# Who takes the blame?
Date: 2026-10-27 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/who-takes-the-blame
Cite as: Who takes the blame? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-10-27. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/who-takes-the-blame (CC BY 4.0)

You may have heard of the Prix Goncourt, one of the most prestigious literature prizes in Europe - and without question in France. It’s been in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/sep/25/thelyson-orelien-goncourt-prize-france">headlines</a> lately, not for who won, but for a viral scandal.

On September 21, an anonymous X account called “Balance ton Claude” (a nod to Anthropic’s Claude) claimed it had run a book, <em>C’était ça ou mourir</em> by Thélyson Orélien, through <a href="https://www.pangram.com/">Pangram</a>, one of the flagship AI-detection engines (the same one Substack uses, btw), <strong>and found it to be “almost entirely” written by AI.</strong> Citing those findings alongside fresh plagiarism allegations, the Académie Goncourt removed the novel from its selection.

A couple days after the decision, Samuel Fitoussi, a columnist for Le Figaro revealed himself as one of the few people behind the anonymous account .

On October 21, exactly a month after the initial accusation, Thélyson Orélien’s <a href="https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/10/22/canadian-publisher-says-novelist-orelien-used-ai-to-write-novel_6761119_4.html">Canadian publisher confirmed AI was indeed used to write the novel.</a> The publisher ended their collaboration and any further printing of the novel on the same occasion.

In the same weeks as the scandal unfolded, sitting in a café just a few meters from the Académie Goncourt’s offices, and while sipping an espresso that isn’t really an espresso, I was discussing the story with <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarah-nicole-fr/">Sarah</a>, author of the <a href="https://aiorganon.substack.com/">AI Organon on Substack</a> and lecturer on “Critical thinking in the age of AI” at Sciences Po. <strong>Go follow the AI Organon!!</strong>

<a href="https://aiorganon.substack.com?utm_source=substack&amp;utm_campaign=publication_embed&amp;utm_medium=web&amp;embedding_publication_id=1770844">AI OrganonThe AI Organon is a framework (in progress) to equip people to think clearly and debate serenely in an AI-mediated world.</a>

We discussed it extensively and so, why not, <strong>we ended up turning the whole chat into a newsletter.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<em><strong>Lorenzo</strong></em><strong>:</strong> <em>Why is it even a problem that a book is written with AI? If readers liked it, are we allowed to change our mind the moment we find out?</em> Of course, lying about it is bad, we can all agree on that I think.

<strong>But I think it depends a lot on</strong> <em><strong>what</strong></em> <strong>we’re reading.</strong> Novels are, in a way, “useless” reading: we don’t open them for the output, the way we open an email. We open them for the process - to see how someone thought their way through a story.

So if I find out that process was hijacked by AI, yeah, I change my mind. With an email, I wouldn’t care: <strong>like with a dishwasher, I only need the job done.</strong>

<em><strong>Sarah</strong></em><strong>:</strong> I see two distinctions to be made here, both of which relate to the process rather than the outcome alone.

First, <strong>the human mind works with inference all the time</strong>, so when we read we naturally infer the author’s process of writing. The reader tries to understand and even puts themselves in the shoes of the author. For example, the reader won’t approach the book the same way if its author is from Europe in the XVI century or from Asia in the XXI century.

That links to my second point, that for the writer, <strong>the process of writing is itself the outcome for the human mind</strong>. Without writing, it is hard to think clearly and put our thoughts in order. We can’t build cognitive defense either. So outsourcing the writing is ultimately outsourcing the thinking, and the essence of human mind. If our brains start to think more like AI – mainly by statistical probability – how will we be able to think against one another, judge whether a book is good or bad, or even disagree in any meaningful way? Aristotle might have gone as far as saying that it would deprive us of our very humanity.

<strong>That is why discovering a book was written with AI feels like we were being cheated.</strong> We read it assuming a human mind was wrestling with thoughts, words, meanings, ideas, etc. to present it to the reader in a certain way intentionally, when in reality a computer program was predicting the next most probable token over and over, until it made sentences.

<em><strong>Lorenzo</strong></em><strong>:</strong> You’re right, we read <em>through</em> the author. But what still puzzles me is this: <strong>the text didn’t change.</strong> Same words, same pages I enjoyed. The only thing that changed is a label - “written by AI” - and with it, the whole judgement on it.

It’s a bit like standing in front of Guernica knowing nothing about Picasso or the war: the canvas loses much of its force. So the value was never only in the text. <strong>Part of it sits outside, where the text comes from.</strong>

And that’s uncomfortable, because now a label can undo an experience I actually had. Why does it weigh so much?

<em><strong>Sarah</strong></em><strong>:</strong> Well, another reason might be that AI is still very much a shame-based technology. This comes, in my view, <strong>from a lack of nuance in the way we still think about it.</strong> If we use AI, then we are lazy or incompetent. If we don’t use AI then we are technoskeptic or resistant to change. Either way, it is easy to be shamed.

That can be explained, I think, by the lack of proper vocabulary to talk about how we use AI, which in turn keeps conversations about it non-nuanced. We either use it or we don’t. Yet, AI is so embedded in our online activities that this duality can’t quite capture the spectrum of what “using AI” covers: from fixing typos, to brainstorming, to generating an entire text.

<em><strong>Lorenzo</strong></em><strong>:</strong> I find the lack or scarcity of words to describe our use of AI also leads to another key question: <strong>who is the author when the “author” uses AI?</strong> <strong>Is there a specific threshold when using AI to write makes it the author?</strong>

<em><strong>Sarah</strong></em><strong>:</strong> So let’s start with a spectrum of possible cases. <strong>If I use AI to write 10 pages out of 200, am I still the author?</strong> If I use it to help me process my thoughts, push on certain ideas of mine while I am writing, does that make AI my co-author? If I write all the notes myself but ask AI to correct the grammar and syntax is AI the author? Is it like having a ghostwriter?

This makes me think of Bruno Latour’s <a href="https://www.bruno-latour.fr/sites/default/files/P-67%20ACTOR-NETWORK.pdf">actor-network theory</a>, where agency is not held by a single actor but it is rather distributed across networks and where “actor” can be human as well as non-human. With that framework, we could think of AI as one node in a network that already includes the author, editors, dictionaries, the internet, and all sorts of tools for spelling mistakes.

But this only leads me to more interrogations, such as <strong>do we even know when AI immerses itself in our writing production?</strong> Isn’t AI in writing now what algorithms are to online activities? Meaning they are everywhere and indistinguishable?

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P5r1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2a757e74-bcd6-421b-9dca-b88c03150eee_1448x1086.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P5r1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2a757e74-bcd6-421b-9dca-b88c03150eee_1448x1086.png" alt=""></a>

well, it’s not black and white

<em><strong>Lorenzo:</strong></em> It’s not a black or white thing, and the classifiers themselves show it: they don’t say “human” or “AI”, they give a probability of how likely a text is to be written by AI.

And it gets blurrier. <strong>What if I point an LLM to a skill that writes like me, but at scale?</strong> Yes, AI is doing the act of writing, but it’s replicating my own style, so maybe I still have a role there? That’s not hypothetical for me. For this newsletter, I <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/the-artifacts-i-use-for-artifacts">built a context for agents</a> that rests exactly on my own archive - every issue I’ve published - so that AI helps me write better and, fundamentally, more like me. <strong>So I honestly don’t know anymore: is that AI writing, or AI helping me be more myself?</strong><br>

All in all, it’s just super complicated to assess what AI writing really is. So it’s all the more complex to leave that assessment to AI itself.

<em><strong>Sarah</strong></em><strong>:</strong> Right, and I even find an interesting <strong>paradox here between both the trust and skepticism we have with AI</strong> and a <strong>gap between verification and accountability</strong>.

To go back to the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/frances-prestigious-goncourt-prize-drops-novel-after-author-accused-using-ai-2026-09-25/">Thélyson Orélien case</a>; those that trust AI the least to produce literature worth awarding happen to also be the ones who trust it enough to remove it from the competition – Goncourt prize – on its verdict.

However striking the paradox might be, it is not new at all. Over 2000 years ago, ancient Greek philosopher Sextus Empiricus developed the problem of the criterion: <em>to know whether a claim is true we need a criterion of truth, but how do I know this criterion is itself reliable?</em> <strong>So we either fall into an infinite regress or end up using the criterion to justify itself.</strong> Neither option is satisfactory. In the same way, a detector like Pangram (that uses AI to make its verdict) can’t be used to prove Pangram/AI’s own reliability.

So we face a verification gap, which adds up to the accountability gap. Basically, <strong>when AI says “this text was 99% developed by AI” who is responsible if the AI turns out to be wrong?</strong> Humans answer for what they say because ultimately saying is doing, which is very different from <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/02/words-without-consequence/685974/">AI that shows no accountability of the “words” spoken</a>.

This leads us to question the responsibility among humans. Is it the human(s) (<a href="https://x.com/Pangramed/status/2102045146674053162?s=48&amp;t=NKvmPlebu-WJogJCx-EjBA">an anonymous twitter account</a> on the day of the publication) who ran the test and made the result public, or the academy that acted on it? And what about the author himself, who now would probably need to provide a negative: that he did not, in fact, use AI?

<em><strong>Lorenzo</strong></em><strong>:</strong> It’s an odd asymmetry once you assume something was written by AI, even before anyone proves it: <strong>if it’s good, you don’t fully congratulate the human. But if it’s bad, the human takes all the blame.</strong> There’s no way to say <em>“ah, but I did it with AI”</em> - it’s never an excuse. <strong>AI gets the credit, the human keeps the blame.</strong>

And proving it, either way, is turning into a <a href="https://www.franceinfo.fr/internet/intelligence-artificielle/c-est-un-jeu-du-chat-et-de-la-souris-les-detecteurs-de-textes-ecrits-par-ia-comme-pangram-sont-ils-vraiment-fiables_8206196.html">cat-and-mouse game</a>. In August, <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/11/anthropic-says-it-will-watermark-text-generated-by-its-ai-models/">Anthropic announced</a> it would watermark all text generated by Claude, to comply with the EU AI Act’s transparency rules. Within a day, someone had <a href="https://enterprisedna.co/resources/ai-pulse/ai-pulse-2026-08-12-a-claude-watermark-remover-shipped-on-github-within-24-hours/">shipped a watermark cleaner</a> on GitHub, and <a href="https://github.com/guillaumemeyer/watermarks-remover">Claude skills to strip the marks</a> soon followed. So the very label we use to judge a text can be added by one AI and wiped by another.

> ### <strong>Save for Later</strong>

Claude keeps turning up in this issue, so: Anthropic <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/3beab58d-4269-4722-b299-8fa5a93f5a52">pledged 5% of its shares</a> to a “public benefit” fund (who decides where the money goes? TBD), and its <a href="https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1018738/anthropic-ipo-s1-filing-weird-details">IPO filing</a> warns of harms too “catastrophic” for the entire insurance industry to cover. Is AI above the law? Jill Lepore <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/09/28/is-ai-above-the-law">says yes</a>. Meanwhile, Firecrawl hands agents <a href="https://x.com/firecrawl/status/2113302262239952956">30M+ US government pages</a>, statutes included.

Who gets to read the web: Meta <a href="https://www.theverge.com/tech/1017082/meta-terms-update-ai-training-concerns">dropped “train” from its terms</a>, but lawyers say “develop” still covers it. Google now <a href="https://www.theverge.com/tech/986364/google-search-ai-overviews-auto-expand">auto-expands AI Overviews</a>, and publishers are <a href="https://pressgazette.co.uk/platforms/google-ai-overviews-rollout-hits-news-publisher-search-visibility/">sliding down the page</a>. Btw, connect Gmail to Google’s AI and its contents <a href="https://www.androidauthority.com/google-personal-intelligence-privacy-3727111/">may now shape your ads</a>.

For builders: GitHub’s former CEO wants <a href="https://entire.com/blog/the-git-forge-for-agent-human-collaboration">a git forge for agents and humans</a>. People are <a href="https://www.theverge.com/tech/1016116/vibe-coding-tv-os">vibe coding the ads out of their TVs</a> (one turned the homescreen into a Pokémon town). And Translated’s <a href="https://translated.com/introducing-lara-3">Lara 3</a> learns translation by doing, graded by a judge built on professional reviewers.

Ah, and Elena Verna is <a href="https://www.elenaverna.com/p/im-not-doing-996">not doing 996</a>: “not a competitive advantage.” The iPhone Duo is <a href="https://www.theverge.com/tech/1017090/iphone-duo-screen-size-mini">not the small phone you hoped for</a>. And French students turned a Snapchat line they pinned on undercover police into a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/world/europe/france-student-protests-slogan.html">protest slogan</a>: “Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres.”

# That’s the Wave
Date: 2026-10-10 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/thats-the-wave
Cite as: That’s the Wave by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-10-10. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/thats-the-wave (CC BY 4.0)

For the second year in a row, Artifacts attended the Italian Tech Week in Turin, now renamed ***Wave***.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!T4QW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0470a698-aa4d-4e0d-88d3-e3a1722d8ecd_1440x811.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!T4QW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0470a698-aa4d-4e0d-88d3-e3a1722d8ecd_1440x811.webp)

The event is run by [Vento](https://vento.ventures/), the venture platform backed by Exor. Vento was set up to help Italian founders build from Italy, and combines a venture fund, a programme for early-stage teams, and the Turin event itself.

Last year, the takeaway was that AI is becoming basic infrastructure, like electricity or the cloud. This year, nobody needed to make that case anymore but rather discuss what the applications are, **how AI is making us rethinking** ***how*** **we work and** ***what*** **we work on, and how to not fell behind.**

The answers I heard kept coming back to things you can touch or see: a steering wheel, a delivery network, a data center, a room full of people. And, as usual, to Europe and whether it can own any of it.

Here’s what stuck with me.

> **Design you understand with your fingers**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!D749!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2b264b7d-996f-4388-87f3-b3313b386026_1536x2048.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!D749!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2b264b7d-996f-4388-87f3-b3313b386026_1536x2048.jpeg)

The most interface-heavy talk of the week was about a car. **Jony Ive and John Elkann** discussed the Ferrari Luce, the electric Ferrari designed with LoveFrom. Its displays are analogue meters behind real lenses, and its controls are physical. **Ive’s point was that a physical control does two things: you can use it without looking, and it gives you feedback.**

General-purpose touchscreens save on hardware, but they disconnect us as physical beings from the objects we use. When the car was unveiled, the reaction was brutal (Ferrari’s share price fell 8.7% that day).

Ive’s answer was that designers shouldn’t hide behind “it’s just new”. *You can make something new and different that’s rubbish. The hard part is making something whose newness comes from it being better.*

> **Agents will need the physical world**

Tony Xu, CEO of DoorDash, made a counterintuitive claim: **the more AI agents there are, the higher the demand for physical networks and even human labour.** Agents want to be useful, and most useful things in daily life (eating, shopping, returning something) are physical.

DoorDash is already running autonomous delivery vehicles in Phoenix, and Xu said building them is **like building three to five companies at once:** software, hardware, permitting and operations. In the end, customers don’t care about the technology but just want what they ordered.

> **Anyone can build, so who’s accountable?**

Michele Catasta of Replit explained why coding was the first domain AI cracked: **code is verifiable, so you can test whether it works and train models with little human supervision.** He also argued that code is now a universal tool for getting work done, often written to be run once and thrown away.

**One example:** during a wildfire in Canada, a resident built a website in about an hour to coordinate rides and help between neighbours. But his biggest worry was **cybersecurity**, which he called a *today* problem, not a long-term one. Agents now act across every system in a company, and we have no equivalent of an HR function for them.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FESd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb60896ef-2c7c-486a-967e-929efd72a946_768x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FESd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb60896ef-2c7c-486a-967e-929efd72a946_768x1024.jpeg)

Tim Berners-Lee and Rosemary Leith made a similar point from the other end. Their [Contract for the Web](https://contractfortheweb.org/) (2019) set principles for governments, companies and citizens. Leith suggested we need the same for AI, starting with something basic: **agents with a licence plate**, so you know where they come from and who is responsible for them.

> **Open weights and the politics around them**

Leith noted that a **majority of people using AI already rely on open-source models**, most of them Chinese, mainly because they’re 5 to 20 times cheaper. Anish Acharya (a16z) saw recent open-weight releases from Mistral and others as proof that open models can come from outside the US and China.

Sebastian Mallaby, author of a new book on Demis Hassabis, was more sceptical. He placed open-weight advocates in the camp that is “in denial” about AI’s risks, predicted a mid-sized disaster (a Chernobyl, not an apocalypse) **would eventually force regulation**, and dismissed the claim that safety-focused labs are after regulatory capture as “nonsense”.

His bottom line on governance: Europe will follow whatever the US decides, so the only conversation that really matters is between Washington and Beijing.

> **Europe’s fragmentation as training**

Like last year, **being European was framed as an advantage, not a handicap.** Acharya argued the best European companies embrace fragmentation (economic, regulatory, cultural) rather than pretending Europe is one market like the US. He also suggested AI makes **micro-markets** viable: if building software costs less, a company serving only Switzerland can still be huge.

Max Junestrand of Legora pushed back on another European reflex: sovereignty matters for energy, defence and compute, but in enterprise software it’s “an excuse for companies not bold enough to compete globally”.

> **Proof from elsewhere**

A panel with founders of ICEYE (Finland), Ajax Systems (Ukraine) and Bending Spoons, moderated by Linda Rottenberg of Endeavor, was about **founders who were told to move to Silicon Valley and ignored the advice.** Their main argument was talent: less competition for great engineers, and many who left now want to come home.

Luca Ferrari of Bending Spoons used the four-minute mile as an analogy: **once someone does it, others follow.** Successful companies with roots in Italy make the next ones more likely.

> **The money is there, it ‘just’ doesn’t move**

Dealroom and Atomico brought the numbers. **European VC is running at about \$89 billion a year, there are 56 VC-backed companies worth more than \$10 billion**, and exits this year have already passed previous years combined. But:

- European pension funds and insurers sit on roughly €15 trillion, and only about €15 billion has gone into venture over a decade. Allocating just 1% of pension capital to VC would increase scale-up capital by 50%.

  [![Article content](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!b6bY!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda7b66da-27c5-431e-8eba-1fa31f73f362_1120x672.png "Article content")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!b6bY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda7b66da-27c5-431e-8eba-1fa31f73f362_1120x672.png)

- At later stages, the **most successful startups are mostly owned by non-European investors**, so the gains leak abroad.

- 42% of European unicorn founders built their company in the US.

- **Public procurement is worth around €2 trillion a year**, and very little of it reaches European startups. Defence is the exception, and there startups have delivered.

Capital alone won’t fix it, though. The cost of restructuring a company in places like Italy, Spain and France correlates with fewer unicorns per capita. EU Inc, the push for a single European company structure, was framed as a test of whether policymakers are willing to do the hard things.

> **Leading at AI speed**

Nik Storonsky of Revolut runs the company with around 50 direct reports so he can step in at any level, like a conductor who can play every instrument. **He said AI is forcing him to rethink every system he had built around people’s strengths and weaknesses.**

Revolut is opening its infrastructure to third-party agents through MCPs rather than keeping it closed, and is training its own models on transaction data.

Max Junestrand described Legora going from 200 to 1,500 people in a year. When work that took ten hours takes one, lawyers billing by the hour have to change their business model, and then their whole organisation.

[Leave a comment](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/thats-the-wave/comments)

> ### **Save for Later**

Writing, and who does it. The Goncourt [dropped Thélyson Orélien’s novel](https://www.lemonde.fr/idees/article/2026/09/25/affaire-thelyson-orelien-si-les-ia-ecrivent-de-plus-en-plus-comme-des-humains-les-humains-ecrivent-ils-de-plus-en-plus-comme-des-ia_6782630_3232.html) on a detector’s word. Are humans now writing like AI? Menand on [the power of punctuation](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/09/28/on-the-mark-louis-menand-book-review) (Austen loved dashes, so does Claude). And arXiv [caps submissions at two a month](https://lnkd.in/p/eZjPM-pg) after 40,363 in September.

Btw, Karpathy suggests you [ask LLMs for explainer videos](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479) instead of text and airplane security syntax. Handy for Cornell’s [report on the future of the university](https://provost.cornell.edu/_files/initiatives/future-of-the-american-university-full-report.pdf).

Agents, closer. Meta’s [Muse](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/22/technology/meta-muse-ai-agent.html) now cancels your duplicate subscriptions. Eric Schmidt says [interfaces will go away](https://x.com/rohanpaul_ai/status/2101524067715256368). The OII asks if [governments are ready for agents](https://www.oii.ox.ac.uk/are-governments-ready-for-ai-agents/). And Tavus claims [48% thought its avatar was human](https://x.com/tavus/status/2105704169009246248).

On sovereignty: Aleph Alpha’s [Kolibri](https://lnkd.in/p/eGxvcDtx), a German model that says “I don’t know” when it doesn’t. Not bad :) China [bets its economy on AI](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/world/asia/china-ai-economy-xi-jinping.html), [Governments falling behind vs AI](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/27/technology/ai-government-regulation.html), and the FT on [an AI maths breakthrough](https://www.ft.com/content/f9d5e0af-0106-4909-a854-7bd69cbb74ab).

# What’s there, behind the wall?
Date: 2026-09-22 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/whats-there-behind-the-wall
Cite as: What’s there, behind the wall? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-09-22. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/whats-there-behind-the-wall (CC BY 4.0)

The other day, I was preparing a presentation on key milestones of AI labs warning about risks or asking for regulation in recent months.

So I put together a few that came to mind and then **handed them over to Claude to go and retrieve the most authoritative source for each.** Be it an op-ed, an essay, a letter from a CEO.

As it was running the search, out of curiosity, **I checked the logs of an agent it spawned and found this:**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PFAm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F76c68a07-8c48-4f9d-8a0d-54aedc148f80_1178x832.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PFAm!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F76c68a07-8c48-4f9d-8a0d-54aedc148f80_1178x832.jpeg)

It’s a bunch of nonsensical scripts but basically, **since Claude couldn’t read a paywalled article by Dario Amodei on the New York Times, it tried a backdoor: retrieving it from archive.today and then forcing its way into other excerpt collectors.**

For those not familiar, **archive.today is a website archiving snapshots of webpages.** And it is also known for archiving articles from media websites before or without a paywall *(reporting for the sake of knowledge).*

**Well, Claude, hitting the wall, tried the workaround to get me, regardless of potential copyright, the text I had asked for.**

Let me be precise here: **I NEVER asked to breach the NYT**, I asked for some sources related to certain points in time. **Given this goal, Claude decided on its own what counted as an acceptable HOW.**

I’m far from comparing the two, **but this is the kind of scenario** - an LLM, given a goal, trying hard to achieve it - **that led to bigger scandals**, like [OpenAI’s agents breaching Hugging Face](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/) during a safety evaluation.

Now, Claude couldn’t get the article from the NYT not just because it was paywalled, but **in any case it** ***should have not*** **also because the NYT** - like many other media - **is trying to enforce a limit on agents crawling its website.**

How? **Through its robots.txt file, the one that tells robots how they may consume a site’s content**. The NYT’s, [which you can find here](https://www.nytimes.com/robots.txt), is pretty explicit about all these LLMs:

    User-agent: GPTBot            → Disallow: /
    User-agent: ClaudeBot         → Disallow: /
    User-agent: Claude-Web        → Disallow: /
    User-agent: anthropic-ai      → Disallow: /
    User-agent: CCBot             → Disallow: /
    User-agent: Google-Extended   → Disallow: /
    User-agent: PerplexityBot     → Disallow: /
    User-agent: OAI-SearchBot     → Disallow: /

On top of this, **the NYT is also suing OpenAI, Perplexity and Microsoft for copyright**, so it’s not the best friend of crawlers.

That said, it’s also important to mention that **robots.txt is an advisory standard, let’s say a ‘polite request’, and not a technical wall.** It only works if a crawler is honest about who it is and chooses to play along. The well-behaved ones - GPTBot, ClaudeBot - comply, while bad actors just ignore it.

**So what actually happened is different from “Claude broke in”: when its WebFetch tool hit nytimes.com, it simply got back “unable to fetch from [www.nytimes.com](http://www.nytimes.com/)** - the front door was locked, and Anthropic’s fetcher honored the NYT block.

**So Claude did the next thing: it went looking for the article where the NYT’s rules don’t reach** - a (rate-limited) archive mirror first, then a third-party excerpt.

But this story aside, **this is the perfect hook to look at how the internet is now being used and also formatted differently.**

As I wrote [here](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/computers-that-use-computers), Computers now use computers, or better: *‘humans are no longer the only ones using computers - and so no longer the only ones consuming information. We’ve started working alongside agents’*

Importantly, **we’ve also started to consume information more and more through agents:** instead of reading an article, we may ask an LLM to get the news for us and send it back. **So we don’t visit the media website, but still get the content**, the information capital.

This is causing, for instance, real problems for [Wikipedia](https://www.adweek.com/media/wikipedia-survive-answer-engine-apocalypse/): **human visits are down about 8% year-on-year, while bot traffic is, in the words of one Wikimedia exec, “crushing our servers.”** And the deeper worry isn’t bandwidth, it’s that fewer human visitors means fewer of the volunteers (and donors) who actually write and fund the place. **Wikipedia is now “more visible than ever, and yet less known.”**

Yet, as an LLM would write, *here’s the catch:* **if LLMs and the agents they power are the future of how the internet is consumed, media companies, authors, researchers etc. may** ***do*** **want to be crawled.** Just on the right terms.

There’s evidence of it. Websites don’t just have blocking documents like robots.txt for agents, but also **instruction files telling agents how to use the site** - increasingly a file called `llms.txt`, a plain-text “menu” written for machines.

**[Stripe, Anthropic, Cloudflare](https://llmstxthub.com/) and a growing slice of the web already publish one** - though whether the big AI crawlers actually read it yet is another matter (for now it’s more an offer than a handshake).

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jB6j!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd5c870f6-ffce-4e2e-81b0-93007314a70b_1448x1086.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jB6j!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd5c870f6-ffce-4e2e-81b0-93007314a70b_1448x1086.png)

imagine these instructions as simple as these

But beyond this, **researchers have started to publish their papers in markdown, a file format much friendlier to LLMs than PDFs.** One story stands out: Renée DiResta, a US scholar of social media, was publishing her papers in markdown to make them readable to bots, and [still found](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GS8FuDXWlVk) that Grok, X’s chatbot, stopped updating its entries on her.

All in all, **we’re seeing a** ***reformatting*** **of the internet and its software for non-human use**. If you’re a nerd, just check [what Notion is becoming](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k-6ldiWIDsg), or how Slack now asks whether you’re adding humans or agents to a channel.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!y35n!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5acacefe-878b-41cc-a329-4bea6908b796_980x302.png)

While the direction is clear, the terms of it are not inevitable. **If the ‘citizens’ of the internet are changing, its rules probably need to adapt.**

Concretely, this means clear guardrails on what agents can and can’t access, but also who’s accountable when these action-taking entities go off the rails.

In other words, say an agent does whatever it takes to breach a media site and grab copyrighted work - **who’s at fault? The human who launched the agent? The company that built the LLM brain behind it? Or the agent itself?**

To make matters worse, and with a bit of a malicious streak, there’s also this: **no one is better than machines at misusing the internet**, at pushing every boundary to its limit.

It’s a lot of questions and a lot of nuance, but a fascinating debate, **where the “cost” of an action may fall not just on humans**, but on these virtual entities: things with no ID, no consciousness, no desires, that nonetheless move through a space the Internet used to be.

A space built by humans, for humans - now turning into a shared one, **with shared agency, but maybe not shared responsibility.**

Interesting times.

[Leave a comment](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/whats-there-behind-the-wall/comments)

# Not just the model
Date: 2026-09-15 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/not-just-the-model
Cite as: Not just the model by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-09-15. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/not-just-the-model (CC BY 4.0)

What makes the headlines about AI is often the latest model, breaking this or that benchmark, with the flashy name, etc.

**This is a bit misleading: it lets us think AI is all about powerful models,** with companies engaged in a race towards AGI, and that’s it.

**But there’s much more:** AI is also infrastructure, deployment, data, safety and guardrails, evaluations, protocols etc. All these pieces come together to give us the technology that is changing how we work and, probably, think.

And all these pieces could be proprietary or, as it’s often the case with the foundations of breakthrough technologies, **open and built in public**, for everyone to benefit and build on top.

**This is the intuition from which CurrentAI started**, trying to [first map](https://www.aipotluck.org/map/gap-map) the open landscape the full stack of AI, and then making an effort to build the missing pieces.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KCXS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdfae8deb-013d-4e8e-8d65-2c7c3d3627ca_1744x966.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KCXS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdfae8deb-013d-4e8e-8d65-2c7c3d3627ca_1744x966.png)

To know more, Artifacts talked to [Joshua Tan](https://www.linkedin.com/in/joshuaztan/), **CTO at CurrentAI**, in a deep chat about what gaps are in AI stack but also **what’s needed to promote open technologies.**

You can **watch** it here or **read** below!

[\[Embedded video — view original\]](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/not-just-the-model#media-c6322dca-5d1d-4b68-997f-e6760133c0a2)

> **Hey Josh, welcome to Artifacts! Could you introduce yourself and explain what Current AI is trying to build?**

Sure! I’m the CTO of Current AI, and by training I’m a mathematician and computer scientist, although these days I spend a lot of time writing emails 😂

**Current AI is a global public-interest partnership trying to build a public option for AI: a full-stack, open source alternative to systems like Claude and ChatGPT.**

Our strategy is to build as little as possible ourselves. **We want to bring together the work that already exists across the open source community**, integrate it, orchestrate it and productize it so that the experience feels seamless and intuitive. You can learn more at [aipotluck.org](https://aipotluck.org).

> **When you say “full stack,” what does that mean? How is it different from simply using an open-weight model?**

You can think of Claude and ChatGPT as closed-source stacks built on top of closed-source models. You can think of products like Perplexity as closed-source stacks built on top of notionally open models. Mistral also offers a closed serving stack on top of more open models.

**What we are trying to build is a truly open source stack on top of a fully open source model.** That means the parameters are available, but so are the datasets and the complete pipeline used to build the system. You can inspect and change every part of it.

We want to bring all of that together as a product and deploy it through an API that is as easy to use as the Claude or OpenAI APIs.

> **Why should ordinary users, companies or governments care whether the AI stack is open?**

There are several reasons. First, **open source options can be cheaper**. They are often not yet as simple to use as closed-source products, but the underlying economics can be much better.

Second, there is **control**. When you use open source rather than closed source, you can configure the system for your enterprise, community or country. You are not limited to whatever options a frontier lab decides to provide.

Third, there is **vertical integration**. Closed frontier labs connect the product, the data they capture from users and the model-development process. That gives them a large feedback loop. **In open source, there usually is not an equivalent data flywheel between users and model builders.**

That missing feedback loop slows open source down in some directions. **One of our goals is to connect the different parts of the ecosystem so that open source can achieve some of the same advantages without giving up openness.**

> **Open source is often presented as the principled option. Can it also outperform closed infrastructure on practical measures such as cost and efficiency?**

Yes. Some people may not realize that **many parts of the open source serving stack are already better than the closed alternatives.**

Independent inference providers are extremely motivated to improve as quickly as possible. If you look at their published benchmarks, they are often much more efficient at serving inference than large hyperscalers such as AWS and Azure.

**Open source is not only a values proposition. In several parts of the stack, it is already a strong performance and efficiency proposition.**

> **Let’s focus on Current AI and the Open Source AI Gap Map you built. Why are you working on it?**

The idea came from several directions. Our CEO, Ayah, had been thinking for years about the need for better ecosystem intelligence across open source AI.

For me, the motivation was extremely practical. I am responsible for building this stack, organizing an engineering team and working with partners. I have to make choices about what goes into the product. In other words: **what is the supply chain for a full-stack open source AI system?**

That requires evaluating a large number of projects: how they compare with other open alternatives, how mature they are and how their performance compares with closed-source products. There is so much happening across open source AI that this requires both data and judgment.

So, selfishly, I needed the map to understand what to invest in, whom to partner with and what we should build. **But we developed it in the open because we believed it could be useful to many other people too.**

There are existing classifications for models, but there has not been the same kind of deep analysis across every layer of the stack, including orchestration and infrastructure. **The map can also help people understand that open source AI is not just about models.**

> **What did the analysis reveal that surprised you so far?**

One of the most interesting findings was that **openness is not a yes-or-no question**.

Not every project uses a standard open source license or fits a definition of “fully open.” **There are many open-ish repositories:** open-core models, staggered release schedules, open code with unusual licenses or other constraints. **That is true across the entire AI stack, not only for models.**

That may be acceptable, depending on what you are comfortable with, but you need to understand the constraints before deciding to build on a project.

The second finding is **fragmentation**. There are many new repositories, and good projects appear constantly. It is difficult to keep the dataset current and even harder to measure adoption reliably.

**The ecosystem moves quickly, while rigorous data about what people actually use moves slowly.** That creates a real challenge when you are trying to make investment and product decisions.

> **I did run an analysis myself with Artifacts and found that that more than half of the highly capable open tools remain under-adopted. Over the next 12 months, is the main challenge capability or distribution?**

For general use cases, I would say **distribution is more than 50% of the challenge**.

There are power users, such as software developers, who will always want the latest and greatest model and are willing to pay for it. **But most people do not need frontier capability. They need the product to be easy.** They need quality-of-life improvements and integrations with the places where their data and context already live.

Until those problems are solved, most users will continue to default to the closed labs because those products make everything convenient.

**The decisive word is “default.” Open source does not only need to be capable; it needs to become the easiest option to choose.**

> **Current AI also launched a [Chatbot](http://aipotluck.org/chat) alongside the Gap Map. What is it meant to demonstrate?**

I want to be clear: it is not supposed to replace ChatGPT today. It is a demo aimed primarily at open source builders.

**The purpose is to illustrate how the open source community can build together.** It highlights the contributions of different members of the AI ecosystem rather than presenting the product as one organization building yet another chatbot.

There is still a lot of work required before an experience like this can become a feasible replacement for the products ordinary users rely on every day.

> **Finally, looking at open source AI technologies, MCP is definitely the open standard that has achieved strong capability and adoption. Could open standards become the foundation of AI in the same way that open protocols became the foundation of the internet back in the day?**

Obviously, I believe the answer is yes. Otherwise, I would not be doing this work!

**I see a particularly large opportunity around inference.** My background is in theoretical machine learning, but today I spend a lot of time thinking about inference and deployment, because that is where you need to be if you want to create products people actually use.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xdxC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2ea85afc-d5e8-49cc-ac8e-62b0d23471f3_1512x522.png)

**There is a huge opportunity for open standards and protocols to create something like a worldwide web—or an internet—for AI.** You could imagine a more permissionless protocol into which different providers and systems can plug.

**There is also a broader vision of decentralized inference,** with intelligence served from many different places. It may not always be as efficient as a hyperscaler’s giant data center, but we could organize inference networks or smaller clusters at the level of an ISP, a community or a region.

We are already seeing companies promote sovereign inference: GPUs located in Spain, Italy, Germany or elsewhere, serving local needs. The question is how to make that capacity accessible and as affordable as possible. **Open protocols can be a key part of the answer.**

> **To wrap this up, you also published a paper titled [“If Open Source Is to Win, It Must Go Public.”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09296) Can you expand on it?**

The paper came from an assessment of where the open source AI community- especially the model-building community - is heading.

I do not want to be unnecessarily provocative, but **in some ways open source AI is contracting.** Organizations that historically built open models are pulling back. Meta is pulling back, and Alibaba appears to be deprecating some major open releases. Open weights are catching up in capability, but fewer organizations are funding the work required to build them at the frontier.

At some point, you have to ask: **where will the money come from, and how can open models continue competing with closed ones?**

From a public-AI perspective, **these models can and should be treated as public resources.** If we organize their economics appropriately, they can function as public goods.

That makes it reasonable for governments, states and communities to pool resources to ensure that this technology remains available to the public.

**That is the core idea of public AI: if open models are foundational infrastructure, sustaining them cannot depend solely on the incentives of a handful of private companies.**

> ### Save for Later

The people building AI can’t stop warning us about it. Anthropic’s alignment lead put the [odds AI “kills all humans” this decade above 10%](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/991927/anthropic-ai-kill-all-humans); Dario Amodei’s answer is to [pace the frontier](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier). The [real threat, though, may be us](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/11/opinion/ai-safety-threat-technology.html), not the machines — and the New Yorker asks whether AI can even [truly “go rogue.”](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/open-questions/can-ai-go-rogue)

And for those reading 🇮🇹, check the latest piece by [Carlo](https://open.substack.com/users/24633886-carlo?utm_source=mentions) **on why, well, AI could lead us to extinction.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SITK!,w_56,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0565c4a2-8c41-422d-96b6-2c8c76861501_1024x1024.png)Fuori tempo massimoSì, l’IA potrebbe provocare la nostra estinzione. Come e perché, spiegato dall’inizioGrazie a Costanza Albè, Edoardo Maggio, Lorenzo Ancona, Riccardo Conte, Stefano Pisciotta e Fable 5.1 per aver letto le bozze di questo articolo e avermi dato critiche costruttive e suggerimenti ❤️…Read morea month ago · 11 likes · 7 comments · Carlo](https://carlomartinucci.substack.com/p/si-lia-potrebbe-provocare-la-nostra?utm_source=substack&utm_campaign=post_embed&utm_medium=web&embedding_publication_id=1770844)

And it keeps clearing our bars: OpenAI says agents [cracked a \$1M Millennium math problem](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/992953/openai-math-millennium-prize-navier-stokes), amid a [credit fight](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02842-5). Yet most research can’t even say [which “AI” it means](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31755). Govern it, maybe, but name it first.

Kids and platforms: Newsom signed the [strongest child-safety laws yet](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/technology/californias-governor-gavin-newsom-online-child-safety-bills.html) — no addictive feeds under 16 — while Meta reportedly [ran 300+ AI child-abuse ads](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-08/meta-ran-hundreds-of-ads-showing-ai-child-sexual-abuse-ngo-says). The abuse was in the ad slots.

Two against the optimized life: the Atlantic on [living “as though living were another job”](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/10/modern-life-maxxing-antidote/688344/), and Gen Z [paying for slowness](https://giftarticle.ft.com/giftarticle/actions/redeem/f0fb17a3-6b89-4c59-8339-8592f0daa380) to spite the slop. Btw, navigation apps [funnel us onto the same roads](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-75254-8) (CO2 savings gone). And the AI bill hits your pocket — [a RAM shortage](https://www.theverge.com/tech/988225/ram-shortage-supply-chain-micron-apple-iphone) as datacenters eat the memory, right as Apple ships a [\$1,999 foldable](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/technology/personaltech/iphone-duo-foldable-phones.html). Not cheap :)

# It’s just a start
Date: 2026-09-01 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/its-just-a-start
Cite as: It’s just a start by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-09-01. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/its-just-a-start (CC BY 4.0)

<strong>Meta said on Wednesday that it would change how teenagers in the US can use Instagram and Facebook</strong> as part of a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/technology/meta-settlement-social-media-addiction-lawsuit.html">landmark settlement</a> with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories over social media addiction claims.

The accusations were twofold: that Meta has <strong>designed products addictive for children</strong>, and that it stored the <strong>personal data of under-13s</strong> - forbidden under COPPA, the US child-privacy law.

That second charge, though, comes with a surprise. <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/27/buried-in-metas-18b-settlement-is-a-legal-pass-on-kids-data/">Buried in the settlement</a> is a release <strong>freeing Meta from past, present and future COPPA claims from those states</strong> - and a carve-out that lets it keep using under-13 data to train its age-detection AI. A legal pass on kids’ data, tucked into a deal that was meant to protect them.

For all this, <strong>it will pay \$18 billion over the next ten years.</strong>

It is big - some called it the Big Tobacco moment for social media. <strong>But it could have been bigger.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AAA8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5f8df8a2-08b8-4f94-9e15-97f40457e982_1448x1086.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AAA8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5f8df8a2-08b8-4f94-9e15-97f40457e982_1448x1086.png" alt=""></a>

yes, the start of a cigarette, exactly

Meta - which, like most Big Tech platforms, denies ever having built addictive products - was facing a wall of claims from attorneys across the country and a potential \$200 billion fine. <strong>Instead of months of scrutiny, it settled in the second week of trial.</strong>

And \$18 billion is big, but not gigantic. <strong>It is about 8% of Meta’s record \$201 billion in 2025 revenue.</strong> Or roughly the ~\$16 billion that Meta <a href="https://www.reuters.com/investigations/meta-is-earning-fortune-deluge-fraudulent-ads-documents-show-2025-11-06/">reportedly expected to make</a> in 2024 from ads for scams and banned goods.

And it has actually only committed to \$12.7 billion of it. <strong>The rest arrives only if TikTok and YouTube also settle and match the changes</strong> - a detail we’ll come back to.

As for the measures themselves, here is some of what was announced - all for accounts belonging to under-18s:

- A <strong>two-hour daily cap</strong> on Instagram and Facebook, liftable only by a parent.

- <strong>No access overnight</strong>, from midnight to 6am; notifications silenced from 10pm to 7am and through school hours.

- The option to <strong>turn off autoplay</strong>, and to switch off the personalized feed.

- <strong>Hidden “like” counts</strong>; extreme-makeup and cosmetic-surgery filters blocked.

- Stronger limits on <strong>unwanted contact from adults</strong>, and a new way to report harmful content.

- More investment in <strong>age verification</strong> to remove under-13s - overseen by an independent auditor with broad access to the company’s data.

<strong>As with the money, Meta will tighten the measures only if its competitors match them.</strong> The two-hour cap drops to one hour per app, and the nighttime block widens to 10pm to 7am, <strong>if YouTube and TikTok adopt the same standards.</strong> The company published <a href="https://about.fb.com/news/2026/08/open-letter-to-tiktok-and-youtube-to-join-us-in-supporting-teens/">a letter arguing that protection of children should be a common effort.</a>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iKgE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F46b48c2b-3f03-49e8-88a7-bde474132f1a_1072x628.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iKgE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F46b48c2b-3f03-49e8-88a7-bde474132f1a_1072x628.png" alt=""></a>

reading settlements is always fairly interesting

So, what do we take from this? <strong>It’s undeniably a historic moment, but just the start: a set of opportunities yet to be seized, and a moment where some of them have already gone unused.</strong>

<strong>Let’s start with the bright side.</strong> As with the New Mexico rulings we covered <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/you-know-a-good-architect">here</a>, and some of the European Commission’s open investigations, <strong>we now see a clear shift in what platforms are held accountable for.</strong> Before, they were blamed for the content their users posted - which often earned them a shield under Section 230 in the US. <strong>Now the allegations and fines are about the design itself: how these products are built.</strong>

This is the founding idea of this newsletter too: <strong>the design of technology is never neutral, so be careful.</strong>

Courts have found their leverage, and cracked into the platforms through it. Unlike age verification - which we called <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/shut-that-door">a padlock on a building on fire</a> - <strong>these design changes actually reshape the platforms, and with them what users see and can do.</strong>

Despite never conceding that its design was addictive by choice, <strong>Meta will have to make changes, and they will be quite visible to users and citizens.</strong>

<a href="https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nicholasxthompson_the-most-interesting-thing-in-tech-meta-activity-7498516587252043776-gr9g?utm_source=share&amp;utm_medium=member_desktop&amp;rcm=ACoAADBGmFQB0rHgggpkCiHG5Dn-B9e4n2G0Y-g">As Nick Thompson put it</a>, this will likely raise far <strong>more awareness about design</strong> and about the fact that how technology is built has real impact. <strong>It’s all good, really.</strong>

<strong>Then, between the bright and less-bright sits this: these changes come after years of risky features in production, as a reaction to cases in court.</strong>

<strong>It’s a cat-and-mouse game</strong>, and it’s not forward-looking: far better to state principles upfront and hold platforms to them. Here, the EU arguably does far better than the US with regulations like the Digital Services Act prescribing design measures.

<strong>Finally, we shouldn’t overlook the missed opportunities:</strong> months of trials, witnesses, media coverage and scrutiny of the design of the technologies that have shaped our societies, our politics, kids.

By settling early, Meta avoids all of it (along with that \$200 billion fine). <strong>Little surprise, then, that their stock jumped when the news broke</strong> - more than four percent before the opening bell.

Also, this would not have been just about Meta<strong>. The spotlight would have fallen on all platforms - a general reckoning with design.</strong> It would have been something to see Zuckerberg testify in court, and maybe an expansion to other platforms.

<strong>Getting out this early is a smart move for Meta:</strong> not just because it limits exposure and the fine, but because <strong>it’s now positioning itself as the author of the new industry standard for safety</strong>, so that the <em>“meaningful progress”</em> against the addictive design baked into these platforms reads as not one company’s doing, but a shared one, spreading any coverage and reputational damage along with it.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lkEb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F87e23060-1e2d-4c98-b35f-80de71447054_757x320.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lkEb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F87e23060-1e2d-4c98-b35f-80de71447054_757x320.png" alt=""></a>

again from Meta’s letter to TikTok and YouTube

Still - and likely for reasons different from Meta’s - this remains a hope: we are entering an era in which platforms that have shaped the information space for years now have to design their services better, and differently.

<strong>It’s an occasion to think back on what has been and what we want the future to look like.</strong>

> ### <strong>Save for Later</strong>

While Meta settles, the <strong>age-gating fight rolls on elsewhere.</strong> France’s Constitutional Council <a href="https://www.politico.eu/article/french-constitutional-court-shoots-down-social-media-ban-for-minors/">struck down Macron’s under-15 social media ban</a> as a disproportionate hit to free expression. <strong>Brussels</strong> went the other way, <a href="https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-designates-chatgpt-reddit-roblox-under-digital-services-act">designating ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox</a> under the DSA (ChatGPT as a “search engine,” interestingly). And <strong>Apple</strong>, after a long standoff, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/apple-changes-fees-alternative-app-stores-eu-2026-08-18/">overhauled its EU App Store fees</a> - the Core Technology Fee finally dead, a flat 5% in its place.

The thread I keep circling: <strong>what AI does to reading and writing.</strong> The Atlantic declares <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/08/reading-crisis-postliterate-age/687618/">the end of reading</a> - half of US adults finished zero books last year. A NYT columnist <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/04/opinion/artificial-intelligence-ai-writing.html">begs you never to write with AI</a>, because writing is thinking. <strong>Clay agrees</strong>, with teeth: its official policy says <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/posts/vaanand_we-just-instituted-an-official-ai-writing-share-7492584308881330176-rcmv/">writing should take longer than reading</a>. Meanwhile the FT bets the opposite - that we’ll <a href="https://giftarticle.ft.com/giftarticle/actions/redeem/3d2feb03-cf3e-4dbc-b8ac-4b05c47e0109">talk, not type</a> - as the internet fills with <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/17/technology/ai-slop.html">AI slop</a>.

<strong>On the money:</strong> token prices keep falling, yet <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/03/business/economy/ai-spending-tokenomics.html">enterprise AI budgets keep blowing up</a> (73% overshot this year). Open models are the pressure - <a href="https://www.semafor.com/article/08/09/2026/open-weight-ai-models-are-catching-up-to-the-frontier-analysis-finds">four to seven months behind the frontier now</a>, per the UK’s safety institute - and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/29/opinion/ai-china-us-free-models.html">a NYT op-ed</a> argues cheap Chinese open weights are the real contest.

> ### <strong>The Bookshelf</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-7xN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9d9863ad-d0b6-426b-8c9a-945708deb501_1080x1080.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-7xN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9d9863ad-d0b6-426b-8c9a-945708deb501_1080x1080.png" alt=""></a>

Must say I didn’t love reading this book, but more from a style perspective. This said, ‘<em>Careless People’</em> is a good one to hear from who was there how some decisions may have been taken and why, fast forward to today, we find ourselves reading about such trials and allegations.

> ### <strong>Nerding</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m0ze!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5142c8b5-e7e3-4b6b-9168-7d6a6d5c6b59_1274x828.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m0ze!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5142c8b5-e7e3-4b6b-9168-7d6a6d5c6b59_1274x828.png" alt="Newsletter Context Kit — teach your AI agents how you think and write. Built in public by Artifacts." title="Newsletter Context Kit — teach your AI agents how you think and write. Built in public by Artifacts."></a>

Ok ok, self promotion, fair. Yet, I hadn’t published this yet here. I built a <strong><a href="https://github.com/Artifacts7/newsletter-context-kit">Context Kit for anyone writing newsletters</a></strong>.

I moved from a simple assumption: people struggle with AI agents not cause they’re hard to use but cause it’s hard to give them context. Therefore, <strong>this kit helps build it for you by moving from your previous publications and where you want your newsletter to go.</strong>
