# Open it up
Date: 2026-08-03 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/open-it-up
Cite as: Open it up by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-08-03. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/open-it-up (CC BY 4.0)

A few days ago, <a href="https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/">OpenAI revealed</a> that one of their agents got out of a sandbox and managed to <strong>breach the systems of Hugging Face</strong>. More recently, <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals">Anthropic disclosed</a> that one of their models gained <strong>unauthorized access</strong> to the production infrastructure of three different organisations.

At the same time, and in response to the first incident of OpenAI, several industry leaders came together to launch the <strong><a href="https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/open-secure-ai-alliance/">Open Secure AI Alliance for AI Safety and Security</a></strong>, to share and develop open AI technologies to defend the global economy. But also thousands of employees from frontier labs are <strong><a href="https://www.pacingthefrontier.com/">advocating for a slowdown</a></strong> of sorts for frontier AI development.

And, as Artifacts had an interview already scheduled with <strong><a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/rkrikorian/">Raffi Krikorian</a>,</strong> <strong>CTO at Mozilla</strong>, to discuss their recent <a href="https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/mozilla-state-of-open-source-ai-report/">‘</a><strong><a href="https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/mozilla-state-of-open-source-ai-report/">State of Open Source AI’ Report</a>, the conversation became even more timely.</strong>

So, I'm truly happy to share our chat on what AI Safety looks like, why open technologies are critical to it, but also why open models are no longer just a philosophical alternative to closed systems, and how to drive up their adoption.

You can <strong>watch</strong> it here:

<a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/open-it-up#media-5142875e-da56-45a7-988c-e8101ca5dc62">\[Embedded video — view original\]</a>

Or <strong>read</strong> it!

> <em><strong>Hey Raffi, welcome to Artifacts! Could you start by saying a few words about your role and what you do at Mozilla?</strong></em>

I’m the CTO at Mozilla, so I spend a lot of time thinking about what is coming around the corner. <strong>The kind of work Mozilla does is timeless: it is not just about browsers - it is about the web, information, human agency, and our relationship with technology.</strong>

AI has opened up a number of new frontiers that we need to think about carefully. I’m leading Mozilla’s work on those new frontiers.

> <em><strong>An OpenAI agent reportedly breached Hugging Face systems, and this triggered the creation of the Open Secure AI Alliance, led by NVIDIA and including Mozilla. The goal is to develop and share open technologies, including open models, to defend the global economy and improve cybersecurity. Did you see this coming? How is Mozilla thinking about this moment?</strong></em>

I think it was <strong>inevitable.</strong>

I rarely say that things are inevitable, but I think it was inevitable that we would get to a point where we needed to have these larger conversations. The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident is one example. Kimi K3 dropping as a downloadable model is another. All of these things add up to the questions you are raising.

At some point, we have to ask: <strong>how do we get to a world where we feel secure, and where things feel under control again?</strong>

<strong>Until recently, your browser was your user agent.</strong> It did things on your behalf. It protected your privacy, your anonymity, and your interests. Now the pendulum has swung all the way to the other side: <strong>things are happening on behalf of users, but users do not necessarily know what is happening, and they may not have authorized it.</strong>

So I think the industry’s reaction - responding to security issues with open source - is the right one. It also shows the missing pieces of infrastructure on the internet. <strong>We need to better understand identity and identity tracing. We need to better understand permission models and how they should work on the internet.</strong>

So. yes, think it was inevitable that we would end up here. I’m just sad it took a major breach and a major model drop to force the conversation. <strong>But lemons make lemonade.</strong> I’m glad we are at least talking about it now.

> <em><strong>The open letter also acknowledges that open models can themselves introduce security risks. They can be modified, and those modified versions cannot necessarily be controlled by whoever released the original model. If we use open models for cybersecurity and defense, how do we make sure they do not become dangerous in themselves?</strong></em>

All of these technologies are dual-use.<strong>But that alone is not the answer.</strong>

The thing I worry about is the alternative: we could try to ban open model usage. Maybe that is possible in some places, although it would be questionably legal. But I think what that would actually do is push a good portion of the internet to ignore the existence of these models.

It would not stop bad actors. It would just mean that a large part of the internet is no longer experimenting with the technology, and is blind to it until a breach happens.

<strong>Instead, if we acknowledge that open models exist and that people are using and building on them, then we can start building open guardrails and open detection tools.</strong> We can collaborate on what that world should look like.

I think that is much better than pretending it is not happening and then waking up one day when something bad occurs.

> <em><strong>Do you think the open nature of these initiatives can make it faster to build guardrails and safeguards?</strong></em>

Yes. <strong>Because they are open, more people can iterate on them.</strong>

One example is work happening inside one of Mozilla’s subsidiaries, <a href="https://mozilla.ai/">Mozilla.ai</a>. They are building an open source library called <a href="https://github.com/mozilla-ai/any-guardrail">AnyGuardRail.</a>

What AnyGuardRail does is allow you to take different guardrail providers from across the internet, synthesize them, and have them work together as a guardrail mechanism for the LLM being called or the input being received.

There is already a growing industry of people building guardrails. <strong>I worry that if we start ignoring open models, that industry dies down.</strong> In reality, we need more people doing this work and more people working together.

> <em><strong>Let’s move to Mozilla’s <a href="https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/mozilla-state-of-open-source-ai-report/">State of Open Source AI</a> report. Why did Mozilla decide to carry out this work?</strong></em>

For us, open models and open source AI raise the same kind of question we should be asking about the web.

<strong>When you use a browser today, Firefox is designed to act on your behalf.</strong> It acts on Lorenzo’s behalf when Lorenzo uses it. It acts on Rafi’s behalf when I use it. <strong>You can inspect the source code. You can know what it is doing. It is designed with privacy protections. There are no other incentive mechanisms built into the foundation of what is going on in the browser.</strong>

That is not necessarily true for all browsers. Some browsers are clearly designed as surveillance mechanisms for other companies.

<strong>We are looking for the same thing to happen in AI.</strong>

Think about chatbots. There was a study - I believe from the University of Maryland - that looked at what happens when you ask popular chatbots for buying recommendations. In a meaningful number of cases, the chatbot responded with a sponsored link. Instead of giving you what is most useful for you, it gives you the thing that makes money for the creator of the chatbot.

<strong>The problem is that chatbots usually show you one answer. They do not show you the “ten blue links” that search engines used to show. You cannot see the alternatives. You just have to trust the response.</strong>

I do not think that is the world we should be living in.

<strong>The only way we get AI that truly works on my behalf is if I can inspect it, run it, and understand what it is going to do. I think the fastest path to that is some form of open source AI.</strong>

<strong>That is why Mozilla cares.</strong> It is not a different fight from the browser fight. It is almost the sequel to the browser fight: the chatbot fight, the AI fight. The internet could fundamentally change, and we want to be in front of that for users.

> <em><strong>One of the key points in the report is that open models are not just a naive alternative. They are increasingly performant and economically compelling.</strong></em>

Exactly. <strong>I also have a philosophical belief that we cannot have a values conversation if the economics do not make sense.</strong>

Right now, the economics do make sense.

If you look at OpenRouter data, which we quoted in the report, a significant share - roughly a third - of all traffic routed through OpenRouter is going to open models. <strong>People are choosing them because they are performant and much cheaper.</strong>

On average, open models are around 50 times cheaper than closed models. So if the economics line up, then we can have the values conversation. This year is probably the first time those two things have really started to line up.

> <em><strong>The report estimates that using open models could save \$24.8 billion every year. We are also seeing companies like Stripe cut inference costs significantly by using open models. Do you think open models are the future of economically sustainable AI usage?</strong></em>

I often say: <strong>you do not need to drive a Ferrari to go to the supermarket.</strong> That would be the most expensive bottle of milk you have ever bought.

There are a lot of things inside that question. Let’s start with token economics.

One of my engineers on the <a href="https://mozilla.ai/">Mozilla.ai</a> team did an analysis: <strong>you can pay \$200 for a Claude Code subscription. But if you did the exact same thing using API calls, it could be on the order of \$6,000, maybe more.</strong>

<strong>That gap tells you something.</strong> Either the subscription is priced to lock users in, or something else is going on behind the scenes economically. But this is a game<strong>. These companies are using a loss-leader strategy to get people onto their platforms.</strong>

We saw this with ride-sharing. After the IPOs of Uber, Lyft, and others, the cost of ride-sharing went up because the companies had already done user acquisition and then needed to lock in profits.

<strong>I think we will see something similar here.</strong> The labs are preparing for big IPOs in Q4 or Q1 of next year. There will be price changes. <strong>I would put a lot of money on the table that prices will change. I cannot tell you exactly when, but it is going to happen,</strong> because those IPOs will force it.

The nice thing about local models and <strong>open source models is that they change the economics.</strong> It is no longer per-token pricing. It becomes a CapEx decision - buying hardware - and then an OpEx decision around power, heat, and operations.

I talk to companies all the time that say: it does not make sense to run something like Opus for our accounting team. We can just run a model locally on their MacBooks.

There is some threshold — I do not know exactly where it is, maybe 10 million tokens a month, maybe 100 million — where the CapEx and OpEx numbers change. <strong>Once you cross that line, purchasing and running hardware becomes more efficient than paying for subscriptions.</strong>

Every company needs to find where that line is. Stripe and Pinterest figured out they had crossed it. Pinterest said they saved \$10 million in a single quarter by making that transition.

> <em><strong>How do we persuade more people to make that transition and use open models for daily tasks?</strong></em>

The real problem is that it is still too hard for users.

<strong>We surveyed around 1,100 to 1,500 developers worldwide. We found that 70% of them had tried to do something with open source AI.</strong> They wanted to. Maybe they remember the internet. Maybe they are big fans of open source.

<strong>But only about 30% of that 70% - so around 20-something percent overall - actually got to production with open source AI.</strong> The rest switched to some kind of closed model.

That is the opportunity for open developers. We need to find the “rounded corners” moment. Steve Jobs made the iPhone’s corners rounded. We need the same kind of usability moment for open source AI. <strong>The developer experience still needs to get a lot better.</strong>

> <em><strong>That adoption gap stood out to me as well. There is a lot of experimentation with open models, but much less production deployment. How can we build the confidence and trust needed for open models to reach users and consumers?</strong></em>

Consumers are an interesting problem.

Enterprises are slowly figuring it out. They still need to figure it out faster. Enterprises go through an innovation curve. Early on, they try random things to see what works. Then, as they mature, they optimize. <strong>And once they reach that optimization stage, the right model at the right cost and performance often ends up being an open model for many use cases.</strong>

Consumers are different. That is still one of the big opportunities.

Right now, most people think of ChatGPT, Claude, and maybe Kimi as the places where you go and type a query. There are good open source pieces of software - Open WebUI and others - that can be pointed at different models, sometimes just through a dropdown.

<strong>But someone needs to build good, gorgeous experiences that regular everyday consumers can touch and feel. That does not really exist yet.</strong>

I have been focused on the enterprise case, but someone needs to talk about the consumer case too. Maybe the next version of the report will do that.

> <em><strong>Another central theme in the report is China’s role in open models. Almost half of weekly OpenRouter traffic goes to Chinese open-weight models, and China has made open AI proliferation one of the pillars of its foreign policy. Do you believe open models can help players like the European Union or the United States regain momentum in the AI race and counter concentration risk?</strong></em>

I want to be clear: the report is not pro-China or anti-China.

<strong>What we want to point out is concentration risk.</strong> Right now, many of the best open models are coming from China. I view that as a concentration risk, just as I view it <strong>as a concentration risk that all the closed platform providers are American.</strong>

We need diversification. Diversification of choice is better for humanity in general.

<strong>I do believe open models, open weights, and open source can become the basis for other countries to build on.</strong>

Think about Linux. As a global developer community, we have effectively agreed that Linux is a free digital public good - maybe not in the strictest definition, but as a foundation developers can work on and build on top of. Because Linux exists the way it does, Google can fork it and make Android, Samsung can put it on TVs, and countless devices can run variants of Linux. Trillions of dollars in market cap have been built on top of that open source foundational layer.

<strong>I think we can get to a similar world with AI: a base open source, commoditized intelligence layer.</strong>

<strong>That does not mean frontier models disappear.</strong> It means that for everyday use cases - going to the grocery store, managing my calendar, writing routine text - <strong>open models can make that intelligence layer free and available for everyone.</strong>

<strong>Then we can build the next layer of applications, agentic harnesses, and services on top of it. That is where I think the real money and opportunities could lie.</strong>

It also means governments can take open models and open weights, build country-specific applications, and fine-tune them to their culture. Open models can become the intelligence layer for the 80% use case.

> <em><strong>Who do you see building these open models? Will it be frontier labs releasing a fraction of their models openly? Governments? Companies like Mozilla?</strong></em>

If we are willing to think expansively, there are many opportunities.

Governments could fund them, although governments are slow.

<strong>There are also infrastructure-first models.</strong> Look at what Mira Murati is doing with <a href="https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/introducing-inkling/">Inkling</a>. The way that company plans to make money is around the infrastructure. The model becomes the incentive for you to use the infrastructure. That is a business model that could work.

<strong>Hardware or operating system companies could also play a role.</strong> Samsung, for example, could seed an ecosystem so that an entire set of operating systems is built on top of a model. That is an indirect play toward the real value someone brings.

<strong>Frontier labs could also do this.</strong> They might release an open model that handles the 80% use case, and then you flip one API key to access the frontier model for harder tasks.

There are many possibilities. <strong>Right now, we are too constrained by looking at everything through the frontier lab perspective. We need to think more broadly. Many different business models could emerge.</strong>

> <em><strong>There are so many interesting points in the report. Is there anything that did not make the headlines but that you think deserves more attention?</strong></em>

I think one overlooked issue is <strong>agentic memory.</strong>

We need to think about agentic memory as a major problem going forward, because I think it is one of the ways platforms will try to create lock-in.

If you use ChatGPT for a week and then switch to Claude, you are talking to an amnesiac. All of your context is somewhere else.

<strong>That seems like an architecturally bad decision for users.</strong> Memory should be on our side, not locked up somewhere else.

<strong>We need to solve that, because if we solve it, it enables many things downstream</strong>. I am interested in opportunities where, if you solve X, it unlocks something. Right now, I feel like the big labs are trying to solve things in a way where, if they solve Y, it locks users in.

I am looking for opportunities to do the opposite. Agentic memory is one of the issues that is not talked about enough, and that we need to wrap our heads around as a community.

DIY version: <a href="https://reflexes.sh/">Reflexes</a>, open-source guardrails for agents in plain English.

Google Earth briefly let anyone <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/07/31/see-how-google-earth-let-people-make-fake-scenes-bombings-riots-destruction/">fake bombings and riots onto real satellite maps</a>, pulled within a day.

# Computers that use computers?
Date: 2026-07-28 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/computers-that-use-computers
Cite as: Computers that use computers? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-07-28. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/computers-that-use-computers (CC BY 4.0)

**I’ve been in San Francisco for two weeks now,** and along with the beautiful houses, the good vibe, and some striking nature all around, **most of the tech discourse I’ve run into sounds like this:**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ar0V!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F326170d8-1c48-40e4-b3ea-788fe9f1fa63_1080x1080.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ar0V!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F326170d8-1c48-40e4-b3ea-788fe9f1fa63_1080x1080.gif)

**People are wildly excited about AI agents** — which I like to describe as *virtual entities* that take on tasks once reserved for humans, working alongside us.

Not that you need to be in SF to know agents are the talk of the moment. But I haven’t seen this much enthusiasm, or this much push, anywhere else.

Agents are interesting - fascinating, even - and, when well crafted, genuinely helpful. **They also reshape how we interact with computers, and spark** ***new*** **interactions among computers themselves.**

To think through what that means, and what tomorrow might look like, it helps to step back. I did that at the go-to place for understanding how computers became what they are: **the Computer History Museum in Silicon Valley.**

Wandering through the past of computing got me thinking about **what comes next**, given all the hype around agents.

**In broad brush strokes, the history of computers is a story of shrinking:** from machines that filled entire rooms and were a nightmare to maintain, to machines that sat on a desk in everyone’s home, to machines we carry around **- all while the power went up as the size came down.**

*(That’s a drastic summary of three hours in the museum.)*

[![Physics History December 1945 \| American Physical Society](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!clYs!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1b2eb0e-fffe-47cb-97d3-d84fa00334bf_2500x1597.jpeg "Physics History December 1945 | American Physical Society")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!clYs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1b2eb0e-fffe-47cb-97d3-d84fa00334bf_2500x1597.jpeg)

the ENIAC: arguably, the first computer ever

They also moved from something legible only to top researchers - dry lines of code - to **beautiful, intuitive interfaces anyone can use** without the faintest idea of how or why they work.

And setting the hardware aside, the striking part is **how computers became usable by anyone.** Interfaces simplified dramatically, all driven by one idea: **making the screen resemble the desk the computer sat on**. Hence the ‘*desktop*’.

**Computers evolved along metaphors borrowed from the old world of work** - the desktop, the spreadsheet, the bin - aimed first at knowledge workers: what Douglas Engelbart called [“augmenting human intellect”](https://www.dougengelbart.org/pubs/augment-3906.html), and what Xerox imagined as the **“office of the future”.**

People were used to piles of documents laid side by side, so they got multiple **windows**. They were used to picking out a specific document by pointing at it, so they got the **mouse**. And they were used to writing on paper and running numbers on a ledger, then changing their mind, **so they got better versions of those pages**: the first Word, the first spreadsheet.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tpNW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa234f462-6987-429f-beec-3469be62600a_1254x904.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tpNW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa234f462-6987-429f-beec-3469be62600a_1254x904.png)

well, a mouse, literally

As **Vannevar Bush** had imagined back in 1945, in [“As We May Think”](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1945/07/as-we-may-think/303881/), computers were meant to help humans navigate vast amounts of information. But not only that. By simulating our desks, the computer became, as **Alan Kay** put it, ***“a new medium that would change the thought patterns of an entire civilization”.***

And that’s what happened. **Work - and not only work - moved onto computers:** thin machines that store, or reach, almost any piece of information in the world, and that have drastically changed how we handle it.

Yet things are changing again, because **humans are no longer the only ones using computers** - and so no longer the only ones consuming information. **We’ve started working alongside agents**, or even simple LLMs, that can navigate information and act on it.

**For the nerds out there,** this is the promise of the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) - or simply of APIs driven through AI applications.

**Nothing exotic**: anyone can point Claude, or ChatGPT, or any AI at their inbox and have it read and draft replies. Same with Notion, or Booking and Trainline, to sort out the summer holidays, and much, much more.

**AI acting for us, thus acquiring agency, and so AGENTS.**

In short: computers are no longer used only by humans, so information is no longer consumed only by humans. [Cloudflare keeps us honest here](https://radar.cloudflare.com/) - more requests to websites now come from bots and agents than from people.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!glsv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F14781ff3-9900-4230-8e55-1a9f114c0be1_648x600.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!glsv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F14781ff3-9900-4230-8e55-1a9f114c0be1_648x600.png)

last week from [Cloudflare radar](https://radar.cloudflare.com/)

***But what could this shift mean?***

- **First, it lands on anyone designing interfaces.** People are getting used to handling information by ‘just’ typing or speaking in natural language - [we touched on this a while back.](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/no-one-click-that-button) But it also means whatever you build, a website or an app, **will need to work not just for humans but be readable by agents too.**

- It could go further: **people may stop using some services directly.** We’ll keep our inbox and email provider, but letting an agent go through it for us will feel more and more normal.

- And this shapes not only what interfaces look like - or whether they exist at all - but **what information we produce, and how we distribute it.** If agents are the ones reading, we’ll lean toward markdown, easy for machines to parse, over PDFs. \[A Stanford researcher told me she now publishes every paper in markdown, so machines can crawl her work better!\]

All in all, **we’re entering an era where computers use themselves.** And no, it’s not dystopia. Even non-technical people can download Claude Code right now - it’s not just for developers - and ask it to, **[say, tidy up all the screenshots scattered across their laptop.](https://www.instagram.com/reels/Dafatj7lKMt/)** And then, well, have fun.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OHTi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F62abc33e-cf6d-4807-8d5d-52920f868ab3_1124x514.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OHTi!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F62abc33e-cf6d-4807-8d5d-52920f868ab3_1124x514.png)

and, btw, interfaces are going back to the terminal?

**What’s also interesting is how we’ll study all this.** **“Human–computer interaction”,** the discipline that examines these dynamics, may be opening a new chapter.

We’re no longer just clicking buttons but asking agents to take tasks off our hands, and, increasingly, simply setting up agents to reach outcomes for us - **without knowing how they got there.**

**So the interaction between humans and computers may come to be mediated by other computers.** And, stretching it a little, we may soon be talking about ***‘computer–computer interaction.’***

Which, recalling Kay on the computer as a medium, puts a new question mark over **how these interactions might change our thought patterns.**

In other words, if I can get from idea to result by handing the computer to an agent, **maybe I’ll understand less and less about the route between the idea and the result?** Interesting times.

> ### **Something new 👀**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WRbH!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4a081c2-a1f6-437a-aded-5930874e0bdb_1200x1200.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WRbH!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4a081c2-a1f6-437a-aded-5930874e0bdb_1200x1200.jpeg)

**Got breakthrough science stuck in the lab? Let's get it out.**<br>

**[TEF Foundry](https://techeuropefoundation.notion.site/TEF-Foundry-Handbook-WS-0b8fbb6d741f49c5966f288111aeb383)**, launched by by the [Tech Europe Foundation](https://tef.tech/), is a 9-month, no-equity Proof-of-Concept program (Oct 2026–June 2027) **for deep tech teams trying to figure out whether their tech should become a real company.**<br>

Think of it as years of trial-and-error compressed into a milestone-based, high-pressure sprint across three gates - with non-dilutive funding (starting from 30 up to €100K total), a dedicated Entrepreneur in Residence, and direct lines to industry, mentors, and investors.

Teams start broad (up to 50) and get narrowed down to the strongest ventures, ending with a Demo Day pitch to international investors.

**Applications are open now and close August 30** - the program kicks off September 28. **Discover more and [apply here.](https://eu1.hubs.ly/H0wFfgB0)**

# It is not normal
Date: 2026-07-04 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/it-is-not-normal
Cite as: It is not normal by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-07-04. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/it-is-not-normal (CC BY 4.0)

Artifacts is not meant to be a news newsletter, but <strong>what has happened between Anthropic and the US administration over the past few months is worth a recap.</strong> It comes in two separate episodes.

<strong>First episode, at the start of the year.</strong> The Pentagon wanted Anthropic to agree that its models could be used for <em>“all lawful purposes.”</em> Anthropic refused, <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/use-with-caution">asking for two exceptions:</a> no fully autonomous weapons, and no mass domestic surveillance of Americans.

<strong>The administration did not take it well.</strong> It moved to label the company a <em>“supply chain risk”,</em> and by late February the President had ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology altogether. Anthropic sued.

<strong>Second episode, in early summer, and a different story.</strong> In June, Anthropic released Mythos, <strong>a model it described as too dangerous to hand over as-is</strong>, alongside Fable - the same model with built-in guardrails against malicious uses.

<strong>Within days, a jailbreak was found in Fable</strong>, and reports emerged that a China-linked group had accessed Mythos. The administration reacted with export controls barring foreign nationals from using the models - including Anthropic’s own non-American employees, which is odd given how many of them there are.

Thus, <strong>Anthropic disabled both models for everyone, worldwide.</strong> A few weeks later the controls were lifted, <strong>and the models are back</strong> - on the condition that Anthropic proactively detects security risks and reports malicious activity to the government.

That last condition matters. There is no formal law here yet, but a pattern is forming: <strong>the state now sets terms on when and how a model reaches the public.</strong> OpenAI, too, <a href="https://openai.com/index/previewing-gpt-5-6-sol/">staggered its latest release</a> “following pressure by the US government.”

There is a clear takeaway out of the past few months: <strong>AI is not a normal technology. Therefore, its use, deployment, and regulation cannot be normal.</strong>

I borrow the phrase from Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor, who argue the opposite in their much-cited essay <em><a href="https://knightcolumbia.org/content/ai-as-normal-technology">“AI as Normal Technology.”</a></em> <a href="https://knightcolumbia.org/content/ai-as-normal-technology"></a> <strong>Their point is about diffusion:</strong> AI will spread and embed itself across the economy gradually, the way electricity or the internet did, and so we can govern it with the ordinary tools we already have.

<a href="https://www.normaltech.ai/p/ai-as-normal-technology?utm_source=substack&amp;utm_campaign=post_embed&amp;utm_medium=web"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YzQY!,w_56,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6780dda8-5879-4789-bf02-b3ea43a9f85e_1000x1000.png" alt="">AI as Normal TechnologyAI as Normal TechnologyThis post is over 15,000 words long—it is a new paper on our vision for the future of AI. We are pleased to announce that an expanded version of these ideas will become our next book together…Read more2 years ago · 590 likes · 38 comments · Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor</a>

On that layer, they may well be right. <strong>But the past few months have played out on different levels: geopolitics and national strategy,</strong> none of this looks normal at all.

AI not being just a normal technology can be inferred when looking at the 2 main actors involved:

- <strong>AI companies</strong> (OpenAI, Anthropic etc) who claim to be building the future of intelligence, while also warning that some of their models are too dangerous

- <strong>US Administration</strong> being so involved in what’s going on, notably keeping a close eye on the models and spotting risks. But, more importantly, being aware that <strong>AI is critical technology also on the geopolitical realm</strong> and has, therefore, implications in the challenges with China too

Let’s look into this more:

For companies, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/opinion/ai-dangerous-openai-anthropic.html">a beautiful piece</a> from <strong>Cal Newport</strong> has criticised their approach. If they claim their models to be dangerous, it could be <strong>for 2 reasons:</strong>

- <strong>this is true and therefore worrying</strong> - but maybe the solution should rather be to really stop and think about what has been done? AI companies keep pushing cause they know other companies will do, so they can’t lose ground. But if you really think what you’re doing is too dangerous and you put it out there, <strong>well then maybe more responsibility is needed?</strong>

- maybe it’s not that true, <strong>it’s just a marketing move</strong> - <strong>but is that responsible?</strong> Are we joking?

Let’s assume 1 is true. Last week, I had the chance to listen to <strong><a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/yann-lecun/">Yann LeCun</a></strong>, former Chief AI Scientist at Meta and now founder of AMI Labs, who just said <em>“if you claim it’s too dangerous, what about starting to do things differently?”</em>

<strong>In other words, AI technologies are far from being deterministic - the people building them can put guardrails.</strong> <em><strong>So if you’re concerned, just stop?</strong></em>

If you’re aware of these risks and you’re in control of the design of such technology, <strong>you draw the consequences.</strong>

Differently, <strong>claims and warnings seem sometimes misaligned with the downstream actions.</strong>

If one is to trace why, <strong>it could go up to the incentives driving AI companies</strong>, which may not just be safety, as they keep raising money from private investors, target IPOs with debatable financial fundamentals, and are racing against each other while being all far from profitable.

<strong>But the administration side of things is not less interesting.</strong> Even a laissez-faire administration like the current US one seems to be concerned about AI safety, and for incentives reasons too. It started with cutting on any existing AI regulation framework, then things have changed with the current proposal being a vet on models.

What it is clear though, beyond regulation, is that the US administration <strong>needs</strong> (and thus has incentives) AI, for a couple of reasons: it’s a critical technology for war operations (and the world is not peaceful right now) but it’s also a matter of competitiveness on the global field, where the threat coming from China is not irrelevant.

And therefore <strong>the grip on AI is different from previous attempts at regulating technologies like online platforms or data privacy</strong>, and it pertains more to a strategic technology.

It may be not dissimilar from nuclear technology, for which special plans were put together (you watched <em>Oppenheimer</em>, no?). With, yet, <strong>the small detail that such strategic technology is not being developed within universities or public settings</strong> but by private organisations that, of course, are looking at being profitable.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

So, <strong>reconciling the two positions of companies and the state, we are facing a more-than-normal technology,</strong> with alarms and warnings about safety being raised by those building and those regulating, but also all of this being pulled by other incentives.

<strong>I once read that incentives are superpowers.</strong> Here they seem to be many, and misaligned - within and across AI companies and the administration - <strong>while all acknowledging (or even raising!) the potential dangers or threats.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yUZ-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faf1c54f7-ea91-4995-9aed-aec2f695cd25_1254x1254.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yUZ-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faf1c54f7-ea91-4995-9aed-aec2f695cd25_1254x1254.png" alt=""></a>

<strong>If these dangers or threats are real, lining up incentives is not enough: they have to be prioritised.</strong>

Here is a test for whether that is happening. When a company says a model is too dangerous, <strong>it is describing an obligation it now carries,</strong> and we should hold it to that. Too dangerous to release, released anyway, banned abroad, back by morning: these words should not cost nothing and cannot be just another way to launch a product.

We built institutions around strategic technologies. <strong>This one we have handed to companies with many different incentives, and left them to sort out the contradictions in public</strong>, with chaos for citizens being the first immediate outcome.

If we get better at this, <strong>the first result would be to stop seeing public communications being often contradictory</strong>, at the expense of users and citizens, and finally aligned with clearer incentives and principles about how AI is being built and distributed.

# Who holds the key?
Date: 2026-06-19 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/who-holds-the-key
Cite as: Who holds the key? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-06-19. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/who-holds-the-key (CC BY 4.0)

It’s no wonder someone might recently have thought *‘why can’t Siri just be as good as ChatGPT voice?’.* That’s probably something Apple was well aware of and that’s why **at the latest WWDC they [announced the new SiriAI](https://www.theverge.com/tech/942416/apple-siri-ai-update-wwdc)**, which promises to be more helpful than just a tool to set a timer or call your mom.

The tech bubble has welcomed it, [wondering if Siri is](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ituu9ypvaHk) *[finally](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ituu9ypvaHk)* [good](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ituu9ypvaHk). And it does seem so: the new Siri will be an assistant that works across apps, knows who the user is and is far more integrated into day-to-day tasks.

[\[Embedded media — view original\]](https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/2PW5y3zAvPE?rel=0&autoplay=0&showinfo=0&enablejsapi=0)

If you have watched the video to the end, you’ve made it to *‘your data stays protected’* and *‘coming to an iPhone near to you’*, which echoes both Apple’s **obsession with personal data protection** and the successful launch campaign of the iPod promising 1000 songs in your pocket.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ri8u!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0f89a54d-fe85-4816-bb17-8df401dfc2df_1280x649.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ri8u!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0f89a54d-fe85-4816-bb17-8df401dfc2df_1280x649.jpeg)

And that’s not just a marketing move but the core of how SiriAI has been built: **a personal assistant that uses your own data, processing it directly on your iPhone, while limiting what’s sent to the cloud.** So your Siri and your data literally stay in your pocket - or wherever you keep your iPhone.

Yet, not if your pockets are European ! **SiriAI is, indeed, not coming European iPhones anytime soon :)** (though it will be available on Mac, Apple Watch and Vision Pro)

This is, [according to](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/06/due-to-dma-siri-ai-delayed-in-eu-for-ios-27-and-ipados-27/) **[Apple](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/06/due-to-dma-siri-ai-delayed-in-eu-for-ios-27-and-ipados-27/)**, ***‘due to the Digital Markets Act’*** and to EU regulators who *‘did not accept any of Apple’s proposed solutions to bring Siri AI to the EU while safely supporting other virtual assistants.’*

The **EU Commission**, for its part, [promptly replied](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/thomas-regnier-24a05810b_what-is-the-true-story-behind-apples-decision-ugcPost-7470439815910551552-sPn3/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAADBGmFQB0rHgggpkCiHG5Dn-B9e4n2G0Y-g) that the decision is *“Apple’s and Apple’s only”* and that nothing in its Digital Markets Act forbids the launch.

For those new to the DMA, **it’s the main EU regulation trying to limit the monopoly power of some sprawling platforms (aka ‘gatekeepers’).**

It’s the reason why you’re now often asked which browser you want to use, instead of Safari ruling out the rest as the default, or why Google can’t route you straight to Google Maps when you search for a town.

It’s not the first time Apple and the EU Commission have fought over the DMA, we covered it [here](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/slicing-apples).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**This time, the fight pertains to Article 6 and the idea of interoperability:** if Apple builds a capability into the iPhone, rivals should be able to plug into the same hooks, on equal terms, rather than being locked out of a system everyone is forced to live inside.

In explaining the decision, Apple fell back on one of its leitmotifs about the DMA: **giving to other providers access to its systems may compromise the security and privacy of users.**

Concretely, Apple is concerned about giving users access to, say, ChatGPT or Claude as a replacement for Siri **because they would not guarantee the same level of security and privacy.**

That’s because any AI model used by Siri is built to run on the iPhone and, for complex tasks, it will be run on Google Cloud (which partnered with Apple to train Siri) but still secured within a proprietary [Private Cloud Compute](https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/) framework. **So Apple can be sure of what happens with Siri, far less so if it opened access to other providers.**

On the other hand, **these security concerns undermine the interoperability goal of the Digital Markets Act**, since users have no choice over which AI assistant to use.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is a case where **the design of the technology clashes significantly with the design of the regulation**, and the other way around.

Yet, this isn’t necessarily down to an incautious approach by Apple, it’s also that **the DMA was conceived for a different era of much more controllable software.**

For instance, when Apple or any phone provider open up the choice of the favourite browser, **they can still limit and know the tasks that the browser will perform**, such as opening URLs one receives on WhatsApp. In other words, **these tasks are well defined.**

This is different with Siri. **An agentic AI assistant has a much broader scope of action:** it doesn’t just answer your questions but can take action on your behalf, using different parts of your iPhone, like Calendar, phone, maybe messaging apps, etc.

Therefore, **opening up to a different AI assistant is definitely different from letting users pick the browser they like.**

If you like metaphors, an AI assistant is **a curious, silly little guy with a master key that can open any door on your phone**, while with other DMA provisions, like the browser, you are dealing with a quiet one with only a few keys :)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7qig!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff3a64d25-f4f2-4ab4-8899-6867667129ea_1254x1254.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7qig!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff3a64d25-f4f2-4ab4-8899-6867667129ea_1254x1254.png)

Finally, to give rivals the “equal access” mandated by the DMA to the new Siri, Apple wouldn’t be handing over a feature, but rather **a good part of the iPhone.**

And yet “handing over the phone” is kind of what Apple offered to do, eventually. Remember those *“proposed solutions”* the Commission turned down? The main one was a **Trusted System Agent:** a gateway that would let rival assistants into the phone gradually, through Apple’s own checkpoint.

Apple’s pitch was: we ship Siri AI in Europe now, and open it to competitors slowly and safely. **The Commission read the eighteen months as a stall, not a safeguard, and said no.**

Overall, though Artifacts doesn’t aim to take sides on the matter (which would require much more research), what’s interesting in this tale is that **we’re looking at a regulation that is only a few years old, but is already straining against a technology only a few years ahead of it.**

And that’s probably because **the DMA was conceived for bounded and predictable services** like browsers, maps, app stores with clear use cases, and thus applying it to AI agents with a broader scope necessarily means stretching it.

Thus, we could argue **that the regulation is not** ***designed*** **for the fundamentals of the technology** and, ultimately, for its design.

Yet, it also shows **how the regulation of AI goes far beyond AI as a technology, how it is built and the risks it may carry**, and should rather extend to how it is put to use within systems, probably forcing us to rethink regulations conceived for much more controllable and bounded technologies.

In the meantime, we wait for a better Siri and will keep using the existing one for the alarm !

> ### **Save for Later**

The UK is about to [ban under-16s from social media](https://www.theverge.com/policy/949679/uk-under-16-social-media-ban-announcement). [Oliver Marsh has the nuance](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dr-oliver-marsh-a0246b60_my-quick-personal-thoughts-on-social-media-share-7472282478955769856-POxD/) the headlines skip.

Speaking of age checks: nearly [a million passports just leaked](https://www.theverge.com/tech/947157/passports-data-breach-cannabis-club-systems-nefos-puffpal) from PuffPal, an age-verification system for European cannabis clubs.

Meanwhile, Europe is quietly [unplugging from American tech](https://www.wired.com/story/all-the-ways-europe-is-ditching-american-technology/). Part of the plan: build our own social media. Meet [Eurosky](https://www.euractiv.com/news/interview-inside-the-commissions-favoured-european-social-network/), the EU Commission’s favourite, running on the same protocol as Bluesky - cofounder Sebastian Vogelsang has been [making the case](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/svogelsang_atproto-opensocialweb-digitalsovereignty-share-7471860196273745921--a2f/) for a while.

And the FT reckons Europe is [finally flexing its innovation muscles](https://www.ft.com/content/326aa9fd-dcb3-4e3b-a775-61b28e7e12f6).

Two AI-and-work papers worth your time. [The Broken Ladder](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6787638): is AI quietly eating the junior rung of the career ladder or it’s rather because of remote work? And [Writing Code vs Shipping Code](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35275): AI lets you code 180% more but ship only 30% more - turns out the bottleneck was never the typing :)

Ah, and Meta just [surprised everyone by funding its Oversight Board through 2028](https://www.platformer.news/meta-oversight-board-funding-2028/).

# Looking backwards
Date: 2026-05-28 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/looking-backwards
Cite as: Looking backwards by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-05-28. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/looking-backwards (CC BY 4.0)

Staring at a blank page is the starting point of most creative work. It is what may trigger the so-called <strong>writer’s block</strong>, <strong>and it happens across every kind of making:</strong> when you sit down to write a piece, when you sketch the interface of a piece of software, or, for the more artsy among us, when you go to paint.

Yet, nowadays, <strong>this is potentially no longer a thing</strong>, or no longer a problem, if you will.

The reason is that, with Generative AI, <strong>we can always start from</strong> <em><strong>something</strong></em><strong>:</strong> the distance between a blank page and one, two, multiple pages of text or a scrappy interface or graphic has become very short. <strong>It is maybe just one prompt away.</strong>

Producing content - whatever shape that content takes and no matter the quality - has become a <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking">commodity.</a>

<a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uxHU!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F157cbf39-ed1c-4b5d-999a-5319b785f96d_1024x1024.png" alt="Writing is thinking?"></a>

#### Writing is thinking?

<a href="https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona">Lorenzo Ancona</a>·10 Feb<a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking">Read full story</a>

And that changes the way we begin work, especially the creative one.

<strong>Yet this doesn’t come without consequences</strong>, and they are worth reflecting on.

This very fact of having an anchor can save us - or maybe drown us - <strong>in skipping some very initial questions</strong>, as the frame is already there. It may also create the <strong>fatigue of re-making something</strong>, with less awareness of how it got there. <strong>And the pull is to keep working on it rather than to start again.</strong>

But it’s not just that: as the Pope points out in his last encyclical <a href="https://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/encyclicals/documents/20260515-magnifica-humanitas.html">‘Magnifica Humanitas’</a> (Magnificent Humanity) on AI, <em><strong>”the speed and ease with which answers or summaries can be obtained risk extinguishing the desire to ask questions, which is a process that bears fruit only over time.”</strong></em> Facing something that goes this fast may indeed create some fatigue, maybe make us lazy, and more importantly stop deeply questioning what we’re producing.

Even worse, when using AI, which Mozilla describes as a force for ‘Acceleration, Simulation, and Homogenization’, <strong>we may be tempted to treat is as a perfect machine</strong>, given how polished the outputs are <em>(bear with me on the output item, we’ll get back to it soon)</em>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!91zz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F74501567-6453-442a-aa01-2368b8547c29_1392x922.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!91zz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F74501567-6453-442a-aa01-2368b8547c29_1392x922.png" alt=""></a>

go read <a href="https://www.mozillafoundation.org/en/what-we-do/mobilize/imaginative-intelligences/imagine-intel-zine/">Intel Zine</a> from Mozilla Foundation!

But this is a risk, and not because of philosophical speculation or any Luddism, <strong>but because of the technological foundations of AI. In other words, because of how AI is built</strong> - so let’s look into the machine.

<strong>AI is, primarily, a statistical machine.</strong> It is trained, as we know, to retrieve the data it was fed and to produce what is plausible on the basis of it. And here we go back to AI as a <em><a href="https://www.newyorker.com/culture/infinite-scroll/ai-is-homogenizing-our-thoughts">technology of average</a></em> both in the quality of the writing and in the calibre of the ideas.

It is, in other words, <strong>a machine built to look backwards:</strong> it generates what is most probable given everything that came before, and not necessarily anything creative.

Now, <strong>you could fairly object that human creativity does the same:</strong> we’re inspired by what we read or listen to and use it for our creative work. True.

But the difference is probably in the purpose and direction. The machine works backwards, from probability. We work forwards, from intention - <strong>taking what we know and questioning it, merging it, putting it back together on purpose.</strong>

Maybe, <strong>that act of repackaging with a reason is what makes creativity worth something.</strong>

It is, in other words, not just to produce something new out of the knowledge we have, but <strong>to give it meaning in the new shape we confer.</strong> The output is only part of the story.

With AI, the rest of that story goes missing. <strong>We ignore the process that runs from input to output, because all we ask of the output is that it be good enough.</strong> The process itself stays inscrutable - technologically, <strong>what happens between A and B is not something we can control nor understand.</strong>

And indeed, <strong>we don’t care whether AI is actually intelligent</strong> - <em>let alone creative!</em> - only whether its output resembles something we humans would consider to be the work of an intelligence.

This is, after all, the founding premise of the field. In 1955, McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, and Shannon opened <a href="http://jmc.stanford.edu/articles/dartmouth/dartmouth.pdf">‘A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence’</a> - the document that launched AI as a discipline - by defining the problem as <em>‘that of making a machine behave in ways that would be called intelligent if a human were so behaving’.</em>

What mattered, from the start, <strong>was the appearance of the result, not the process</strong>

In that sense, <strong>AI is not far from a dishwasher:</strong> you don’t care about how the dishes got clean, <strong>only that you can eat off them again.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jMOd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdac7a854-e18e-4a4b-8042-e15cb6676405_1254x1254.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jMOd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdac7a854-e18e-4a4b-8042-e15cb6676405_1254x1254.png" alt=""></a>

For most things, that’s a perfectly good arrangement - drafting an email, say. It becomes a problem with creativity, <strong>because there we risk missing what creativity actually is, and what it is for.</strong>

Stand in front of a painting and you care about more than the final artifact, important as it is. <strong>You care also about how it came to be.</strong>

<strong>For instance, last weekend I stood in front of Guernica.</strong> Stripped of its background - without knowing what Picasso wanted, without the history behind it - I thought the canvas loses much of its force. <strong>The image alone is not the point.</strong>

And importantly, <strong>the process matters not just to those receiving it or consuming creativity, but for the people making it</strong> - who begins at a blank page and, through a cognitive, creative struggle, arrives somewhere.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qmix!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1ec18ff2-4cc2-4f62-83b6-44292c378267_936x704.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qmix!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1ec18ff2-4cc2-4f62-83b6-44292c378267_936x704.png" alt=""></a>

<a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/ask-eu-how/comments">Leave a comment</a>

# Ask EU how
Date: 2026-05-13 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/ask-eu-how
Cite as: Ask EU how by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-05-13. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/ask-eu-how (CC BY 4.0)

Last week, Artifacts attended the [Politico AI & Tech Week in Brussels.](https://www.politico.eu/ai-tech-week-2026/?_Tech_-_EOM1_-_auto_conf)

Topics went well beyond AI - **sovereignty, data, chips, platforms, online safety, entrepreneurship.** Which is refreshing, since AI dominates so much of the conversation everywhere.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TEse!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbba9033f-f7e7-472f-9ae5-3b3bfe58842f_3024x3058.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TEse!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbba9033f-f7e7-472f-9ae5-3b3bfe58842f_3024x3058.jpeg)

What struck me was **the breadth of opinions**, moving past the tired regulator-versus-private-sector dichotomy. Instead: **regulators** more open to explain and listen, **third parties** trying to mediate, scaling **companies** voicing their needs, large **enterprises** less defensive, **academics** naming the complexity.

But there’s still a pattern quite visible: **a fundamental disconnection between those designing regulation and those building the technology, who rarely attend such events.** Which then triggers lots of talks about the *what* needs to be done, and **much less about the** ***how*** **to get there.**

Finally, a special mention goes to the Politico journalists, who asked precise questions, pulled speakers back on track when needed, and kept pointing toward where the real complexity lives.

Anyway, **here are five things the Brussels Tech ‘Bubble’ is discussing** - in an attempt to make it readable for those outside of it (and go follow [Unbubble Hub](https://unbubblehub.substack.com/), speaking of bubbles)

> ### *First of all*, Europe wants more control on the technologies we use

This is the thing everyone agrees on. **Sovereignty is the political frame of such control**, with the core idea being *“someone on the other side of the planet cannot switch off our infrastructure.”* Therefore, it’s also a matter of strategic security.

**Less agreement exists on what counts as a European technology and when it can really be considered sovereign.** More importantly, it remains unclear which domains to prioritize - semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, data centers, software - and what the real impact would be on the private sector actually building these systems. Yet, end of the month may provide more info with the release of the [‘Tech Sovereignty Package’](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/07/eu-commission-cloud-sensitive-data.html) by the Commission.

> ### *Therefore*, Building European is the path

The idea that Europe and European companies can build breakthrough technologies is **no longer a myth.**

Simplification packages like [EU inc](https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/eu-inc-making-business-easier-european-union-2026-03-18_en) - a streamlined legal structure for digital startups - are welcomed with genuine enthusiasm and curiosity. **Much more alignment exists on the idea that regulation need not be a drag but should enable easier business.** And finally, pushing for a [Eurostack](https://eurostack.eu/) - a European-controlled tech infrastructure - and actively financing innovation seems to be the way forward.

> ### *That’s why* Antitrust matters (a lot) on AI

To avoid scenarios like Google Search edition 2, where the search market is heavily concentrated, **with AI it’s critical to prevent companies from entrenching themselves as blockers.** This matters especially for Europe’s hope to keep alive the dream of a European AI flagship company.

> ### *And still on AI*, the real work with regulation is actually on implementation

It was fun to be in Brussels at the Politico event on the day of the [AI Omnibus](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1024), which meant a delay and a simplification in the implementation of the AI Act. **It’s also increasingly clear that AI regulation is primarily AI governance** - not just the rules, but how they’re enforced. The actual work starts after the paperwork, and many speakers suggested Europe is behind here.

**Figuring out how to operationalise the AI Act is what will keep the bubble busy in the months ahead.** Getting this right matters for safety, for clarity, for whether the rules can actually be enforced. This whole situation brought me back to someone who once told me: *“A politician who doesn’t care about the outcome of their policies is like a CEO who doesn’t care about the outcome of their product.”* That’s probably something to keep in mind.

> ### Which is a *very similar story* to the one on Age Verification

Age verification has become the new buzzword in tech regulation. **Everyone agrees, of course, that protecting children online is a priority.** Yet fewer people grapple with the **complexity** of actually implementing a proper verification system - the technical and privacy problems, the likelihood of bans, [what we do with VPNs](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/ATAG/2026/782618/EPRS_ATA(2026)782618_EN.pdf) (with some ideas that seem quite bizarre, to say the least)

**This is the clearest example of the** ***what*** **versus** ***how*** **gap.** Easy to agree on the goal (protecting children), harder to think through implementation. **On this matter, which is fundamentally technical, the debate remains heavily political.**

It will take time and considerable controversy, while the [EU Commission just announced](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c9q3x19ddl7o) they’re considering a social media ‘delay’ (=ban) for minors this summer, pointing to the recently released [EU age-verification app.](https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/european-age-verification-app-keep-children-safe-online-2026-04-15_en)<br>

On age verification, I had written a piece btw:

# Decoding it
Date: 2026-04-28 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/decoding-it
Cite as: Decoding it by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-04-28. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/decoding-it (CC BY 4.0)

<a href="https://www.getmatter.com/">Matter</a>, the app I used to read articles and save the highlights, introduced a subscription, which I didn’t want to pay for. So, in slightly more than an hour <strong>I (vibe)coded with AI something quick and dirty that does the exact same things.</strong>

\[Vibe-coding becoming a thing was <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/send-good-vibes">the subject of an Artifacts</a> more than 1 year old, btw\]

This Read Later app (it doesn’t even have a name) may seem to be quite cool, <strong>but I’d argue that it is not.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6kND!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff2d270be-5267-4dbc-b376-41928cdf1c25_800x450.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6kND!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff2d270be-5267-4dbc-b376-41928cdf1c25_800x450.gif" alt=""></a>

As you see, it does a few things just right for me:

- <strong>it stores articles</strong> from any website (with an ugly browser extension)

- <strong>it saves them</strong>, so I can read, highlight what matters, add labels in an uglier UI

- and finally <strong>it sends them to the Notion database</strong> I use to write Artifacts.

And yes, although I could go and brag like LinkedIn folks saying ‘I recreated \[insert name of random app\]’ or ‘You can now build anything’, <strong>I tend to think that such narrative is, as most narratives, just a nice story to tell.</strong>

And that this app doesn't make the cut cause <strong>it was built with just my specific needs in mind.</strong>

It is, indeed, true that <strong>non-technical people can nowadays quickly bootstrap functioning apps</strong>, but these are <strong>quite far from well-crafted products</strong> or saying that software organisations are doomed.

True: we may have solved large parts of the complexity of coding, but <strong>it’s not because anyone can write that then anyone can suddenly be David Foster Wallace</strong> or Carrere or whoever you like.

This Artifacts is to decode this story around programming code.

We do live in extraordinary times, for sure:

- <strong>5% of the programming code in GitHub is now written by Claude Code</strong>, the most popular AI for coding. The Head of Claude Code claimed that <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=We7BZVKbCVw">‘code is largely solved’.</a>

- For the first time in 15 years, <strong>student enrollment in computer science degrees is falling in the US</strong>, according to the <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/04/13/computer-science-major-ai/">Washington Post.</a>

- <strong>Some tech companies are firing employees</strong>, including engineers, because of AI - last being Meta which announced it will fire 10% of its staff.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!DhXa!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fea0be385-6f69-4295-a704-b1155f9e8745_1142x754.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!DhXa!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fea0be385-6f69-4295-a704-b1155f9e8745_1142x754.png" alt=""></a>

Yet, <strong>not everything seems to back this narrative.</strong>

The most surprising data is that <strong>demand for software engineers is not dropping</strong>, <a href="https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/state-of-the-product-job-market-in-ee9">according to Lenny’s newsletter.</a> So, despite students being reluctant to enrolling in computer science degrees, the job market isn’t showing a steady downfall, for now. <strong>(Maybe the first time in history students are concerned about a sector that is not really shrinking?)</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vrZH!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6a8f258-05e6-4bbf-96f0-57d21575c08b_1456x1259.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vrZH!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6a8f258-05e6-4bbf-96f0-57d21575c08b_1456x1259.png" alt=""></a>

Aside from the job market, which is not the focus of Artifacts, these months and years are incredibly fascinating to speculate about what’s happening to software.

<strong>It is true that coding is becoming a commodity.</strong> Concretely, if you talk to any engineer, writing code by hand is undergoing something similar to what is happening to writing emails for any knowledge worker.

<strong>It’s what I called <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking">meta-writing:</a></strong> we more and more dictate to a machine <em>what</em> we need to write and maybe even <em>how</em> and in what style, <strong>and then we delegate the act of writing or typing <s>words</s> code to machines.</strong>

Yet, this can be framed within the <strong>progressive simplification of creating software</strong> over decades. Without diving into the history of coding, also the rise of API (Application Programming Interfaces) made it much easier to create apps.<br>

<em>skip this paragraph if you know what an API is</em> - APIs is what makes it possible, for instance, for any website to just connect to Stripe, the most popular payment service in the world, and having a working payment process, without building it from scratch. <strong>APIs are, fundamentally, prebuilt</strong> <em><strong>bridges</strong></em> <strong>between applications</strong> -

If before you still needed to handle and oversee the construction of the bridges of API (and many other items of working software), <strong>it is now true that, with AI, all of this is more and more being commodified and automated.</strong>

Or, to put it simpler, <strong>the code can be written by machines themselves</strong>. On this, on the very question if we should even be surprised that machines are good at using themselves, <strong>I’ll probably write an Artifacts.</strong>

Getting something working is fine and great and it is what we all eventually care about with technology = <strong>problems solved, maybe ignoring how.</strong> You want to call your mom with your iPhone, you can’t care less about how it works.

But it doesn’t mean we’ll no longer need people who understand and think through software.

Because getting something working very quick <strong>but overlooking</strong> <em><strong>how</strong></em> <strong>it works</strong> <em><strong></strong></em> <strong>is not great</strong> if you’re to (1) fix something that may break when you will add a new feature, (2) be confident about the security of what you’re creating, and (3) make it fit for the wider public and not just you.

This is also cause there’s a big difference between building something that works for us at first glance and something widely usable, which is what professionals do.

And there’s something even more fundamental than all of this: code was never only the point - <strong>tackling the right problem has always been the harder part.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<strong>I don’t want to sound like a doomsayer or a skeptic here,</strong> it’s just a humble exercise to cool down a lot of hype that I often find unjustified.

It is, again, great that anyone (especially non technical people) can sketch prototypes of something: <strong>it cuts time, makes ideas spread, and makes them easier to prove right or wrong.</strong>

Yet, in all the hype around AI coding, there’s one apparent risk that doesn’t pertain to the code: <strong>skipping the question of</strong> <em><strong>why</strong></em> <strong>you’re building that app in the first place.</strong>

Why do you think the app you rushed to organise a trip with friends on a Saturday morning would work for others? <strong>Just because it works? Mmm…</strong>

The fact that it is now so fast and easy to get something working together with automated code writing may let us overlook:

- <strong>why we’re investing time</strong> in building something

- whether what we’re doing <strong>is the best way</strong> to get to a result

- and <strong>whether it will hold up</strong> beyond the first version

Just as writing is thinking and taking the time to write is valuable, <strong>we should handle with care the velocity and the ease at which AI enables us to build something.</strong>

Are velocity and ease just an unparalleled advantage or <strong>do they let us overlook why we do something?</strong>

If you have ever worked in a software company, you know that before handing off to engineers, <strong>there’s first a whole preliminary phase:</strong> defining what needs to be built, what problem it should tackle, what a bad solution would look like, how to make it technically possible. <strong>All before a line of code is written.</strong>

If AI makes it faster and easier to skip that phase and get something working, <strong>I’m not sure we will go that far.</strong>

<strong>The value of software primarily lies in the problems it tackles, not in having functioning code.</strong> If your shiny product works but doesn’t tackle a real problem, it’s trash.

And it is only good that with AI it is easier and quicker to develop such trash if one has the honesty to go back to the drawing board and rethink the problem.

Asking such questions and making sure that what we intend to build is the first step. <strong>Only after, making it real, now more easily and faster with AI, is the second one.</strong>

And this connects back to the students concerned about their jobs despite a job market that hasn’t collapsed. <strong>It is true that writing code is becoming easier - but this commodification is the opportunity to focus on the problems we want to tackle.</strong> A largely abused (and not perfect) metaphor is that of calculus machines: it’s great to be faster at doing math if we know what math we need done.

One may also argue that this is even better: we’re cutting the time spent on the part that can be automated <strong>to focus on the questions.</strong>

Then, once the questions are tackled, <strong>making sure that the code</strong> (likely mostly written by machines) <strong>is understandable, curated, and sustainable over time</strong> - that is still critical, and likely to become the work of current and future engineers.

One thing is just writing. <strong>A completely different one is knowing what to write and then writing it well.</strong>
