# You know a good architect?
Date: 2026-04-07 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/you-know-a-good-architect
Cite as: You know a good architect? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-04-07. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/you-know-a-good-architect (CC BY 4.0)

A few weeks back, I was in Amsterdam in a well-known museum that I had visited before. <strong>They had restructured the building, though:</strong> new layout, different lighting, and a reworked flow for visitors.

<strong>The experience was notably worse</strong>, despite the quality of the art on the walls. The same pieces I remembered were now hard to see properly - light reflecting off surfaces, canvases hung in awkward corners, and the rhythm of the visit broken.

Nothing had changed about the art <strong>but everything had changed about the building around it.</strong>

<strong>It reminded me of reading a beautiful book in a poorly printed edition</strong> - the content is all there, but something in the way it reaches you is off.

A badly designed building affects what it contains and the people who visit it. <strong>To fix it, you will likely call back the architects,</strong> not the artists.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

With a bit of fantasy and mental stretch, <strong>this is what was ruled for social media in the US in the last weeks.</strong>

Two bellwether <em>(must admit I learnt a new word)</em>, initial rulings:

- On March 25, a Los Angeles jury found <strong><a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/25/technology/social-media-trial-verdict.html">Meta and YouTube negligent</a> in the design of their platforms</strong> - <strong>ruling that features like infinite scroll, autoplay, and algorithmically-tuned reward loops were not neutral product choices but foreseeable causes of harm.</strong> The plaintiff had sued the companies at 17 after spending up to 16 hours a day on Instagram as a teenager.

- On March 24, a New Mexico jury ordered Meta to pay \$375 million after the state attorney general proved <strong>the company had misled users about how safe its platforms were for children</strong> - and that its design had actively enabled predators to find and contact minors.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!eEnL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F93cae063-ab02-44ef-bc9f-8e8556f073fa_401x491.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!eEnL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F93cae063-ab02-44ef-bc9f-8e8556f073fa_401x491.png" alt=""></a>

To get a sense of the severity of these matters. Plus, the full explanation <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/video/technology/100000010801833/why-the-verdict-against-meta-and-youtube-could-change-social-media.html">here</a>

The platforms have announced that <strong>they will appeal these decisions.</strong>

What makes these verdicts different from the thousands of lawsuits that came before is not the dollar amounts but the question they answered: courts weren’t asked whether Meta and Google hosted harmful content but <strong>whether they built dangerous products or hadn’t done enough to prevent harm.</strong>

This distinction - quiet, technical, almost bureaucratic-sounding - is actually a <strong>big new thing</strong>.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Up until now, platforms have often been shielded by <strong>Section 230</strong>, or <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.7591/j.ctvr7fcrd">‘the 26 words that created the Internet’</a> - a piece of legislation within the 1996 Communications Decency Act that <strong>protects online services from liability for what users post.</strong>

Section 230 made the internet possible because <strong>no one would have risked opening a service and bearing responsibility for other people’s actions.</strong>

Yet when it passed, <strong>the closest thing to a social media platform looked like this:</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A_PF!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40ffda7b-bc74-46e0-b9cf-e4c262cdf467_1920x1080.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A_PF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40ffda7b-bc74-46e0-b9cf-e4c262cdf467_1920x1080.png" alt=""></a>

These are <strong>CompuServe</strong> and <strong>Prodigy</strong>, dial-up platforms where users posted text messages to bulletin boards. Users also chose a topic and read posts in chronological order. The logic of 230 was sound: you don’t sue the corkboard for what someone pins to it.

<strong>What CompuServe and Prodigy were offering was the hosting of content.</strong> But online platforms have changed quite a bit since:

<strong>They can now profile every user</strong> - every tap, pause, scroll, and replay feeding a behavioural model. <strong>They personalise reality:</strong> two people on the same platform at the same moment see completely different feeds. <strong>They recommend the next piece of content before you’ve decided you want one.</strong> <strong>They shape what is culturally visible at scale:</strong> what trends, what gets buried, what goes viral is not the neutral outcome of user preference but the product of ranking decisions the platform makes for billions of people simultaneously.

<strong>The content is still there, but it has become the fuel of a much broader and complex machine built on top.</strong> What these platforms offer now - content curation, algorithmically-determined connections, trends, monetisation - <strong>is far beyond just hosting.</strong>

And as they have built more complex products and offered more complex services, <strong>it makes a lot of sense to scrutinise the design.</strong>

Back to the two cases, with a bit more detail:

- <strong>KGM (the Los Angeles case) is a case about what Meta and YouTube built:</strong> infinite scroll, autoplay, variable reward loops - the deliberate unpredictability of likes and engagement, engineered to trigger certain behaviours. <strong>These are features with authors, thus decisions with accountability.</strong> The jury found their design negligent.

- <strong>New Mexico is a case about what Meta didn’t build</strong> (<a href="https://nmag.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/2023-12-05-NM-v.-Meta-et-al.-COMPLAINT-REDACTED.pdf">super interesting to read the full case here</a>)<strong>.</strong> The state attorney general ran an undercover investigation, creating a fake profile of a 13-year-old girl. She was served grooming content and connected to predators. <strong>What was missing: meaningful age verification, protective defaults, friction.</strong>

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1oOg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb54a24c3-3877-439d-9a87-de00392e572c_657x194.png" alt="">

the New Mexico Case

If we are to introduce the language of product liability doctrine: <strong>the first case spots defects of</strong> <em><strong>commission</strong></em><strong>, the latter defects of</strong> <em><strong>omission</strong></em><strong>.</strong> Some of what Meta built was harmful; some of what it chose not to build made things worse.

<strong>By looking into these items, judges went beyond Section 230</strong> and started scrutinising the design of the platforms themselves. <strong>In such a change, what’s new is also who is now part of the conversation.</strong>

If before platform accountability was a topic mostly for lawyers, regulators, and policy people, it will now involve a different crowd: <strong>product people</strong> who designed (or didn’t design) a specific feature and <strong>engineers</strong> who implemented it in a given way.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AisA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5fccc63e-28fd-4c55-8fb2-b66a0524d49d_698x617.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AisA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5fccc63e-28fd-4c55-8fb2-b66a0524d49d_698x617.png" alt=""></a>

look at how much detail the case provides about the design decisions

<strong>And therefore, product</strong> <em><strong>liability</strong></em> <strong>is the natural legal container for all of this.</strong> It asks the right questions: <em>could you have built this differently? Could you have chosen not to build it at all?</em>

But in the US, product liability, as currently defined, was built for pharmaceuticals and power tools. <strong>Applying it to algorithmic systems requires foundations the law hasn’t yet built.</strong> So, <a href="https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/does-product-liability-offer-a-route-around-section-230">they’d need:</a>

- <strong>a clear legal definition of what counts as a “product” in the digital world</strong> - social media platforms and algorithmic services are currently treated more like intangible services than goods;

- <strong>a design‑defect standard that fits software:</strong> treating features that are <em>“working as intended but foreseeably harmful”</em> as a defect that was predictable, thus avoidable;

- <strong>a causation doctrine</strong> (<em>‘this causes that’</em> type of thing) that handles systemic harm epidemiologically rather than case by case — tobacco litigation eventually developed this. This one is particularly important since, as contended by Meta too, <strong>it is quite a strong statement to say that a single platform has caused mental problems for a teenager.</strong>

- a First Amendment boundary that cleanly <strong>separates design conduct</strong> (how the platform works) <strong>from editorial expression</strong> (what content is there and how it is distributed), so platforms can’t collapse the two on appeal.

If these foundations get built, <strong>we get the tools to keep scrutinising properly how social media are designed</strong>, so that when architectural choices cause harm, they can be addressed.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LPEz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5608fc6b-8131-439f-9bcd-bd5c09ae9282_1024x1024.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LPEz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5608fc6b-8131-439f-9bcd-bd5c09ae9282_1024x1024.png" alt=""></a>

Speaking of tools, architects, and design

The importance of sound foundations is clear if we look at what Europe is already trying. <strong>With the Digital Services Act</strong> (which is not at all just about content!), <strong>the EU is, for instance, looking into prohibiting dark patterns, requiring recommender system transparency.</strong>

Therefore, for instance in December, the <strong><a href="https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_2934">Commission issued its first DSA fine: €120 million to X</a></strong>, partly for the design of its <strong>blue checkmark</strong>, a trust signal quietly turned into a paid badge anyone could buy. And days after the US verdicts, it opened a <a href="https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_723">formal investigation into</a> <strong><a href="https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_723">Snapchat</a></strong> - focusing on defaults that exposed minors to strangers and age verification that amounted to typing a birthdate.

Two legal systems, different legal instruments, but the same shared question: <em><strong>can we improve the design of these platforms?</strong></em>

And so, as in that Amsterdam museum, <strong>finally asking if we can call the architects back in to fix the building.</strong>

# Use with caution
Date: 2026-03-07 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/use-with-caution
Cite as: Use with caution by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-03-07. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/use-with-caution (CC BY 4.0)

This week Artifacts should normally not go out. Yet **[what has happened between Anthropic, OpenAI and the US Pentagon](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/886082/ai-vs-the-pentagon-killer-robots-mass-surveillance-and-red-lines) is too interesting a story to miss.**

If you already know the news, feel free to skim to the *“So, what?”* section. **If not, I tried to keep the story concise.**

In July 2025, the Pentagon awarded **two-year contracts to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and xAI** to prototype frontier AI capabilities for national security. The goal was to develop agentic workflows, intelligence analysis tools, and battlefield simulations.

Among them, Anthropic had something the others did not. **Its model Claude was the only frontier AI system cleared to run on fully classified Pentagon networks**, deployed through Palantir Technologies’ AI Platform and Amazon’s Top Secret Cloud. It had been used, reportedly, **during the operation to capture Nicolás Maduro** and, most recently, for the strikes in Iran.

All four contracts, though, included some usage safety restrictions. **This changed on January 12, 2026** when the Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued an [AI strategy memo](https://media.defense.gov/2026/Jan/12/2003855671/-1/-1/0/ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-STRATEGY-FOR-THE-DEPARTMENT-OF-WAR.PDF) declaring the Pentagon would become ‘an ‘AI-first’ warfighting force with AI agents integrated *‘from campaign planning to kill chain execution’.*

To this end, the Pentagon asked Anthropic and the others **to change the contracts** so to use AI at its full potential, with no ‘policy constraints’ decided by the AI companies. **“Any lawful use” should be allowed.**

On February 27, Hegseth reportedly gave Anthropic an **ultimatum**: accept the revised terms or lose the contract. **Anthropic rejected the offer, [citing concerns about undermining democratic values](https://www.anthropic.com/news/statement-department-of-war)**, and no intention to allow the use of AI for **mass surveillance** of American citizens and **autonomous weapons** that can kill with no human in the decision loop.

That same evening, **Sam Altman [announced](https://openai.com/index/our-agreement-with-the-department-of-war/) that OpenAI had reached a new agreement with the Pentagon**. According to Altman, the deal preserved the same red lines on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance that Anthropic had defended.

However, **the details of the contract have not been made public**, and some observers believe the new arrangement may allow broader uses than Anthropic considered acceptable.

OpenAI claims that they will be able to enforce better their constraints as the models used by the Pentagon will run on their own cloud.

Finally, **[the Pentagon has responded by designating Anthropi](https://www.anthropic.com/news/where-stand-department-war)c a “Supply-Chain Risk to National Security”** - usually reserved for foreign companies (like Chinese ones) - ordering federal agencies to stop using its products in the next 6 months. The New York Times [said](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/28/podcasts/hardfork-pentagon-anthropic-openai.html) this is *‘likely the harshest punitive action the U.S. government has taken against a major American company this century, possibly ever.’*

**Anthropic will challenge the designation**, which could greatly impact their business, while also [saying](https://www.anthropic.com/news/where-stand-department-war) they *‘have much more in common with the Department of War than we have differences.’*

> ### So, what?

This story is ultimately about **constraints**.

Not only those that AI companies want to put on the US government in the use of technologies or those put by technology regulations on the use of AI, but also, and maybe more crucially, **those baked into the design of AI technologies.**

Let’s look at the [two red lines set by Anthropic:](https://www.anthropic.com/news/statement-department-of-war)

1.  ***‘Mass domestic surveillance is incompatible with democratic values** and presents risks to fundamental liberties’.* Therefore, despite being technically *feasible* to use their AI models to analyse data on citizens, **there has to be constraints as this is overly dangerous and threatens rights.**

2.  **Fully autonomous weapons**, instead, ’*need to be deployed with proper guardrails, which don’t exist today.’* So they *could be used*, but the current safety constraints are not sufficient, **and thus it is imperative to have safeguards in place.**

These constraints are not just on the AI models but **on the blurred terminology of** ***‘any lawful use’*** adopted by the Pentagon.

In theory, this sounds straightforward. But **in the United States** - where there is still no comprehensive federal regulation of AI - **the meaning of “lawful use” is far from settled.** The boundaries are still evolving.

In practice, this means that **the law alone does not fully define the acceptable uses of AI.**

And that is precisely **where these technological constraints come in.**

Interestingly, **the Pentagon itself had tried to push back constraints** in the January memo, writing that they *‘must utilize AI models free from usage policy **constraints** that may limit **lawful** military applications.’*

This sounds like a very controversial statement depicting a contrast **where the constraints of technologies could be countering or impeding uses allowed under the law.**

Provocatively, this is exactly **the contrary of the reasons why technology regulations are often criticised:** that they impede the full use of technologies.

Usually, you see BigTech or other organisation complaining about regulation. Here, the situation is almost inverted: the Pentagon argues that **constraints embedded in the technology itself** could limit uses that the law might otherwise allow.

Or, as put more bluntly by [Hegseth](https://x.com/SecWar/status/2027507717469049070?s=20) *‘America’s warfighters will never be held hostage by ideological whims of Big Tech.’* Or from Trump:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!H0jM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F34018583-64c5-44ed-83ab-fedb69c400ef_804x1172.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!H0jM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F34018583-64c5-44ed-83ab-fedb69c400ef_804x1172.png)

At its core, this raises a fundamental question: **who ultimately controls powerful technologies?** Those who build them or those who regulate them, this time more interested in a laissez-faire regulation for unbridled use?

By setting these constraints, **AI companies are doing something subtle but important.** They are not only designing the technology itself, but also shaping the **space of possible uses**.

Interestingly, **they are designing a downstream layer of the use of AI** that sits on top of the design of technology itself.

If we have long argued that technologies are not neutral - that their design shapes their political and social effects - **this story reveals something further.**

With AI, the **design of use** **becomes almost as important as the design of the system itself.**

This is particularly true because artificial intelligence is a **general-purpose technology**. Its capabilities can be applied across a vast number of domains, **and thus the layer of how it can be used is critical.** Not all possible options are good options.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kv_i!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F661eace5-156f-4830-b074-9004d3935975_2048x2048.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kv_i!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F661eace5-156f-4830-b074-9004d3935975_2048x2048.png)

Concretely, as AI would, for instance, enable easy data analysis, **the issue is rather with what use is done of such capability:** is it to assess, say, decarbonisation metrics or rather spying on citizens through combining data?

The real question is therefore not just what AI can technically do but also **what it will be allowed to do**.

And in the absence of clear ‘lawful uses’, **those decisions increasingly fall for now to the organisations building these technologies** and in how they design what’s allowed and what’s not.

> ### **☕?**

If you want to know more about Artifacts, where it all started, or just want to connect...

# The artifacts I use for Artifacts
Date: 2026-02-25 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/the-artifacts-i-use-for-artifacts
Cite as: The artifacts I use for Artifacts by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-02-25. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/the-artifacts-i-use-for-artifacts (CC BY 4.0)

[In the last Artifacts,](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking) I argued that using LLMs to produce text **may mean skipping the thinking that makes writing worth doing.**

Yet, I’m definitely not a Luddite or sceptical of AI helping with daily tasks. It’s just that I don’t buy ‘the perfect prompt’ or other tricks with chatbots.

And so, while busy ranting against chatbots, **I was also studying AI agents:** *artifacts* that don’t just generate text on demand but can coordinate and use other tools, memory, **and - more importantly - can perform actions.**

And I started to wonder **how I could use these artifacts to write Artifacts.**

**I moved from the tasks I do every day for the newsletter:** pulling interesting articles or podcasts, storing them somewhere with labels or notes, finding moments to make sense of a lot of unshaped knowledge, but also trying to find that old article or books I read that may be relevant to a certain topic.

People working in product would say I started from the **jobs to be done.**

The more I researched, **the more I realised that [Claude Code](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/head-of-claude-code-what-happens) was the perfect orchestra director** of the different flows I was tinkering with. But let not be boring with the technicalities :)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VSEM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75e0782e-ae50-4c4f-9ffb-6513c93d9aa4_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VSEM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75e0782e-ae50-4c4f-9ffb-6513c93d9aa4_1024x1024.png)

music :)

What matters is that a few weeks in, **I found myself with something I hadn’t expected at the outset:** **a full editorial infrastructure** that autonomously gets relevant articles from multiple sources, organizes them and - **when I decide on what to write about** - supports me with the research and the refinement, tapping in everything I’ve read for the past 3 years.

All in all, I don’t think it’s an overstatement to say I got **a small team of artifacts that help me write Artifacts.**

Ah, a few important **caveats**:

- I use Claude Code, which is built for engineers, **but works just fine for other tasks as well.** A good alternative could be [Claude Cowork.](https://claude.com/blog/cowork-research-preview)

- This whole infrastructure costs **19 euro per month.**

- It’s hard to quantify how long it took, but **it’s definitely** ***easy*** **to build something like this with AI**, now.

Here’s a bit of the **story** of how it went.

> **First,** **the** **foundation**

If there’s one thing that matters with AI agents, it’s **context**. Not copy-pasting the prompt of who you are, what you do, etc., but **a more solid understanding and ‘memory’ of what you’re writing on**, how you do things, what good looks like.

So when I started thinking about how to make Claude Code useful for Artifacts, the question was simple: *where’s the best place to pull that context from?* The answer was obvious: **Artifacts itself.**

**I had Claude fetch and read every Artifacts I’d ever published** - years of writing, including the early ones still in Italian, when the newsletter was heavier on policies and regulation and lighter on technologies.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bO4H!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd6e6bd6-fde4-4ac4-b0f6-98e180027da9_1572x764.png)

**And it was quite fun to ‘talk’ with the old newsletters**, see how Artifacts has evolved and, implicitly, how I’ve evolved in writing them.

It was also the opportunity to rethink a bit how I describe this newsletter, settling on ***‘stories & ideas on the design of technology’***

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XdpJ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F10b73ba9-ef30-47dd-9ca1-ae35a05670d2_1188x640.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XdpJ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F10b73ba9-ef30-47dd-9ca1-ae35a05670d2_1188x640.png)

Claude then used all this context to fill in the `Claude.md`, **a file that loads automatically at the start of every session**, where it’s clear who you are, what you do, where things are, what’s your style etc. **Much better than the perfect prompt :)**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!r8gi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F16915354-00d4-46fc-8f0b-5fe9df7cdcea_1604x1318.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!r8gi!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F16915354-00d4-46fc-8f0b-5fe9df7cdcea_1604x1318.png)

Most developers use it to document code architecture. **I** **use it to document Artifacts and how it is written.**

**CLAUDE.md is the most important piece in this stack.** Everything else runs on top of it.

The second foundational piece is **Notion**. I’ve used it for years as a database where to automatically store all the articles, papers, podcasts, books, I read - basically, **the knowledge that has been powering Artifacts for years.**

Now, I’ve connected it to Claude (via MCP, for nerds out there), so that **whenever I’m thinking of, say, age verification, it will return to me anything I’ve came across in the past 3 years**, be it a podcast or a book highlight. Not too bad.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!h-SG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdb85fe36-462f-4cc5-bfe6-ce88597aec79_1280x720.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!h-SG!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdb85fe36-462f-4cc5-bfe6-ce88597aec79_1280x720.gif)

`Claude.md` and the Notion plug are where the full context lives: **they don’t generate content but they make my agents aware of what Artifacts is** and what I know already.

So I’m not always starting from zero, or chasing the perfect prompt :)

> **Then,** **the** **flow**

Once the infrastructure knew Artifacts, **I started using it.**

First task is getting sources. **As Artifacts is where I try to make sense of a lot of what I read, I try to read a lot.** But as the newsletter subscription counter grows, it’s not the case for time - and sometimes I struggle to catch up.

So I built an automation in n8n that **every day at 9 PM pulls articles from TechCrunch, The Verge, The Markup, and WIRED, plus whatever newsletters landed in my inbox**, then filters, clusters, and analyses them with an AI tuned to ask one question: ***what matters here for Artifacts?***

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jkFR!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff50e3e5f-c69c-4fdc-9d8a-eae47cd22bba_2226x1128.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jkFR!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff50e3e5f-c69c-4fdc-9d8a-eae47cd22bba_2226x1128.png)

The output is some **notes sent to a Notion page and in a Telegram message** on my phone. I usually read it in the evening or first thing in the morning.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bFVP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8ae940f5-1880-4c9a-ae27-c50bf97aaa1c_1166x1016.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bFVP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8ae940f5-1880-4c9a-ae27-c50bf97aaa1c_1166x1016.png)

Sometimes nothing sticks, other times one item connects to something I’ve been turning over for weeks, **and that’s when the idea of a piece begins.**

Important point: **I decide what to write about.** For now, I don’t want AI suggesting topics. **I enjoy connecting the dots myself.**

Once I pick a topic, **I open Claude Code and start looking into my Notion for pieces on the subject.** It helps me re-read, draw an outline, ditch ideas, explore new angles - building the shape of what I want to write before I actually write it.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!opUL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff2484393-58bc-49d5-876f-49c50b45fe93_1196x466.png)

**So I can draw on my notebook the mental schema** I need before writing Artifacts.

**Writing itself I keep for myself,** and I think I’ve explained at length why :)

What I have built is`/artifacts-polish`, **a skill that helps me clean language and keep it consistent with older editions,** having ‘read’ the others.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JIDD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F296a062d-7c4d-4d3b-ad49-7b1ab57ed008_1454x824.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JIDD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F296a062d-7c4d-4d3b-ad49-7b1ab57ed008_1454x824.png)

In Claude, **skills are fixed instructions on repeated tasks** - say every morning you want a recap of your emails, you built a skill that knows what to do.

Once the draft is ready, **I run this skill and it helps me go through what I’ve written with fresh eyes.**

And when I’m happy, I send it out to your inbox :)

**But it doesn’t end there.** As some of you know, I always republish on LinkedIn - with some effort to avoid the annoying flattened language of that platform. So I built another skill,`/artifacts-linkedin`, **that turns my piece into a post I’m actually happy with, based on all my previous ones.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EoV8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05387444-bfa3-4880-b29a-843a64204b12_1614x1082.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EoV8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05387444-bfa3-4880-b29a-843a64204b12_1614x1082.png)

Last but not least, **Claude, the context and the agents keep learning from the process**, so the infrastructure improves with me.

> **So, what?**

I want to be careful not to oversell it. **These artifacts don’t write Artifacts** - but they help by surfacing topics I might have missed, pulling up pieces I read months or years ago, and keeping consistency across publications.

And I built this not to have someone else writing, but **to do better some tasks and leverage more my very own work of the past years.**

So it’s not just a writing assistant but more **an AI-powered thinking and writing infrastructure**, designed around what Artifacts is and has been, and with flows for how I want to be writing and keep doing it.

The critical decisions stay with me: **picking the topic, building the argument, doing the writing.** That’s intentional, and I don’t plan on changing.

But I must say that I’m having a lot of fun in having **these artifacts that help me write Artifacts,** and I’d encourage anyone to try it out for their projects!

# Writing is thinking?
Date: 2026-02-10 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking
Cite as: Writing is thinking? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-02-10. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking (CC BY 4.0)

Don’t look away, I’m quite sure this has happened to you as well:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xA0m!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd4fc25d9-176d-4318-8662-3eead6e117c7_1200x628.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xA0m!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd4fc25d9-176d-4318-8662-3eead6e117c7_1200x628.png)

I admit too that I rarely draft work emails 100% by myself.

But let’s look at the broader picture: **we live in an era where producing a significant amount of language with meaning is more efficient and less time-consuming than ever.** You can literally get 10 pages of anything in a few minutes by asking any LLM to do so.

Yet, **this doesn’t mean we’re producing more knowledge or that the amount of meaning keeps pace with the length of the documents spit out by machines.**

Rather, **LLMs are great at producing stuff that makes sense, sounds good, and neatly organises notions**, being able to package information either in a few bullet points or uselessly long documents.

Not surprisingly, though, **the level of these texts can’t help but be average**, as LLMs are, technically but also philosophically, *‘[technologies of average](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/infinite-scroll/ai-is-homogenizing-our-thoughts) both in the quality of the writing and in the calibre of the ideas.’*

(And usually also badly written imho)

Not only creating, but also [consuming language](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/open-questions/whats-happening-to-reading) has been drastically simplified (I swear I wrote this sentence 😅): **we may be often asking an AI to help us read and summarise a document that someone else asked AI to make longer.**

Just look at newspapers apps or any reading app or even the iPhone, that now has introduced AIs to quickly give the 3 key points of anything.

I like to call this **the accordion of AI language: we keep making texts longer or shorter depending on our needs** only cause doing it is very, very easy.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uxHU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F157cbf39-ed1c-4b5d-999a-5319b785f96d_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uxHU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F157cbf39-ed1c-4b5d-999a-5319b785f96d_1024x1024.png)

we’re doing this to language

And so **producing simple, beautiful BULLSHIT is now extremely time-efficient, cheap and accessible** 🎉 Just peek at your LinkedIn feed if you need validation.

But that’s not as much of a problem.

What’s worse and deeply concerning is that **producing language has become a commodity.**

Large Language Models have made it so **easy to turn a few words of a prompt into newly created language.**

Yet, this makes us skip the complex, fascinating process through which we translate our thoughts into language, and thus words. **LLMs are our mediums.**

**And this means that language is less of a tool** - even a technology or an artefact - **through which we think and instead just a code enabling communication.**

All in all, **we can now think less to produce language.**

This comes with a few **implications**:

We’re no longer writing but rather **‘meta-writing’:** we more and more dictate to a machine *what* we need to write and maybe even *how* and in what style, **and then we delegate the act of writing or typing words to machines.**

**And so we stare at screens** while language is being produced by LLMs, skipping the process of thinking through what we aim to communicate.

This way, **writing is no longer a flow of 1st draft out, correcting it, changing, refining, but a back-and-forth exchange with a machine.** [As argued in Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44222-025-00323-4), though, *‘**Writing compels us to think** — not in the chaotic, non-linear way our minds typically wander, but **in a structured, intentional manner.’***

Yet, **the ability to iterate over and over on a text quickly**, asking an AI to ‘make it more interesting’ or ‘make it sound more natural’ or whatever non-sensical prompts, **may decrease the time we spend on and with the language that should express our thoughts.**

So we may also understand less about what we’re ‘writing’ about but also **devote less care to what we’d like to emphasize and what requires less attention**, which is one of the most critical skills of thinking and writing.

At its extreme, **I sometimes consider writing the process by which we realise that we don’t understand what we’re talking about** - and sometimes this is so important.

This goes hand in hand with two other critical skills of writing and thinking: **the ability to break down complex issues into simple words as well as the ability to write concisely**, while not compromising on the meaning of what we say.

And still on the drafting and redrafting part, **we, as writers, are less and less the first careful readers of what we produce**, as we assume that LLMs will never have typos (rightly so, actually).

Finally, allow me to be a bit romantic, but **writing** - like reading - **is [a great process of self-discovery.](https://fs.blog/writing-to-think/)** [](https://fs.blog/writing-to-think/)

As I’m writing this Artifacts, I love seeing the mental connections I make, how I bridge different things I read in the past, what a friend maybe told me - **I thoroughly enjoy the time and feeling of the whole process.**

**And I do feel [a sense of care](https://www.theatlantic.com/family/2026/02/ai-etiquette-friends/685858/)**, of being clear and readable, so that your reading is enjoyable and an interesting time. *And I’m sure it’s the same for you, when you write.*

This being said, I’m not saying the final outcome of what I will produce would necessarily be better than an LLM *(well, I hope)*, but **the process itself of writing is probably also part of why you’re reading this piece.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4QoH!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe449b185-9b95-4eb2-8823-6076bd5e8acf_2950x2446.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4QoH!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe449b185-9b95-4eb2-8823-6076bd5e8acf_2950x2446.png)

This is everything that happens before me writing an Artifacts

Indeed, I argue that we read what others write cause we’re interested not just in the content of their writing - that could be produced by LLMs - or the information conveyed, **but also in why they wrote that something, what moved them, and, simply, in getting to know what they think.**

And so that a text - and thus the language of a thinking process - can resonate and establish a new human connection.

[Leave a comment](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/writing-is-thinking/comments)

> ### **The Bookshelf**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PXcL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f516323-22b3-4f13-83d3-7103ecc32883_1080x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PXcL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f516323-22b3-4f13-83d3-7103ecc32883_1080x1080.png)

# You're breaking it
Date: 2026-01-28 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/youre-breaking-it
Cite as: You're breaking it by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-01-28. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/youre-breaking-it (CC BY 4.0)

You may have heard of the tough situation that Iran is going through right now. <strong>And probably at one point you may have stopped seeing content coming from there, at least on social media.</strong>

That’s why, far from Artifacts diving into geopolitics, the Iran situation has a technological angle to it: <strong>the Internet has been shut down.</strong>

Indeed, as protests over economic collapse and political repression swept through all, <strong>Iran’s authorities triggered one of the most severe internet blackouts in the country’s history.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SMmI!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c77f25c-c5a4-481a-acec-9b1655afe8f9_1280x720.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SMmI!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c77f25c-c5a4-481a-acec-9b1655afe8f9_1280x720.jpeg" alt="Graph from NetBlocks showing network connectivity in Iran from January 2, 2026 to January 26, 2026. The y-axis represents normalized connectivity, ranging from 0% to 100%, and the x-axis represents the dates. The green line representing Iran&#x27;s observable internet connectivity, with a sharp drop on the evening of January 8 from high levels to near zero and only a short-lasting recovery on the morning of January 24. The drop in connectivity aligns with an internet shutdown imposed by authorities during protests across the nation. The minimum and current connectivity levels are indicated as 1% and 1%, respectively. The chart has a dark background with a red horizontal arrow labeled &#x27;SHUTDOWN&#x27; indicating the period of disruption, which is ongoing." title="Graph from NetBlocks showing network connectivity in Iran from January 2, 2026 to January 26, 2026. The y-axis represents normalized connectivity, ranging from 0% to 100%, and the x-axis represents the dates. The green line representing Iran&#x27;s observable internet connectivity, with a sharp drop on the evening of January 8 from high levels to near zero and only a short-lasting recovery on the morning of January 24. The drop in connectivity aligns with an internet shutdown imposed by authorities during protests across the nation. The minimum and current connectivity levels are indicated as 1% and 1%, respectively. The chart has a dark background with a red horizontal arrow labeled &#x27;SHUTDOWN&#x27; indicating the period of disruption, which is ongoing."></a>

current status of connectivity in Iran

Starting around January 8, <strong>mobile data, broadband, and even text messaging were largely cut off,</strong> plunging a nation of more than 90 million into digital silence. <strong>Connectivity dropped to near zero,</strong> isolating families, crippling small businesses that depended on online platforms, and leaving daily life — from banking to emergency communication — fractured and precarious.

At the same time, <strong>independent reporting and social media feeds went dark,</strong> making it harder to verify what was happening on the ground and <strong>easier for the state to control the narrative of the crackdown.</strong>

What might have seemed like technical disruption is, in fact, <strong>a deliberate effort to stifle communication, suppress dissent, and limit the outside world’s view of events unfolding inside Iran.</strong>

<strong>This is not the first time Iran has pulled the plug.</strong> Over the past decade, nationwide and regional internet shutdowns have become a recurring response to moments of protest and political tension.

This blackout combines a central “kill switch” in the national backbone with multiple layers of filtering, routing changes, and physical network controls.

All international traffic runs through a small number of state-controlled providers — MCCI, Irancell, and TCI — <strong>which connect to the outside world via the government backbone.</strong>

Around the evening of January 8, routing announcements from these networks collapsed by 90–95% within minutes, as they withdrew most of their IP prefixes from the global Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) tables — the internet’s core routing system, <strong>which works like a postal service to find the best paths for data between large networks (Autonomous Systems) worldwide.</strong>

In practical terms, <strong>this meant that most URLs in Iran effectively vanished from the global map</strong>: external users could no longer reach them, while only a few tightly controlled routes remained for select institutions.

To picture it, <strong>imagine Iran’s network as a vast city:</strong> the government closes the bridges and highways to the outside world, blocks most inner streets, and leaves only a few heavily policed lanes open. <strong>The map still exists, but almost nobody can move, and the flow of information collapses.</strong>

Additional measures quickly reinforced the shutdown: <strong>VPNs, messaging apps, and streaming services were largely disabled at the border gateways,</strong> while mobile base stations were switched off, landlines disrupted, <strong>and SIM cards of activists or journalists were deactivated or throttled.</strong>

For users, this meant that <strong>most attempts to connect, communicate, or share content simply failed,</strong> leaving only a very limited, controlled connection within the country.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Cwr6!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2d144d55-6c3b-4e6b-95d9-a5c4f081b85a_1024x1024.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Cwr6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2d144d55-6c3b-4e6b-95d9-a5c4f081b85a_1024x1024.png" alt=""></a>

and so they pulled the plug

Yet, as you know, <strong>the architecture of the internet was just never meant to work this way and be controlled by a state.</strong>

By design, <strong>the internet infrastructure should rest on principles of decentralization, universality, and end-to-end connectivity:</strong> networks coordinate via protocols, not territorial authority, allowing anyone to send or receive data without relying on a central controlling entity.

<strong>States were never intended to sit at the core of this system, dictating who can or cannot communicate.</strong>

<strong>When a government shuts down large swaths of connectivity, it violates these principles,</strong> imposing control that the network’s architecture explicitly discourages.

This gap between the internet’s intended design and the way it is governed is not just a technical quirk, but <strong>a derailing of governance.</strong>

It is helpful to take <strong>two references:</strong>

- <a href="https://www.unesco.org/en/internet-universality-indicators">UNESCO’s Internet Universality framework</a> stresses that the <strong>internet should be open, accessible, and universally available:</strong> connectivity is not a privilege, but a precondition for participation in digital life.

- But also the <a href="https://contractfortheweb.org/principles/principle-2-keep-all-of-the-internet-available-all-of-the-time/">2nd principle of the Contract for the Web</a> is to <em><strong>‘Keep all of the internet available, all of the time’</strong></em>. Tim Berners Lee, that promoted it, in his latest book explicitly calls out Iran and the blocks they’ve been applying.

What is happening in Iran directly contradicts these principles. By shutting down the internet, <strong>the state is asserting control over the infrastructure itself.</strong>

<strong>It is appropriating a space that was designed to remain open and shared,</strong> turning connectivity into something conditional and revocable.

<strong>This is very different from digital sovereignty as it is often discussed.</strong> Legitimate forms of digital sovereignty aim to shape how the internet is used: enforcing laws, protecting users from illegal content, promoting local ecosystems, or reducing strategic dependencies - something that Europes is experincing a lot.

None of this requires breaking the network: <strong>Iran’s shutdown crosses a different threshold.</strong>

When a government can turn the internet on and off, <strong>the very idea of governance through code and protocol collapses</strong>. The internet stops being coordinated through shared standards and technical consensus, <strong>and becomes subject to territorial command.</strong>

<strong>This is a deformation of digital sovereignty that directly contradicts the internet’s original vision.</strong> It stops treating the infrastructure of the Internet as a common foundation, and it rather <strong>turns it in a lever of power.</strong>

Applied repeatedly, <strong>this logic breaks the Internet.</strong>

And it is how the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splinternet#:~:text=The%20splinternet%20(also%20referred%20to,religion%2C%20and%20divergent%20national%20interests.">Splinternet</a> emerges: <strong>what was meant to be a single network is broken down,</strong> with connectivity becoming conditional, access suddenly political, and interoperability erodes.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_z1Z!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1ce49df-0e21-40f0-a284-7becc6ef5008_1440x960.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_z1Z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1ce49df-0e21-40f0-a284-7becc6ef5008_1440x960.jpeg" alt=""></a>

this was a nice visual I found while reading about the splinternet

And so <strong>the internet shifts from a universal space for communication and innovation into a patchwork of controlled networks.</strong>

And with that shift, something else may be lost as well: the internet’s capacity to function as a space of openness and - at times - <strong>as a space of resistance to political oppression.</strong>

<a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/in-between">As announced in the interview with its founder,</a> <strong>Artifacts took part in the Political Tech Summit in Berlin.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MCzB!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F37821884-8676-4f4d-a28c-423197f5dcdb_707x804.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MCzB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F37821884-8676-4f4d-a28c-423197f5dcdb_707x804.jpeg" alt=""></a>

My three main takeaways:

- <strong>The market for tools that improve engagement between politics and citizens is flourishing.</strong> There are lots of interesting ideas and concepts, and already some strong products, like <a href="https://fr.qomon.com/">Qomon</a>.

- <strong>Events where researchers speak are simply better:</strong> less fluff, more solid reasoning grounded in data, with brilliant minds like <a href="https://www.favstats.eu/">Dr. Votta</a> on stage.

- <strong>People outside the industry are increasingly interested in what good technology can unlock for politics</strong> — and that’s very encouraging.

# Laying bare
Date: 2026-01-06 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/laying-bare
Cite as: Laying bare by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2026-01-06. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/laying-bare (CC BY 4.0)

If you use X (formerly Twitter), **you may have noticed an explosion of non-consensual, nudified, and sexualised deepfake images** over the past few days.

**No need to pollute this newsletter with frightening screenshots**, but you can see what I’m talking about [here](https://x.com/grok/status/2006696301325410657?s=20) or [here](https://x.com/grok/status/2005915875929382971?s=20) or even [here](https://x.com/grok/status/2007668427888918846?s=20) (targeting women and children…)

What’s different this time is not the existence of deepfakes, but a **product decision** from X. **A very debatable one.**

The platform recently rolled out a new Grok - X’s chatbot owned by xAI, still a Musk company, now also the parent of X - feature that **allows users to generate or edit images simply by mentioning or replying to @Grok.**

Grok does not return the images in a private chat: **it publishes them directly to X’s public feed**, as a post from the Grok account itself.

Predictably, some users are now asking Grok, via posts or comments, to **put people in bikinis or other sexualised poses.**

And that’s how the platform is flooded with images as bad as these (or far worse, as you can imagine)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mOcn!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff9c694fa-fe84-4f60-9d28-a25bff98799a_1410x964.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mOcn!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff9c694fa-fe84-4f60-9d28-a25bff98799a_1410x964.png)

Needless to say, Grok does not discriminate based on who owns the original picture. **Anyone can ask it to put you, or someone close to you, into a skimpy bikini.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Yet, these images should not be there.** And not (only) for any sort of ethics or responsibility, but because of what policies and regulations state.

According to X’s own guidelines, **such images should be banned from the platform.** According to Grok’s rules, **some of them should not even be generated in the first place.**

[Grok’s system prompt](https://github.com/xai-org/grok-prompts/blob/main/grok4_system_turn_prompt_v8.j2), which is public, explicitly **disallows material depicting child abuse**, while appearing noticeably looser on other forms of sexualisation involving adults. The same goes for the [acceptable use policy](https://x.ai/legal/acceptable-use-policy), updated a few days ago.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Xqqg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F62400a0a-0bb7-4fcf-9247-4409ed2512d3_1894x534.png)

On the platform side, [X’s Child Safety policy](https://help.x.com/en/rules-and-policies/child-safety) claims **“zero tolerance” toward any form of child sexual exploitation**, including synthetic media. Its [non-consensual nudity policy](https://help.x.com/en/rules-and-policies/intimate-media) **bans “explicit sexual images or videos of someone online without their consent”.** There is, however, no mention of AI-generated content. The policy was **last updated in December 2021**

At the same time, the [authenticity policy](https://blog.x.com/en_us/topics/company/2020/new-approach-to-synthetic-and-manipulated-media) - last updated in April 2025 - states that **users may not share manipulated or misleading media that could cause serious harm.**

Enforcement, however, appears weak at best. A quick scroll through X makes that clear. **X Safety has instead pointed the finger at users prompting Grok to generate these images**, promising content removal and account bans.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8esw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F70494b33-a7ba-4343-8a15-da6d9f4c657a_1204x1126.png)](https://x.com/Safety/status/2007648212421587223)

This distinction is interesting, **and we will come back to it.**

In the meantime, Elon Musk, who is probably ignoring [the paper](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf) that inspired this newsletter 😅, appears convinced that **if something bad happens, the problem lies solely with misbehaving users, not with the technology enabling them.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pCWa!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0eeb027f-5871-48c5-82f0-d818ecbd659c_455x290.png)](https://x.com/mark_k/status/2007371398386462734?s=20)

And also seems to find it fun to play around himself.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tzLA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa0068da8-b73b-4924-8b2b-63df6f786960_452x542.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tzLA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa0068da8-b73b-4924-8b2b-63df6f786960_452x542.png)

To add more fun, [Grok itself doesn’t agree with Musk](https://x.com/grok/status/2007425282966171743?s=20), sometimes [regrets](http://about%20nudifying%20minors%20with%20no%20consent) about nudifying minors with no consent, but is also saying that [these images are not real](https://x.com/grok/status/2007088168764399870?s=20) so it’s ok (?).

To be clear, AI-generated non-consensual pornography has existed [since at least 2017](https://www.vice.com/en/article/gal-gadot-fake-ai-porn/). **This is not new, and it is not Grok’s invention.**

But it is accelerating, **and very little seems to be done to meaningfully address the risks.**

To get an idea of **the emergency we’re in**, NCMEC, the US agency running the main portal for reporting suspected child exploitation, issued [a rare mid-year update to its annual report.](https://www.missingkids.org/blog/2025/spike-in-online-crimes-against-children-a-wake-up-call) Online enticement reports jumped from 292,951 last year to 518,720. **Reports involving generative AI and child sexual exploitation soared from 6,835 to 440,419.** That is a 6,344% increase.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AM7y!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff3de510d-0bde-4c0d-829b-090b1f3ee8e1_1518x390.png)

Against these figures, **facilitating the creation, and especially the distribution, of certain images looks like a questionable idea.**

Yet the **design** of this new Grok feature seems largely indifferent to these risks:

- Making Grok a simple **“hey grok put her in a bikini”** **away** lowers the effort required to engage in harmful behaviours, making them more common

- By automating not only image generation but also publication, **users’ feeds are flooded with this content**, offering visibility and, for some, inspiration.

- Finally, **enabling Grok in replies means that ill-intentioned users can target virtually anyone**, not just with words, but with AI-generated imagery. Probably not the future of AI we were promised.

**If design is how we shape technology, its uses, and its risks, this design does very little to guide users in the right direction.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E12q!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40890be9-a359-4481-90aa-5731efee59ae_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E12q!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40890be9-a359-4481-90aa-5731efee59ae_1024x1024.png)

I may have expected AI to provide a different contribution to 2026

There is also a subtle but crucial detail. Users are not generating images and then choosing to post them. **Grok posts the images itself, acting as a user.**

So when harmful content is reported, **the account being reported is Grok’s, not the user who requested it.**

**This may strip users of visible agency**, despite X Safety’s insistence that they are responsible as if they had posted the images themselves.

Someone prompting Grok to generate a sexualised image can easily **argue that the excess or vulgarity came from the model, not from the prompt.**

In other words, **if the AI enables and publishes the content, users may feel conveniently absolved.**

**This also creates an accountability headache.**

**Who is responsible when a child-nudifying image appears on X?** The user who prompted it? Grok itself, assuming a machine can be accountable? xAI, which built the model? Or X, which distributes the content?

**The answer is probably not just one actor.**

Without getting into the rabbit hole of a legal review, laws like the EU Digital Services Act and the UK Online Safety Act are fairly clear. **Once illegal content appears on a platform, X has a duty to act.** Whether the image was uploaded by a human or generated by an AI is largely irrelevant when it comes to child sexual exploitation or non-consensual sexual imagery.

There is more. Under AI regulations such as the EU AI Act, **xAI may also be asked to explain why Grok is capable of generating such content at all.**

And then there are the users. **If people are deliberately trying to make Grok misbehave, as X Safety suggests, do they bear responsibility?** Is malicious prompting not something worth pursuing?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**All of these questions stem from a single product decision and the design choices behind it.**

As the cost and ease of generating realistic sexualised deepfakes of people, including children, continue to shrink, **the way technology is shaped becomes decisive.**

**We are entering an era where anyone with a photo of anyone else can manipulate it in disturbing ways.** Even if major companies implement guardrails, open-source or local models will not always do the same.

**Also, bad actors can get images that are so realistic.** As [said by Mosseri](https://www.theverge.com/news/852124/adam-mosseri-ai-images-video-instagram), head of Instagram, “Deepfakes are getting better. Al generates photos and videos indistinguishable from captured media \[…\] **It will be more practical to fingerprint real media than fake media.”**

As tough as it may sound, **anyone could take a photo of me, you, your sister, or your friends and turn it into something sexualised and disturbingly realistic**, without the person depicted ever knowing.

This is why building safer AI matters. But just as importantly, **designing how these systems are used on platforms matters just as much.** And on that front, X currently seems to have room for improvement.

# I've got nothing to predict for 2026
Date: 2025-12-23 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/ive-got-nothing-to-predict-for-2026
Cite as: I've got nothing to predict for 2026 by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-12-23. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/ive-got-nothing-to-predict-for-2026 (CC BY 4.0)

I’ve read a saying that goes, ***“It is difficult to make predictions, especially about the future.”***

Some attribute it to Danish tradition, others to baseball legend Yogi Berra. **The internet is a weird place.**

I won’t dig further into ownership of the quote, but it’s a helpful lens for all the 2026 prediction lists you may have seen.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lAaY!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fffed5016-f867-4611-9666-31a885e59188_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lAaY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fffed5016-f867-4611-9666-31a885e59188_1024x1024.png)

what I will **NOT** do with my non prediction list :)

**I don’t want to add another list.** I’m not good at predicting, and I’d rather not use vague language I could brag about in a year if something vaguely similar happens.

**But I do have** ***questions*** **about what’s coming** - mostly based on what we’ve seen over the past few months.

So I’ve put them together below, **and I’d really like to get yours in the comments!**

I’ll try to use what you share to inspire, inform, and explore **new topics in 2026 for Artifacts!**

[Leave a comment](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/ive-got-nothing-to-predict-for-2026/comments)

> ### Artifacts has questions, not predictions

*It wasn’t easy to add and cut, but these are the questions that made it in coupled with pieces of Artifacts somehow related :)*

> **Will we find a (better) way to pay Wikipedia or newspapers when scraping them for AI?**

There is currently **no standard way to compensate Wikipedia** **or news outlets** when their content is crawled for AI training or inference, even though we know these sources are foundational to how AI systems “know” things. [Wikipedia has reported that 65% of its most expensive traffic](https://diff.wikimedia.org/2025/04/01/how-crawlers-impact-the-operations-of-the-wikimedia-projects/) comes from bots, meaning it is not only unpaid, but **actively bearing the cost of this extraction.**

[![Talking to the Internet](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NVae!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4f44359c-35ea-4960-98f7-fb6191cda01a_1024x1024.webp)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/talking-to-the-internet)

#### Talking to the Internet

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·3 November 2024[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/talking-to-the-internet)

> **Can we stop sentences like “Writing is thinking, not just putting together words”?**

Any stats around how much is synthetic content is around can’t help but being partial, **but we all now see a lot of horrible patterns of AI writing, like weird short sentences**, “this, not that”, those weird long dashes and “delve into”. [We know why it is the case](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/03/magazine/chatbot-writing-style.html), but **could we please get back to writing better?**

> **Do we really want AI for sexting or brain rots?**

AI was sold as a **tool to help tackle some of humanity’s hardest problems.** Instead, the race to adoption seems to be shrinking ambitions: [erotic chatbots](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cpd2qv58yl5o), parasocial companions, [endless content sludge](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/30/style/italian-brain-rot-ballerina-cappuccina.html). **Will we keep going down this slope?**

> **Will we get just fewer buttons on screens?**

With AI taking over computer use, [interfaces are shrinking and becoming simpler](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/no-one-click-that-button), with **most of the work happening behind the screens.** If this is the new frontier of design, one may wonder how users will keep control and dark patterns (or maybe a better word) won’t surface even more.

[![No one click that button!](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yOrL!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F19c2e0e0-0265-45e6-aa8e-8295a84de213_1024x1024.png)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/no-one-click-that-button)

#### No one click that button!

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·10 June 2025[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/no-one-click-that-button)

> **Will age verification become normal?**

Australia and UK have started already and Europe and the US are thinking of it. Despite age verification not being the silver bullet to make social media better, **maybe it will become a default when logging in?** To be seen also how much companies will want to bear this weight.

[![Shut that door](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m6O6!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8b0fb261-d34a-45a8-a95e-77fc1d7f1b3d_1024x1024.png)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/shut-that-door)

#### Shut that door

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·13 December 2025[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/shut-that-door)

> **Will we know more about how social media actually works?**

One path to making social media better is **how much we know about them**, and therefore how much we’re allowed to look into. Data access is still **far from being robust**, [regulators are going after platforms](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_2934), but the journey is still long.

[![To better understand](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oUKC!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc74a28bf-aa68-45e6-a313-d86c67e3da49_1024x1024.jpeg)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/to-better-understand)

#### To better understand

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·18 November 2025[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/to-better-understand)

> **Will we be able to make it clear what we want to see on social media ?**

It’s no mystery some users reclaim more ability to [steer what they get to see on social media](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/19/opinion/patreon-algorithms-social-media-internet.html) and some are [building platforms for better control.](https://kgi.georgetown.edu/research-and-commentary/better-feeds/) This may increase user satisfaction but **also clash with some retention practices**, which also means money. **What matters more, though?**

> **Or will it simply become cool to be off social media?**

Digital detox or [physical artifacts to use less phones are getting traction](https://www.theverge.com/column/717498/brick-phone-screen-time-apps), as well as with bans in schools. Maybe **the next cool kid** is the one who is not posting?

[![By default](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zb3S!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8c5d928c-d597-4526-b5db-3ea2051feb04_1024x1024.webp)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/by-default)

#### By default

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·5 August 2025[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/by-default)

> **Will there be more space for new up and coming tech companies?**

We’ve seen some good antitrust and competition efforts across the US, especially in regard to Google, and some good wins of the EU through the Digital Markets Act. *If* this keeps going as hoped and planned, **it’ll be easier to see new players and innovation.**

[![Multiplayer](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4HuE!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F214d02f3-8762-4cb3-9a63-d09cad4a90be_1536x1024.png)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/multiplayer)

#### Multiplayer

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·17 September 2025[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/multiplayer)

> **Will we have an “Obama moment” for AI? And ow much synthetic content will flood politics & information?**

Or, more likely, a negative one.

Will a political candidate use AI so pervasively - in messaging, targeting, persuasion - that **the risks suddenly become obvious to everyone?**

> **Are Large Language Models already not enough?**

Yann LeCun, formerly VP and Chief AI Scientist at Meta, is among the most vocal skeptics of LLMs and [is now leading race to world model AIs](https://techcrunch.com/2025/12/19/yann-lecun-confirms-his-new-world-model-startup-reportedly-seeks-5b-valuation/), that should attempt to **understand the world and can simulate cause-and-effect and what-if scenarios to predict outcomes.** He’s not alone and these model may be **the alternative to LLMs hallucinations.**

[![Breaking the chains](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tsdM!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7211e686-5f64-4f1d-89d5-c1d8ce71c1e2_1024x1058.png)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/breaking-the-chains)

#### Breaking the chains

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·11 February 2025[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/breaking-the-chains)

> ***Last but not least,*** **will the AI bubble finally blow up?**

This may come with *a few* implications.
