# Shut that door
Date: 2025-12-13 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/shut-that-door
Cite as: Shut that door by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-12-13. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/shut-that-door (CC BY 4.0)

In these days, in Australia <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/media/2025/dec/10/social-media-ban-australia-explained-banned-apps-list-guide">anyone under 16 will lose access to the usual parade of social platforms</a>: Snap, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, etc.

Little by little, <strong>those companies will start poking at their users’ identities,</strong> watching for signs like device changes, behavioural patterns, or even a stranger’s report that a kid looks a little too kid-like.

When suspicion hits, <strong>the user will be nudged toward age checks,</strong> using a selfie, an ID, or even a payment card. If they fail, they’re suspended or removed. <strong>If platforms fail, they’re fined up to A\$50 million.</strong>

The ruling comes from <a href="https://www.esafety.gov.au/">Australia’s eSafety Commissioner,</a> <strong>but it isn’t some lone regulatory outburst.</strong>

In the US, <a href="https://www.tomsguide.com/computing/online-security/online-age-verification-timeline">25 states</a> have passed a form of age verification laws, <strong>with now discussions to have a <a href="https://www.theverge.com/policy/830877/app-store-age-verification-act-pinterest-endorsement">federal regulation.</a></strong>

In the UK, the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2025/apr/24/ofcom-rules-protect-keep-children-safe-online">Online Safety Act blocks minors from platforms carrying adult or self-harm content.</a> That covers obvious material, like porn, <strong>but also less obvious cases like Bluesky.</strong>

In the EU, France and Italy are imposing checks on porn sites, and several members of the European Parliament want a <strong>minimum age of 16 for social platforms</strong>, <a href="https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20251120IPR31496/children-should-be-at-least-16-to-access-social-media-say-meps">citing mental-health concerns.</a>

After a few years of evidence of the potential risks of algorithmic-driven platforms (not only) for children, <strong>regulators are waking up.</strong>

Better later than never.

And that’s why now <strong>you may have seen a lot around age verification technologies.</strong> It is, though, a complex issue, especially from a technological perspective.

For one, <strong>there’s a difference between verification and estimation:</strong> the first tries to place someone precisely on the virtual timeline, the second just guesses whether you fall on the right side of a threshold.

Multiple methods exist, <strong>each with its own tradeoffs:</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mIU9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7432775f-1bbe-4538-a95d-b56d28990f32_804x1080.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mIU9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7432775f-1bbe-4538-a95d-b56d28990f32_804x1080.png" alt=""></a>

cool report <a href="https://cetas.turing.ac.uk/publications/age-assurance-technologies-and-online-safety">here</a>

A thriving market of third-party providers promises to help platforms comply, and somewhere down the line governments may issue digital wallets that let people prove their age more securely.

And <strong><a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/12/10-not-so-hidden-dangers-age-verification">none of the current techniques are flawless:</a></strong> <a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/12/10-not-so-hidden-dangers-age-verification"></a> from not recognising people with disabilities or belonging to minorities to not supporting who has no IDs (quite frequent in the US) to even <strong>questionable ways of storing personal and sensitive data.</strong>

To make matters worse, <strong>workarounds are popping up: i</strong>n the UK, <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/vpn-use-spike-age-verification-laws-uk/?bxid=5f43a3c889a7356e7e1b2114&amp;cndid=61968307&amp;hasha=dca445e23e26114858a48ad35040e287&amp;hashc=2107626209cd615da922d357ec59a2f4a769eeec7e75a95e874cf17f98f1a7c1&amp;esrc=MARTECH_ORDERFORM">VPN</a> usage among teens have spiked (no, kids are not all of a sudden wary of their IP secrecy) but also <strong>simply minors taking pictures of their parents on the first log-in.</strong>

All of this raises a <strong>few thorny questions.</strong>

- <strong>At what level should age checks happen?</strong> Should every platform run or buy its own system, or should the app store handle it? Or maybe the device itself? No one seems particularly eager to own the problem.

- <em>And therefore,</em> <strong>who is</strong> <em><strong>accountable</strong></em> <strong>if a children goes around the checks?</strong> Is it the social media platform or the external service used to verify the age? Or maybe the parents of the children that were not that attentive?

<strong>Still, the existence of loopholes doesn’t invalidate the purpose.</strong> Protecting minors from digital environments full of potential risks is a sensible, overdue ambition.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Yet - <strong></strong> and this is the real purpose of this Artifacts - <strong>age verification goes far beyond minors.</strong>

<strong>All users will, in one way or another, need to prove their age.</strong> But, more importantly, this should make us think of what regulators are actually trying to protect all of us from: <strong>digital spaces that are,</strong> <em><strong>by design</strong></em><strong>, likely to be risky.</strong>

In this sense, age verification is good, desirable, overdue - <strong>but also a bit of a smokescreen.</strong>

It’s a bit like preventing access to <strong>a building that may catch fire at any moment.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m6O6!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8b0fb261-d34a-45a8-a95e-77fc1d7f1b3d_1024x1024.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m6O6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8b0fb261-d34a-45a8-a95e-77fc1d7f1b3d_1024x1024.png" alt=""></a>

You can stop some people from entering, <strong>but we’re still not doing anything about the fire itself and the people who are already inside.</strong> Maybe they (we) should worry?

If a building is unsafe, we should be looking at its structure. The same is true for platforms: <strong>how do we prevent the fires that may come up?</strong>

<strong>It comes down to their design, and the risks this design carries.</strong> As simple as it sounds, <strong>digital harms stem from design decisions</strong>, namely policy choices with social consequences.

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-Cc6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3332ae2b-cf3a-492b-b3b3-1ee96837f687_1752x206.png" alt="">

<a href="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68ba1281b6406dbd18597dab/68c31612d1d0dd45ea02d046_Blueprint-on-Prosocial-Tech-Design-Governance-May-2025.pdf">go read this!</a>

As raised by Mark Scott, if minors are not safe in accessing, then <strong>maybe we should be asking a question or two about the nature of these spaces in the first place.</strong>

And this is where age verification shouldn’t distract from the deeper issue.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

What these regulatory shifts really point toward is <strong>design governance of online platforms.</strong> Not just more rules, but <strong>persuading who’s building platforms to take a step back.</strong>

This means asking very concrete questions: <strong>What incentives shape a platform’s architecture?</strong> What risks follow from those incentives? <strong>Why do those risks exist in the first place?</strong>

Maybe it’d be the moment to stop building algorithms for <strong>engagement</strong> - time spent, clicks - and think of user satisfaction. Perhaps time spent isn’t a positive signal at all, but the result of addictive design patterns.

And we could also ask more <strong>how much control users really have.</strong> How aware are they - not just minors, but everyone - of the algorithms that decide what keeps them scrolling?

Crucially, why not exploring alternatives to engagement-based recommendation models and <strong>give users more choice in what they see?</strong>

If platforms were truly providing beneficial, meaningful content, <strong>maybe we should even let minors use them more - why not?</strong> If value is what they get, why restrict access?

This is, intentionally, provocative. But it’s to underline a simple point: <strong>being in spaces where you have no control over what you see can be dangerous, regardless of your age.</strong> And of course, limited control is especially harmful for those who haven’t yet developed full awareness or confidence - which is why age verification is more than welcome.

Still, as <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/19/opinion/patreon-algorithms-social-media-internet.html">the CEO of Patreon put it,</a> <em><strong>“it is possible for algorithms to serve people instead of people serving algorithms.”</strong></em> That can happen only if we shift away from attention-based systems and towards designs that foster genuine human connection.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This would be <strong>a good start</strong> in thinking of architecture of these digital buildings.

If we followed through on that ambition, <strong>a few useful changes would kick in.</strong>

We would, for instance, <strong>start measuring signals like real user satisfaction,</strong> <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/f3a785e4-37c9-4108-b88a-0970eb6314be">trust</a> or the quality of connection created.

A system built on these principles would <strong>likely be more favourable to researchers</strong>, who could finally peek under the hood instead of guessing how these engines run.

And finally, instead of just shutting the door and keeping minors away, <strong>we’d end up constructing spaces where real literacy can happen because users have more control.</strong> With minors (and not only!) not just passive to algorithms suggesting things but actively involved in what information they consume.

To put it plainly, maybe the right way of looking at age verification is not the restriction itself but what it may hint at: <strong>access to spaces that need better design for users to be more in control and, thus, safer.</strong>

# To better understand
Date: 2025-11-18 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/to-better-understand
Cite as: To better understand by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-11-18. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/to-better-understand (CC BY 4.0)

Ok, the Mozilla Festival is **probably the coolest tech event I’ve ever been to.**

I went there with Artifacts last week (proudly wearing a **press badge**!) and spent the days bouncing between great conversations, sharp sessions on building better tech, and the general buzz of a community that **still believes technology can be good.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MFba!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F04c15402-01b7-4ec2-bb2a-78f2512b2c46_3021x2811.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MFba!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F04c15402-01b7-4ec2-bb2a-78f2512b2c46_3021x2811.jpeg)

Barcelona is amazing btw

I came home with so many notes that I knew I needed a moment to let things cool, sift through everything, and figure out what it all meant.

**This edition of Artifacts is that attempt.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!urS1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6a898627-0dbe-4e8e-9be9-6021f7b9a7f4_360x392.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!urS1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6a898627-0dbe-4e8e-9be9-6021f7b9a7f4_360x392.jpeg)

The location was just beautiful

If I had to summarise the Festival in one word, it would be: **data**.

Not a shock, maybe, but it kept surfacing in almost every conversation. F**air access to data, transparency around it, and actual ownership of it** came up again and again as the real foundations of a healthier internet, especially in an AI era powered by the very data we barely control.

That’s also the thinking behind **Mozilla’s new [Data Collective](https://datacollective.mozillafoundation.org/)**, a platform for responsible data exchange for AI training.

As E.M. Lewis-Jong, the Director, said when announcing it: *“Data is power and that power should belong to the people and organizations who are creating that data”.*

The same idea appeared in one of the most entertaining sessions, **“The Wikipedia Test”**, a game-lab by the Wikimedia Foundation that asks participants to invent policies to compensate Wikipedia for all the scraping it endures from AI companies.

(go checkout the [Wikipedia test](https://wikimediafoundation.org/news/2025/06/27/the-wikipedia-test/), it’s a fun one!)

The point is simple. **How data is shared and used isn’t a side issue.** It’s critical if we want a digital world that isn’t just extractive.

Finally, probably my favourite conversation was the **“Unlearning Data Barriers: A New Framework for Access to High-Influence Public Platform Data”**, led by Knight Georgetown Foundation and joined by Brandi Geurkink (**interview below!**), Carlos Hernández-Echevarria (Maldita.es), and LK Seiling (DSA Data Access Collaboratory).

We talked about how to secure better access to platform data, what the landscape looks like now, and why researchers and citizens still lack visibility into the places where our digital lives unfold.

We started from the [Framework](https://kgi.georgetown.edu/research-and-commentary/better-access/) developed by the Knight Georgetown Foundation, that is focused on:

- **what** data is critical to get (in yellow)

- and also **how** to develop efficient and immediate access points (in green)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qcQh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faaf04418-0257-4551-b5b6-1271d6ddd91e_1956x1214.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qcQh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faaf04418-0257-4551-b5b6-1271d6ddd91e_1956x1214.png)

The bottom line? Regulations mandating data access, like the Digital Services Act, do help, but platforms are still opposing too resistance: **the way for a fair data access is still long!**

**But we may have already gone a bit too far.**

To give you a sense of why data access, why it matters, and what we could all do with it, I’m so happy to share the conversation I’ve had with **Brandi Geurkink,** currently the Executive Director of the [Coalition for Independent Technology Research](https://independenttechresearch.org/), who is on a mission to empower researchers to better study the online world!

Good read :)

> ### **The Interview**

*For clarity and readability, the transcript has been reviewed and lightly edited.*

> ***Why data access?***

For technology to be shaped by and informed by the people who use it, **we need to be able to ask questions that reflect their experiences—and surface negative experiences.**

Data access is how we see into what people actually see. Tech companies are driven by making money, which leaves a ton out of the equation. Independent researchers and journalists - rooted in communities that are ignored and underserved - provide a critical counterweight to the industry.

**Data access levels the playing field and opens a window where companies have intentionally created a black box.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oUKC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc74a28bf-aa68-45e6-a313-d86c67e3da49_1024x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oUKC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc74a28bf-aa68-45e6-a313-d86c67e3da49_1024x1024.jpeg)

> ***And what do we get?***

**Better questions and better ideas.** Under the Digital Services Act, for example, companies have to develop mitigations for harm; **to know if those mitigations are actually working, you need the data to evaluate them.**

> ***What data should be accessed, and what would you look into?***

A solid baseline of public social media data, aligned with the new framework that sets a gold standard for public data access for researchers and journalists.

**We should know that tiny sliver of “highly disseminated public content” with disproportionate reach** - what are the most viral things people are seeing, whose viewpoints they’re coming from, and whether there are paid motivations behind them. That’s essential if we want a more informed media ecosystem.

> ***If we had unlimited platform data access, which behaviors, patterns, or features are critical to investigate right now?***

Whether user controls actually work against recommendation systems. In [my YouTube research with Mozilla](https://www.mozillafoundation.org/en/research/library/user-controls/report/nothing-changed-a-qualitative-analysis-of-youtubes-user-controls/), we built a browser extension and saw people getting recommendations that violated guidelines or simply weren’t wanted. YouTube said, “we have user controls.” We tested them. **Largely, they didn’t work.**

A concrete example: “Don’t recommend this channel” might block the main channel, but users still got flooded with near-duplicate clip channels - so they kept seeing what they’d said they didn’t want. **That’s technology not working for people.**

> ***You talked of the “Data Desert”: over 60% of independent researchers face significant barriers. What are the obstacles?***

**Platforms have deliberately killed or walled off useful tools** - CrowdTangle going away, X pricing its API at \$42,000 a month, Reddit making API access extremely difficult.

We’ve also seen legal intimidation: cease-and-desists, lawsuits, suspensions of researcher accounts. And even where regulation exists, like the DSA, platforms still deny requests or create excessive gates.

> ***You’ve said data access helps break monopoly power and conflicts of interest- and that platform data isn’t purely proprietary. Why should citizens care?***

**Because this is about how power operates.** Look at the Romanian election: research into TikTok helped explain a candidate who seemed to come out of nowhere, and whether that activity aligned with electoral rules.

Digital spaces aren’t just online battlegrounds - **they shape real-world outcomes.** If we’re blindfolded, the power sits with states and platforms.

**Researchers act as middleware** - like the long fight for government transparency - **so that citizens get a window into the mechanisms affecting their lives.**

> ***Are regulations like the Digital Services Act (that mandates data access for researchers) enough? What would you improve?***

They help, but **we need clear guidelines or best practices for what good compliance it looks like.** Right now, platforms interpret “without undue delay” however they want and **retain as much control as possible** - asking for things like your birthday or requiring a Facebook account. That doesn’t match the spirit of the law.

The DSA is why these programs exist at all, which is good, **but the point is enabling researchers to identify systemic risks and check whether platforms are actually mitigating them.**

> ***What’s your dream research project if you had unlimited data access?***

Research into **monopoly power** - especially Google’s. The discovery in current cases has shown how much we didn’t know. With proper access, independent research - particularly from economists - could push this forward in a big way.

[Leave a comment](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/to-better-understand/comments)

> ### **The Bookshelf**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AaFs!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f92a2d5-ab83-4db4-8bab-a0b6e8b67080_1080x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AaFs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f92a2d5-ab83-4db4-8bab-a0b6e8b67080_1080x1080.png)

# In between
Date: 2025-11-04 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/in-between
Cite as: In between by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-11-04. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/in-between (CC BY 4.0)

One of the reasons why Artifacts was born is to look into the people and organisations building tech products not just for consumers, but also for citizens.

**How technology can enable a better democracy and participation.**

**Which is not just digital public services,** as we discussed [with the former Head of Design of the Italian Government](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/services-that-serve), but **any artifact aimed at citizens and their public and political life.**

That’s why talking to **[Josef Lentsch](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jlentsch/)**, the CEO and Founder of the **[Political Tech Summit](https://www.politicaltech.eu),** has been so interesting.

It opened up the concept of ***“political tech”,*** how we can make it work, and what they’re already doing and will be discussing further on **23–24 January 2026 in Berlin.**

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!UM5i!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F70bcb993-d822-421c-a9bb-bd39bc44f5ce_730x178.png)

**[A lot more info on their website here!](https://www.politicaltech.eu)**

If you’d like to join, there’s a **discount code reserved for Artifacts readers!**

[Join the Political Tech Summit!](https://pretix.eu/partisan/pts26/redeem?voucher=PEF5FMBM2ARTIFACTS)

And if you want to read and know more, **you can read Josef’s own words below.**

*See you in Berlin, I hope!*

> ### The Interview

*For clarity and readability, the transcript has been reviewed and lightly edited.*

> ***What exactly is “political tech”?***

In democracies, governments and citizens each have their own technologies: GovTech digitizes public services and administration, while CivicTech empowers citizens. In between sit intermediaries - political parties, unions, associations, NGOs - operating in a distinct political sphere with its own needs. **Political tech is the specific software, data, and tools used by these organizations, reflecting that unique space.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5JQn!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fceda1135-1f05-40fd-9ba2-adfe0b749669_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5JQn!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fceda1135-1f05-40fd-9ba2-adfe0b749669_1024x1024.png)

Well, a bridge…bridging

> ***What was the spark moment behind creating the Political Tech Summit - and why now?***

It wasn’t one moment but many. Working with political organizations, we kept seeing the potential to elevate their work through technology, yet **too many relied on in‑house tools that weren’t up to the task - hurting mobilization and communications.** As someone told me,

*“there’s so much money being burned… there’s a mismatch between what’s being used in political organizations and what should be used.”*

The summit addresses this by creating a **marketplace** - of ideas, products, and services - **so people and solutions can connect and improve outcomes for politics and citizens.**

> ***What’s your elevator pitch for someone unsure whether to attend?***

We create connections where none existed and offer the only comprehensive market overview in the space. By **linking peers across political families and sectors and facilitating new business relationships**, we deliver both impact and scalability. The model works economically - we capture some of the value we create - and attendees keep returning because they see that value.

> ***So, what will one get from coming?***

**Exhibitors, partners, and vendors meet political professionals actively seeking methods, tools, and analysis**. The result is tangible adoption and new collaborations that wouldn’t happen otherwise. Most partners are returning year over year, new ones are joining, **the event has grown to two days**, and we’re building a year‑round networking platform to extend that value beyond the summit.

> ***Who should attend?***

**The primary audience is political professionals - staff, operatives, executives, department heads, and directors. Citizens are welcome too**, and they’ll find a counter‑narrative to tech dystopia: practical examples of technology improving politics by making democracy more agile, faster, and more inclusive - think AI‑assisted citizen dialogues and assemblies. **It’s also highly international, with participants from 40+ countries.**

> ***From a tech perspective, what solutions are there?***

You can get **a broad mix:** CRMs for activist and constituent data, content moderation, data analysis, monitoring of political processes, and more.

> ***What will we be talking about this year?***

There will be 3 key themes:

- **Power**: Everything about winning and governing with legitimacy - campaign tech stacks, rapid-response content, field ops, and measurement. Like voter data integration, message testing, targeting, and the workflows that turn volunteers into repeat mobilizers.

- **Protection:** Keeping institutions, campaigns, and communities safe - Trust & Safety, incident response, threat intelligence, and counter-disinformation. And so content moderation tooling, deepfake detection/labelling, and narrative monitoring across platforms.

- **Participation:** Broadening who gets heard - youth engagement, AI-assisted citizen dialogues, digital assemblies, and inclusive product design. This covers onboarding funnels that meet young people where they are (TikTok/YouTube/Discord), trust-building content, and feedback loops that convert attention into sustained participation.

> ***Top sessions to watch?***

A returning favorite is the **hands‑on masterclass on the power of newsletters** (“The Power of Newsletters: Lessons from Journalism for Political Parties in the Anti-Social Media Age”) in a small group, 15–20 people, pre‑registration required. Expect equally practical main‑stage sessions, including participation from the Parliamentary State Secretary for Digitization, Thomas Jarzombek (Federal Ministry for Digital and Transport).

> ***If someone wants old‑school “policy talk,” what won’t they find?***

You won’t find endless discussions - **sessions are capped at 45 minutes** - and you won’t see the usual suspects. Instead, you’ll see new faces and **plenty of practitioners who want to dig into how things actually work.**

> ***Magic wand for next year’s edition: what’s the one thing you’d do?***

I’d bring **all the international officers from political organizations into the same room.** Those cross‑party, cross‑country exchanges are where the energy and the potential really are.

[Join the Political Tech Summit!](https://pretix.eu/partisan/pts26/redeem?voucher=PEF5FMBM2ARTIFACTS)

# Press Command
Date: 2025-10-22 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/press-command
Cite as: Press Command by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-10-22. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/press-command (CC BY 4.0)

Over the past few days, many have claimed that AI companies are doing with chatbots what Apple did with the iPhone in 2008: turning their product into a platform where users go to access apps. **It’s a fair comparison, but also a partial and shortsighted one.**

We’re witnessing something broader. *Let’s see how.*

**I’ve argued that chatbots often miss the mark:** you have to start from scratch, paste text and images, and constantly feed them context.

That’s why I’ve been (and still am) fascinated by AI-powered browsers - like [the one OpenAI just launched](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-atlas/) - where AI lives in your tabs, next to you. **A joystick for the Internet.**

[![Out of context](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Gh4!,w_140,h_140,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F98ceaca6-72b1-47a1-b298-046b88d38f60_1536x1024.png)](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/out-of-context)

#### Out of context

[Lorenzo Ancona](https://substack.com/profile/142944754-lorenzo-ancona)·29 July 2025[Read full story](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/out-of-context)

**But we may be going beyond this already.**

A few days ago, OpenAI announced [apps for ChatGPT:](https://openai.com/index/introducing-apps-in-chatgpt/)

[\[Embedded media — view original\]](https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/2C4Cs6503gw?rel=0&autoplay=0&showinfo=0&enablejsapi=0)

From the chat, you can now, for instance:

- Book a hotel on **Booking**

- Get a personalised playlist on **Spotify**

- Turn your idea into slides with **Canva**

- *and many more to come*

Anthropic, meanwhile, launched **[“Skills,”](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/800868/anthropic-claude-skills-ai-agents#comments)** which can, for instance, generate marketing materials consistent with your brand without you repeating yourself. And, a year ago, they introduced the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**, a standard that lets chatbots interface with apps. I even used it to rebuild Artifacts’ database by telling Cursor how to reorganize my Notion!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

So yes, the direction charted by many *seems* clear: **chatbots are shifting from being endpoints of conversations with users to platforms mediating interactions with other users,** who are renting rooms on Booking, or uploading music on Spotify, or offering courses on Coursera.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IURq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97bc7d60-3a49-4de5-a618-190410dd7f69_2500x800.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IURq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97bc7d60-3a49-4de5-a618-190410dd7f69_2500x800.png)

how the shift is portrayed

**Still, that’s not the full story.**

What we’re witnessing goes beyond and is **a new layer of Internet use.**

**Yes, the “platform” analogy works economically** - chatbots fit the [OECD’s definition](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2019/05/an-introduction-to-online-platforms-and-their-role-in-the-digital-transformation_970fc377/53e5f593-en.pdf) of platforms as *“digital services that facilitate interactions between two or more distinct but interdependent sets of users who interact through the service via the Internet”.*

But they aim to be much more than just **gatekeepers or intermediaries with other users or services,** as many claimed these days.

Indeed, from a technical perspective, **they want to give a new way to use the Internet:**

- **they’re not replacing (all) existing platforms** but rather using these, like Spotify or Booking

- **by concentrating the access points into one single place**: **a chat,** which is notably easier to use than finding specific intermediaries,

- **so the chatbot is more than a platform:** **it’s a new layer of the Internet** - dependent on existing platforms, but promising to make them easier and more natural to ***use***, **not just access.**

The model looks more like this:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ddcf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa215a5ab-5457-4a01-a686-67188f4fa9dd_1920x901.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ddcf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa215a5ab-5457-4a01-a686-67188f4fa9dd_1920x901.png)

with services being used by AI

Where, yes, acting as the bridge between ends is the key but **it’s more a bridge to other existing bridges** (aka platforms) to which we’re accustomed and where we already have our accounts, preferences, information stored.

Think of it less as an access point, more as a command center, even an **[operating system.](https://stratechery.com/2025/openais-windows-play/)**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This more-than-platforms shift has **some very fascinating implications** from different angles:

**Technologically**, **the model is the product.** Great platforms have always been [great products first](https://www5.qa.hbr.org/2016/04/products-to-platforms-making-the-leap) - and here, **the product is intelligence itself.** The AI model translates your words into actions, pressing the buttons of other services for you. Complexity is hidden away; apps become silent tools working behind the curtain.

Therefore, ***from a design perspective,*** **interfaces either shrink or vanish**. Your new interface is a text box, with no time spent on getting how it works and **with the best interaction medium: plain words.**

No need to figure out how a playlist is created on an app, you’ll get it back on your clean chat interface.

Also, if I may, it’s truly striking ***from an epistemological perspective***. We could now interact with platforms as if they were people - your designer, your music geek, your travel agent - to whom we talk.

**Economically, though, things get tricky.** If chatbots centralise Internet use while drawing data and services from elsewhere, **who gets paid? And how?** **The problem echoes AI search:** chatbots depend on external services for information as much as (if not more than) the services depend on chatbots for distribution.

*How is Booking compensated when ChatGPT handles the booking? And how will OpenAI decide which platforms to privilege?*

This points to a deeper tension: **the “new layer” of chatbots still rests entirely on old stacks.** ChatGPT wants to be *the* place where users are - controlling distribution and nudging developers to build for this new gravity point.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!61X_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F330d2523-e772-4e51-bcab-e70a8acc747c_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!61X_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F330d2523-e772-4e51-bcab-e70a8acc747c_1024x1024.png)

But for all the elegance of booking a hotel or designing slides from a chat window, **ChatGPT still relies on other people’s infrastructure:** APIs, tokens, accounts, and services owned elsewhere.

In other words, the minute Booking.com (or others!) shut their doors or block access, this new operating system loses its function.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

And that raises the final question: **if chatbots become not just intermediaries but the very** ***way*** **we use other services, what will those services look like next?**

*Will they still be built and designed for humans clicking buttons - **or for AIs clicking them on our behalf?***

Fascinating times, way beyond platforms ;)

# Take IT(W) Away
Date: 2025-10-06 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/take-itw-away
Cite as: Take IT(W) Away by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-10-06. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/take-itw-away (CC BY 4.0)

**Artifacts went to the Italian Tech Week in Turin** - and will definitely go again. :)

**It’s a surprisingly well-balanced event:** the right number of people, the right mix of big names and niche players, a broad and interesting set of topics, and a crowd that neatly spans **startups, VCs, Big Tech, institutions, and media.**

Finally, a genuinely **international gathering** - not just in its lineup of speakers, but in its audience too. **People actually flew in from other countries.** Maybe that’s why the mood was so upbeat.

**There’s a growing sense that Europe might finally be finding its own rhythm in tech.**

I took notes on a few sharp ideas shared both on stage and in side chats - **here’s what stuck with me:**

(And yes, **it was great to meet people from the Artifacts community there!** Let’s do this more often.)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RN2k!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0a603f66-5a5a-49f1-b1d2-149735db068c_1536x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RN2k!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0a603f66-5a5a-49f1-b1d2-149735db068c_1536x1024.png)

> ***First of all,*** **AI is becoming a basic service - like electricity or cloud.**

[Laura Modiano](https://www.linkedin.com/in/laura-modiano/?originalSubdomain=uk), Head of Startups EMEA at OpenAI, said it bluntly: **they’re already powering the next generation of European startups**, like Granola. These companies are building directly on AI, not just with it.

So AI is unleashing a a fractal of applications:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ClYx!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1f0ad299-790a-485f-9738-83f7ea1be234_3024x1646.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ClYx!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1f0ad299-790a-485f-9738-83f7ea1be234_3024x1646.jpeg)

> ***But also,*** **AI is the baby of technologies, yet it’s already teaching its parents.**

AI is also the last wave of technologies, built on cloud, data, semiconductors, and systems - **but it’s also reshaping how those technologies are designed and used.**

Think of data: we’re now able to “speak” with a database through AI. Or SaaS, that are moving faster with AI.

> ***But no,*** **engineers aren’t going anywhere.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G7Cz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe75597f8-3d53-43da-af1c-b7627c47be8d_3024x2274.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G7Cz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe75597f8-3d53-43da-af1c-b7627c47be8d_3024x2274.jpeg)

As super well explained by [Ravi Mehta](https://open.substack.com/users/9223401-ravi-mehta?utm_source=mentions) [here](https://blog.ravi-mehta.com/p/building-ai-products?hide_intro_popup=true), future is less reinventing the wheel and more **embedding AI intelligently within existing systems to solve real customers / citizens problems.**

And this is what forward deployed engineers will bring!

> ***Then,*** **Italian startups are…too Italian**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!j7hG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe9e2dddf-90a8-4486-8893-9113142ed60d_2880x1325.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!j7hG!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe9e2dddf-90a8-4486-8893-9113142ed60d_2880x1325.png)

**This comes with some critical issues:** market size is very limited while it should be (at least) the whole Europe, non-italian talents don’t come build / found in Italy, fundings as well are too reliant on a small ecosystem.

[![No alternative text description for this image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3Kb3!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F216673f4-c9b0-4b38-8f84-992a85d3d1e7_1920x960.jpeg "No alternative text description for this image")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3Kb3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F216673f4-c9b0-4b38-8f84-992a85d3d1e7_1920x960.jpeg)

> ***But that’s why*** **Italy may be the poster child for EU INC**

**Startups that think European from day one** - in product, team, and capital - **will move faster.** That’s true for early-stage ecosystems like Italy’s, but also for more mature ones across the continent.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kwBC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F907ce21b-e63d-44e5-b7b0-1c8d64c0d1eb_768x634.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kwBC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F907ce21b-e63d-44e5-b7b0-1c8d64c0d1eb_768x634.jpeg)

> ***Also because,*** **building and scaling in Europe makes it easier to scale in other countries**

As signalled by Sequoia and OpenAI, winning and tackling the complexity of 27 markets and 24 languages (before we get to EU INC and the 28th regime) is tough, **but it trains startups that make it to then go and conquer other markets with ease.**

> ***Yet, for this to happen,*** **institutions need to drive and lead innovation - top-down, even.**

A recurring theme was **how far institutions still are from driving real innovation**, despite Ursula von der Leyen’s presence.

Public leadership matters. Governments and the EU can (and should) set the tone, supporting those already trying to build in Europe. A great panel on this point had local institutions debating how to bridge that gap, moderated by [Virginia](https://open.substack.com/users/151607-virginia?utm_source=mentions) !

> ***On top of this,*** **innovation** ***in*** **and** ***from*** **the public sector is what makes governments more agile and the tech ecosystem quicker in thriving**

Probably my favorite panel had [Leonardo Quattrucci](https://open.substack.com/users/194414315-leonardo-quattrucci?utm_source=mentions) in conversation with **Diego Piacentini** (ex Apple & Amazon, and then leading GovTech for the 🇮🇹 Government) reminding that we need more tech-savvy people in government (maybe more than lawyers 😅).

And he dropped the line of the week: ***“A politician who doesn’t care about the outcome of their policies is like a CEO who doesn’t care about the outcome of their product.”***

> ***Especially if*** **complexity is preventing businesses from scaling.**

As found by FutureProofSociety and shared by [Alessandro Tommasi](https://open.substack.com/users/36549296-alessandro-tommasi?utm_source=mentions), over 80% of businesses have missed out on growth opportunities due to excessive bureaucracy, one in three spend more than €30,000 a year on burocratic compliance, and on average, entrepreneurs dedicate seven hours a week to it. **Time to move ahead!**

> ***And finally,*** **the world is divided in scientists and artists, and we need both!**

A friend told me this - great quote :)

# Multiplayer
Date: 2025-09-17 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/multiplayer
Cite as: Multiplayer by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-09-17. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/multiplayer (CC BY 4.0)

***“Google is a monopolist,** and it has acted as one to maintain its monopoly\[…\]in general search services and search text advertising **through a web of anticompetitive practices**”,* [wrote Judge Amit Mehta back in August 2024](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/05/technology/google-antitrust-ruling.html). That line set the tone for what was supposed to be the biggest antitrust reckoning in tech since Microsoft in the 90s.

And so it started the evaluation of some **remedies** proposed by the U.S. Department of Justice, that [we covered extensively in Artifacts](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/pulling-linchpins) last year.

They included what may read like a Silicon Valley nightmare: **force Google to sell Chrome, tear up its default search deal with Apple, maybe even split off Android.**

This could’ve been HUGE. **But it wasn’t, eventually.**

A couple of days ago, the **Judge Mehta published a 223-page case with all the remedies significantly watered down:**

- **No Chrome sale.** According to Mehta, breaking it off wouldn’t restore competition, and in any case it wouldn’t feel “natural.” **Alphabet keeps its browser**, which happens to be the gateway for 7 out of 10 internet users (with Google as the default search engine)

- **No end to default search deals.** Apple will keep cashing Google’s checks (20 billion dollars a year, for the record) and Google will keep getting all that iPhone traffic.

- The one real concession: **Google must share parts of its search index data** with rivals like DuckDuckGo, Yahoo, OpenAI, and Perplexity.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**But really, the reason things didn’t go further is external**. There’s a new elephant in the room - two letters: **AI.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KCnl!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F923619e7-3511-4671-8fe9-b5b4de6e4989_1290x652.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KCnl!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F923619e7-3511-4671-8fe9-b5b4de6e4989_1290x652.png)

Yep, we read the 223-page doc, **[and you find it highlighted here!](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1OxJZsRuomagGP3rEkAVYRvPdHuLzdHpk/view?usp=sharing)**

Mehta put it clearly: this case started in a different (search) world: **back when “search” meant typing words into a box and getting ten blue links.**

**Today, AI has scrambled the field.** The remedies that made sense in 2020 would be useless in 2025. **You don’t fix yesterday’s monopoly if tomorrow’s competition looks completely different.**

And therefore,

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!B5cc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffc164cb4-a5d2-4611-b6ae-e6d543670fbc_1272x386.png)

You need “**humility”** as you cannot **“gaze into a crystal ball”.**

And as the issues you’re dealing with changed in a direction you cannot forecast, **the remedies need to change as well.**

Here’s the real takeaway: **one of tech’s landmark antitrust cases ended, not with fireworks, but because AI stepped onto the field.** Suddenly, the competition is between a whole new cast of players.

**And if we’re to give AI search a shot,** as I wrote back in November 2024 😇, *[“Piecemeal solutions won’t be enough.](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/talking-to-the-internet) **[Structural remedies are needed.”](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/talking-to-the-internet)***

------------------------------------------------------------------------

That’s why the meaty remedies - Chrome, Android, Apple deals - vanished. **The only thing left standing is data sharing**, a bet that competition in the AI search era won’t be about who has the best lawyers or the biggest checks to Apple, **but who has the fuel to train models.**

***What data?*** Google will need to share **parts of its search index, the corpus of web pages and information that feeds its results page.** But this does not include other data associated with those results, including information about the quality of web pages.

***Why data?*** Because it might finally level the field. Smaller rivals like Perplexity or DuckDuckGo have the smarts but not the raw material. Without access to a real index of the web, they’ll never catch up to Google’s decades of crawling and ranking. **With some extra fuel, they just might.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4HuE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F214d02f3-8762-4cb3-9a63-d09cad4a90be_1536x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4HuE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F214d02f3-8762-4cb3-9a63-d09cad4a90be_1536x1024.png)

yeah okay data may not be like fuel cause they are potentially endless but you get it.

The DOJ put it bluntly: a newcomer can probably build a search system that answers 80% of queries in the short run. **It’s the remaining 20%** - the weird, hyper-specific, often forgotten corners of the internet - **that Google has locked down.**

**Sharing data is supposed to fill that gap.** Maybe.

This way, the competition should shift from who has, inevitably, the best data (Google) to **who’s best at AI.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LxNk!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe905a94f-a8be-4528-8d78-00bb686142f9_1248x870.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LxNk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe905a94f-a8be-4528-8d78-00bb686142f9_1248x870.png)

as claimed by Eddy Cue, VP at Apple

The playing field hasn’t changed much - **it’s still about who can pull quality search data and deliver it to users.** The pros call this the ***“ecosystem of information retrieval.”*** Now, though, there’s a new player you can’t ignore.

For AI to succeed at parsing, ingesting, and refactoring information, **it needs more than just smarter algorithms.**

If AI is ever going to become a normal part of how information gets distributed, **it has to reach a level where it can actually compete.**

**All of this is through data**, and a remedy that acknowledges that, regardless of AI potential, its **adoption** will make it a thing, for real.

And that’s where antitrust comes in: **it’s less about fixing the past than making sure tomorrow is open** - whatever it ends up looking like.

Will sharing data be enough to make information retrieval different? *Too soon to say.*

# By default
Date: 2025-08-05 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/by-default
Cite as: By default by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-08-05. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/by-default (CC BY 4.0)

I’m generally convinced that **the phone is, by default, an integral part of our lives.** In two ways.

First, **we check or use it as the first thing when we take our attention away** from work, study, or even writing a newsletter. We literally *default* to it.

Second, **it’s a default element of daily life** - so obvious, like house keys or a wallet.

There’s nothing inherently wrong with this. It’s just a fact, but **one I think is worth reflecting on.**

Summer, vacations, and holidays are probably the right time to do that.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zb3S!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8c5d928c-d597-4526-b5db-3ea2051feb04_1024x1024.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zb3S!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8c5d928c-d597-4526-b5db-3ea2051feb04_1024x1024.webp)

Sometimes the phone can become the emergency button

Through what some call a **“digital detox”** - a period where you limit this default, distance yourself from your phone, understand this constant interactive relationship, and maybe give it a new shape.

I actually did this 2 years ago, [and wrote about it.](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/una-settimana-senza-algoritmi)

(Fun fact: the name “Artifacts” actually came to me during those detox days.)

So, today in Artifacts, a few tips and techniques for building your own digital detox. Which, really, is just how I imagined mine!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The core idea is that of **“Digital Minimalism”** proposed by Cal Newport: A philosophy of technology use where we focus our online time on a small number of truly important activities, and are **happy to miss out on everything else.**

A few ground rules for how I thought about the Artifacts digital detox: ￼

- **No total phone ban**. It would be too easy to just leave it at home, but that would simulate an unrepeatable condition - so not very useful or replicable. **The phone stays in your pocket or next to you, but you use it more consciously.**

- **Not just a social media detox.** Sure, without social media the phone is basically a brick, but the idea is also to change how you use it and your habits - like using it as soon as you wake up or checking it at a stoplight (yes, I’m back in Rome).

These are very general suggestions - everyone can adapt them as they like.

**The goals I see**, and that I personally set for myself:

- **Better understand** my use of and relationship with my phone.

- **Eliminate or minimize external inputs** - especially those physically distant from me (in other words, notifications).

- Develop a **proactive approach to phone use,** not a reactive one. I want to be the one who decides when to use it, not just react to it.

- **Build new defaults, new habits.** It’s not enough to just create empty spaces where you don’t use your phone - you have to figure out how to use that time. **Even if it’s just doing nothing, but doing it consciously.**

With the ground rules and goals clear, let’s get concrete: how do you actually do this digital detox?￼

***Before you start***

- **Step 1 – Initial assessment: Which part of your screen time feels toxic?** For me, it’s the habit of opening Twitter or LinkedIn almost unconsciously and constantly checking notifications.

- **Step 2 – Define your goal: Ask yourself what the purpose of your detox is - and also of your vacation**. To relax? To have new experiences? To spend time together? To escape routine? In other words, what do you really want to do with your time? **Write down your goal, take a photo, and set it as your lock screen image** so you’re reminded every time you instinctively pick up your phone.

- **Step 3 – Have a plan:** Create a realistic plan to minimize the negative behaviors you identified.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

***10 + 1 Tips, Tricks, and Ideas ￼***

1.  Each time you’re tempted to reach for your phone, ask: ***“What else could I do instead?”.***

2.  **Prepare alternatives** - books, aimless walks, a Rubik’s cube, anything else you can turn your attention to.

3.  **Embrace solitude** — reduce the inputs coming at you, and as Cal Newport puts it, be happy about what you’re “missing out” on.

4.  **Get over yourself - don’t take yourself too seriously.** Most of the time, it’s unlikely that someone needs to reach you for something truly urgent or essential.

5.  **Create no-phone zones:** For example, no phone at the table, before bed, or right after waking up. Keep it physically distant.

6.  **Rethink your habits:** If you’re traveling, ask locals where to eat or download offline maps so you can keep your phone in airplane mode. The goal is to limit how often you pick up your phone.

7.  **Make it a game:** If you’re with friends or a partner, get them involved and set up fun penalties - like buying ice cream for the group if someone fails. If you can’t stick to the detox, at least you eat well.

8.  **Schedule screen time:** If we usually schedule work or study and then fill the gaps with our phones, try saying, “10 minutes to check my phone at lunch, and another 10 at dinner.”

9.  **Reorganize your apps:** Only keep the essential ones on your home screen so you’re not tempted by the others.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y3As!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff9d5f6dd-6afc-4222-a1aa-fd9f6c58bbc2_1920x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y3As!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff9d5f6dd-6afc-4222-a1aa-fd9f6c58bbc2_1920x1080.png)

like this!

10. **Let the sunset be a sunset.** It’ll still happen even if you don’t photograph it. Not every beautiful thing needs to be documented to be real.

11. **Only Human Intelligence. This one’s personal: I’m aiming to go AI-free for a bit.** I’ve realized how deeply I rely on it - and I want to see what life feels like with just my own brain for company, like it’s 2019 again.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

*And then what?*

I think it’s helpful to **keep track of your feelings and thoughts during these days** away from your phone’s default routines. Of course, it’s best to jot them down on paper.

And at the end, **maybe write down what you’ve realized**, what you’ve learned, and - if there’s anything - what you’d like to improve after your digital detox.

Because yes, the phone is the default, it’s essential, and it’s incredibly useful. But **maybe we all have a little something we could tweak.**

# Out of context
Date: 2025-07-29 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/out-of-context
Cite as: Out of context by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-07-29. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/out-of-context (CC BY 4.0)

<strong>I’ve been testing what the future of browsing the internet might look like</strong> - why LLMs alone aren’t enough, and why something better, built on top of the Internet, isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds.

It’s been a fascinating journey. <strong>Here are my first takeaways.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The big problem with large language models - and chatbots, their most popular use - is simple: <strong>they lack context.</strong>

<strong>Every time you start a task, you have to explain everything from scratch.</strong> What you’re doing, why, what you’ve already done. You end up copy-pasting fragments and <strong>repeating yourself just to get the chatbot to perform reasonably well.</strong>

A lot of the good results you might get depend less on the model and more on you - <strong>on how good you are at gathering information, giving instructions, prompting it right.</strong>

Which is why ChatGPT’s (and others) ability to (1) store long-term instructions about who you are and (2) remember things across sessions is hailed as such a big deal.

<strong>But even that’s not enough.</strong> Because what we really want is AI to <em>live inside</em> the document, slide, or code we’re working on <em>right now.</em>

Call it a companion, co-pilot, or just a helpful mate - <strong>it needs to be</strong> <em><strong>in the context</strong>,</em> not waiting on the sidelines for us to bring it up to speed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

And where does that context live, most of the time? <strong>In our browser.</strong>

Whether it’s Chrome, Safari, or something more niche, our tabs contain the bulk of what we’re doing. <strong>In many ways, the browser has become the operating system of our digital lives.</strong>

That’s why <strong>it makes so much sense for AI to be baked into our browsers</strong> - not as another tab, but <em>within</em> the flow of everything else

AI should sit <em>next to</em> whatever we’re doing. Reading what we’re reading. Seeing what we’re seeing. <strong>Getting the context</strong>, without having to be spoon-fed.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VKxL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9e4bfbb6-e93c-4133-95f6-2118b4aaa722_2928x1640.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VKxL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9e4bfbb6-e93c-4133-95f6-2118b4aaa722_2928x1640.png" alt=""></a>

this is from Dia!

This has one immediate implication: <strong>the ChatGPT-style interface is already outdated.</strong>

What we’re moving toward is AI not as a standalone tool, but as a <em><strong>normal technology</strong></em> - integrated into the technologies we already use. <strong>The browser, this time, is front and center.</strong>

And it’s about time. Browsers haven’t changed much in the past 15 years. Sure, Chrome is slicker than Internet Explorer - but functionally, they’re not that different.

As browsers evolve into full-fledged operating systems for our online lives, <strong>AI becomes the joystick we use to play with them.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Gh4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F98ceaca6-72b1-47a1-b298-046b88d38f60_1536x1024.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Gh4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F98ceaca6-72b1-47a1-b298-046b88d38f60_1536x1024.png" alt=""></a>

such an old-style one

Or, to quote the genius tagline from The Browser Company: <strong>“You’ll never explain yourself again.”</strong> (Also, you’ll get amazing branzinos.)

<a href="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/YVOw0TAO9ok?rel=0&amp;autoplay=0&amp;showinfo=0&amp;enablejsapi=0">\[Embedded media — view original\]</a>

<strong>This isn’t speculation: the industry is already headed there.</strong>

Over the past month, I’ve been testing two AI-powered browsers. One is <strong>Dia</strong>, from The Browser Company (yes, the folks behind Arc). The other is <strong>Comet</strong>, by Perplexity - the AI company Artifacts readers should already know well.

What I’ve seen is madness.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Mj7F!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5f6b3f7c-2e71-4cc2-868b-ac3ddee2c7e7_1920x1080.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Mj7F!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5f6b3f7c-2e71-4cc2-868b-ac3ddee2c7e7_1920x1080.png" alt=""></a>

Both share a powerful new feature: <strong>you can</strong> <em><strong>chat with your tabs</strong></em><strong>.</strong> And the chat sits right next to what you’re doing.

But it’s not just a UI gimmick with a dumb chatbot bolted on. <strong>These chats can</strong> <em><strong>see</strong></em> <strong>what you’re doing</strong> - so when you ask something, there’s no need to explain: “I’m writing this thing for this reason…” They already know.

Watching a YouTube video? <strong>You can chat with it.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y-Bb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa10a5a52-0b6d-491b-838b-770812ad3f2e_800x514.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y-Bb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa10a5a52-0b6d-491b-838b-770812ad3f2e_800x514.gif" alt=""></a>

this is so good

Planning a holiday across multiple tabs? <strong>These browsers can compare destinations for you.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VHoQ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0a30ce34-791b-403b-8f33-9444bfc39e05_800x450.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VHoQ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0a30ce34-791b-403b-8f33-9444bfc39e05_800x450.gif" alt=""></a>

<strong>Still working?</strong> Tag the document you’re editing, ask to review against a few articles you’re reading, and draft an email to ask for clarification.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ET2C!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0e0a8e2c-bdcb-4d97-aa41-d7e2dadb87ff_2514x1598.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ET2C!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0e0a8e2c-bdcb-4d97-aa41-d7e2dadb87ff_2514x1598.png" alt=""></a>

<strong>All of this removes the usual back-and-forth with ChatGPT.</strong> No more copy-pasting. No need to pick a model - because honestly, for low-intensity tasks like drafting messages, any LLM will do.

So you just care about technology solving your problems, <strong>less about the</strong> <em><strong>how.</strong></em>

Ah, Comet doesn’t just <em>read</em> what you’re doing - <strong>it can</strong> <em><strong>take action for you:</strong></em>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nqVz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8be9566e-9a1d-46f0-845a-78b1aa751b4e_600x338.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nqVz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8be9566e-9a1d-46f0-845a-78b1aa751b4e_600x338.gif" alt=""></a>

I don’t have a favourite yet. But here’s what I know so far:

<a href="https://x.com/lorenzo_ancona/status/1947020603166204326"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oI6i!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4beeee1f-9250-42fd-8ba9-832690742859_1080x382.png" alt=""></a>

check it out <a href="https://x.com/lorenzo_ancona/status/1947020603166204326">here</a>

What these browsers are doing is refreshingly simple: <strong>they make AI feel normal.</strong> Not magic. Not hype. Just useful.

The browser still looks like a browser - <strong>but now AI sits quietly on the side, ready when you need it.</strong> No dramatic reinvention or steep learning curve. <strong>Just a new layer of capability built into the place you already live online.</strong>

And honestly, that’s where AI belongs. <strong>In the flow of your everyday browsing,</strong> enhancing what you’re already doing - without making you start from zero every time.

<strong>No context-switching.</strong> Not for us, and not for our tools.

# Paying for it
Date: 2025-06-25 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/paying-for-it
Cite as: Paying for it by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-06-25. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/paying-for-it (CC BY 4.0)

I've been thinking of this piece for quite a while.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NKy1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcfeb3b90-af7f-4eb0-8a3f-51fe7e0708df_800x1422.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NKy1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcfeb3b90-af7f-4eb0-8a3f-51fe7e0708df_800x1422.gif)

And on a flight, with a great LLM local model to brainstorm with, I finally put it together

**We’re all struggling with attention:** we turn off notifications, put phone away, try pomodoro technique. **Cause we don't want to be distracted.**

At the same time, we turn off notifications, put our phones away, and seek out isolation to temporarily escape our daily worries and concerns. **To stop being attentive to everything**, to get distracted, eventually.

**And yet, we’re told we live in a non-attentive era.** An age of dwindling focus, of jump cuts and doomscrolls. [Some data claims so.](https://magazine.columbia.edu/article/cant-concentrate-heres-how-focus-digital-age#:~:text=People%20have%20gradually%20spent%20more%20and%20more,focus%20because%20it%20provides%20infinite%20external%20distractions.&text=So%20even%20if%20we%20turn%20off%20audio,check%20social%20media%20is%20difficult%20to%20ignore.)

I agree. **But also, I don’t.**

**What if we’re actually the most attentive era in history?** What if our problem isn’t that we lack attention, but that we’re incapable of doing nothing at all?

We don’t sit still anymore. We don’t zone out. **We fill every idle moment.** Not necessarily with meaningful things, but certainly with something. And isn’t that a kind of attention?

Here’s the kicker: **attention and distraction aren’t opposites.**

**Think of attention as a state** - a focused, intentional effort to direct your mind. It’s a posture, a discipline. **Distraction, by contrast, is a motion.** It’s what happens when attention moves elsewhere, often against our will, hijacked by push alerts, autoplay, or curiosity about whether your football team is, in fact, winning.

**Take doomscrolling. It feels like distraction, but it’s actually a kind of feral attentiveness.** You’re absorbed. Focused, even. Just not on anything that nourishes you. We’ve confused being directed with being distracted.

So maybe we're diverting our attention away from work, **but we're succeeding on focusing on something else.**

And this is probably something brought to us by the internet and phones. They make us, potentially, always available. And, therefore, **potentially attentive to something else than the current status quo.**

It's getting harder to lie down on a park and focus just on a book.

**One may wonder what were we doing before phones?** [Probably nothing.](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2023/07/before-smartphones-boredom/674631/)

**Now, every place - even what used to be a non-place - can be a place for some attention**, often limited, in bits, but still attention to some input

Queue to board a flight? You scroll. Waiting for the metro? Let's check email. Your partner went to the bathroom at a restaurant? Let me check if my football team is winning the game.

**(Maybe we just can't wait for someone / something?)**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**So yes, we’ve developed a new kind of attention** - one attuned to a specific kind of information:

- **We attend to bits.** Tiny fragments. Reels, tweets, thumbnails. Things with no context, no follow-up. Easy in, easy out.

- **We attend to ephemera.** If you blink, it’s gone. That TikTok won’t show up again, even if you want it to.

- **And we attend to what the algorithm serves**, not what we sought out. It’s attention without agency.

**Technically, we’re getting what we want.** Statistically, at least. But [as Harry Frankfurt](https://mbird.com/week-in-review/feb-22-28/) put it: **getting what we want, not what we want to want** - perhaps the unofficial motto of digital life.

So yes, we’re attentive. Constantly. And distracted. Constantly. Because the medium of our attention - the phone - is engineered to reward impulsive urges, not reflective desires. **We say we want to read. But we scroll.**

**Some have said we’ve closed the [Gutenberg parenthesis](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2023/aug/02/the-gutenberg-parenthesis-the-age-of-print-and-its-lessons-for-the-age-of-the-internet-by-jeff-jarvis-review)** - that stretch of history dominated by print - and stepped back into an oral era. Others, with less subtlety, call it the Zuckerberg era.

The first was a time of books, or at least of things that stayed still long enough to be read - even if printed on a screen. The second, the one we’re in now, is softer around the edges. **It’s oral not in the sense of conversation, but in the way content is absorbed:** listened to, watched, passively consumed. It demands less from us. Less effort. Less attention. Just eyes and ears.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v9GL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F863c7200-309a-42d6-b7c9-9b971944884e_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v9GL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F863c7200-309a-42d6-b7c9-9b971944884e_1024x1024.png)

you know the ‘do not disturb’?

**And yet, one artifact resists: the book.**

**Books don’t come to you.** They don’t notify, nudge, or suggest. They just sit there. Silent. Flat. Dead weight, literally and metaphorically, until you crack them open.

**Books ask something rare: undivided attention.** Not to skim, not to swipe, but to read - line by line, and between them too. **No curation, no autoplay, no “you might also like.”** Just your choice, and your risk: to engage or not.

**If you think of them as an interface, it's one that is not replying back.** It's there, dead. No input if we don't choose to do so or get one. In that sense, **books are less like social media and more like a chatbot.**

And so they sit. Closed, mute, overlooked (sometimes). **Still requiring attention in an era of distracted attention.**
