# No one click that button!
Date: 2025-06-10 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/no-one-click-that-button
Cite as: No one click that button! by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-06-10. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/no-one-click-that-button (CC BY 4.0)

This may soon be outdated:

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZlVN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F219b9bef-85a1-4da1-9d80-ff5463a98751_1920x1080.png" alt="Some insert features in Word are greyed out, like Screenshot, - Microsoft Community" title="Some insert features in Word are greyed out, like Screenshot, - Microsoft  Community">

But it’s unlikely to be replaced by this:

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gZ7x!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F32da0cce-246d-4754-af01-89a5f3736eb4_2262x1466.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gZ7x!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F32da0cce-246d-4754-af01-89a5f3736eb4_2262x1466.png" alt=""></a>

Or at least, <strong>if AI really is the future of tools, it probably won’t arrive wearing a chatbot mask</strong> - the one that took the world by storm just a few years ago.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Let’s think through this.

<strong>Take Word, for instance.</strong> When was the last time you started a document without at least checking in with an AI for ideas, a structure, or a template? And if you <em>did</em> start solo, how long before you copied your rough draft into ChatGPT (or your LLM of choice) to get feedback, edit suggestions, or just a nudge?

<strong>So the least we can expect is to have that AI companion</strong> <em><strong>already there</strong></em>. Present not just in spirit or on another tab, but right inside the interface itself.

<strong>Now look at chatbots.</strong> The generic ones, the tab-switching kind, that require instructions for every new project. The ones that don’t know what you’re working on, what you’ve written before, or what your app even <em>does</em>. <strong>That’s not a sleek user experience.</strong>

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!85mj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff59ee897-8882-41ad-b89b-646685f42a60_220x146.gif" alt="Bad Computer GIFs | Tenor" title="Bad Computer GIFs | Tenor">

when you start the back and forth with chatbots

Word is <em>just</em> an example of this. It’s a much broader matter: <strong>how AI may shape and change interfaces.</strong>

Or, put differently, <strong>how the AI revolution may be, before anything else, an interface revolution.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Let’s pivot to a different example.

<strong>I hate pickles.</strong> I also hate figuring out how to remove them from burgers in food delivery apps.

Sometimes the customization options appear upfront. Sometimes they’re buried before checkout. Sometimes it’s a list of toggles. Sometimes it’s a freeform text box. Every app a new quest.

<strong>What if I could just</strong> <em><strong>say</strong></em> <strong>what I want?</strong> Like: <em>“No pickles. Make it rare. Also, extra crispy fries.”</em>

Natural language. No hunting around in weird menus. No decoding the logic of some designer’s idea of “flow.”

Overall, <strong>without</strong> <em><strong>discovering</strong></em> <strong>and</strong> <em><strong>understanding</strong></em> <strong>the app</strong> but just by <em>typing</em> in my own words.

In this case, <strong>AI isn’t the interface itself (like in a chatbot).</strong> <strong>It’s the medium through which I interact with the app.</strong>

<strong>I don’t need to go and click around to understand how to customise my order.</strong> And the same applies to, say, interpreting a complex data set I’ve been given to analyse or a multi-step process I need to set up for the sales strategy of my company.

<strong>Instead of translating my intentions into clicks, I use my words</strong> — and the AI translates them into actions. It’s a <strong>different paradigm</strong>.

This shift means interfaces can become <strong>simpler, less crowded</strong>, and more intuitive. <strong>We don’t need to understand</strong> <em><strong>how</strong></em> <strong>they work.</strong> We just need them to work <em>with</em> us.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HRVK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8539240f-4a60-4b61-bad2-ec2e0ff05ec7_2868x2217.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HRVK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8539240f-4a60-4b61-bad2-ec2e0ff05ec7_2868x2217.png" alt="Image" title="Image"></a>

<a href="https://x.com/felixhhaas/status/1928489808797511832">Maybe?</a>

<strong>Because not everyone necessarily cares about an interface.</strong> We care more about what it lets us do.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

You might argue: <em>“Okay, but aren’t these just AI agents? Nothing (too) new.”</em>

Not quite. <strong>Agents are the next level</strong> - the background operators that respond to context, act autonomously, send emails, book meetings. They’re backstage.

<strong>What we’re talking about here is the stage itself.</strong> The front-of-house experience. The AI-as-mediator, the one that <em>sits between you and the interface</em>, reshaping how you get things done.

<strong>In this framing, AI isn’t about unlocking new capabilities.</strong> It’s about <strong>reframing old ones</strong> — taking the exact same workflows (ordering food, writing a doc, configuring sales tools) and making them smoother.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<strong>All of this has some consequences.</strong>

Using plain language to interact with technological artifacts <strong>should be easier</strong>, and could make our lives easier.

<strong>This could mean screens that don’t just</strong> <em><strong>display</strong></em> <strong>things, but respond.</strong> Nudge. Adapt.

Like Netflix suggestions - which, let’s face it, were doing AI before it was cool. <strong>We could get screens that adapt to our needs</strong> and try accompany us towards what is inferred to be our desired outcome.

Start a doc on the history of politics? It offers a timeline template. Launch a sales plan? It reminds you of last quarter’s targets.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yr8S!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F79ca9a32-4db1-4159-ae82-30e133a84c49_800x485.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yr8S!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F79ca9a32-4db1-4159-ae82-30e133a84c49_800x485.gif" alt=""></a>

this is already something else - ah, they called it Artifacts :)

Of course, <strong>there are risks.</strong>

<strong>Where’s the line of agency?</strong> What does the AI get to do without your explicit approval? How do you <em>know</em> what it’s doing? Can you override it? <strong>Can you understand</strong> <em><strong>why</strong></em> <strong>it made the choices it made?</strong>

<strong>Not only: what control do we have over</strong> <em><strong>processes</strong></em> <strong>themselves?</strong> If the AI I’m using to co-write a document gets to weird conclusions, how can I see and steer it? Explainability is a thing, and <a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/breaking-the-chains">has already been in Artifacts !</a>

<strong>More importantly, what about failure?</strong> What if the AI can’t get rid of the pickles? Do I still have a backup way to manually fix it? <strong>Will there still be buttons for when things go sideways?</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yOrL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F19c2e0e0-0265-45e6-aa8e-8295a84de213_1024x1024.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yOrL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F19c2e0e0-0265-45e6-aa8e-8295a84de213_1024x1024.png" alt=""></a>

no please no!

And, yes, <strong>eventually voice</strong> <em><strong>might</strong></em> <strong>be the final form of this interaction,</strong> instead of text<strong>.</strong> But do we really want to work in offices where everyone is talking out loud to their computer like they’re casting spells? <em>There’ll be time to look into this in future Artifacts.</em>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

But let’s not go to some sci-fi singularity.

We may not become radically more efficient beings, <strong>but we’re likely to be</strong> <em><strong>doing things differently</strong></em><strong>.</strong>

Because the way we interface with tools is adapting to a new kind of medium - one that can understand us more directly.

It’s not the chatbot or AI that matters.

<strong>It’s what happens when the interface starts speaking our language,</strong> thanks to what is in between and mediates the relationship between us and artifacts.

📚 <strong>All the books</strong> I’ve read and recommended in Artifacts are <a href="https://airtable.com/appK7fMPX1DMkQYzL/shrRh8TgI7GtmgBxM">here.</a>

> ### <strong>Nerding</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CfyP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd2b1c49-6a18-4d92-85e8-09d8aad71f7e_1080x1080.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CfyP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd2b1c49-6a18-4d92-85e8-09d8aad71f7e_1080x1080.png" alt=""></a>

We used to design interfaces, now you can prompt them with a few words. <a href="https://www.magicpath.ai/">MagicPath</a> just launched but it’s already <strong>enabling people to create the best buttons</strong> (if we’ll keep using them) and much more.

# Open a new tab
Date: 2025-05-29 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/open-a-new-tab
Cite as: Open a new tab by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-05-29. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/open-a-new-tab (CC BY 4.0)

Searching on Google will soon be <strong>like this:</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!usGS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39a20ed5-87a7-4b15-8e46-32089b5a07d1_432x432.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!usGS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39a20ed5-87a7-4b15-8e46-32089b5a07d1_432x432.gif" alt=""></a>

Not just because the <a href="https://www.zdnet.com/article/googles-im-feeling-lucky-button-might-soon-be-replaced-by-ai-mode/">“I’m feeling lucky” button is disappearing</a>, but because <strong>Google has officially introduced <a href="https://blog.google/products/search/ai-mode-search/">something it calls “AI Mode.”</a></strong>

This means that instead of just tossing you a list of blue links, <strong>Google Search will now host a conversational AI assistant.</strong> Ask it questions, follow up with more, get crisp, synthesized responses (with small numbers referencing websites)

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Uc5z!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe7dcc66c-b226-4ecf-a084-b813c962f6e8_1920x1080.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Uc5z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe7dcc66c-b226-4ecf-a084-b813c962f6e8_1920x1080.png" alt=""></a>

Think of it less like searching the web and more like… <strong>chatting with it.</strong>

(And, well, they also rolled out a bunch of other stuff nicely wrapped up in a <a href="https://notebooklm.google.com/notebook/953b658a-579b-4b3c-b280-43b3781babf3">mind map</a> by - of course - NotebookLM, one of Google’s own AI tools.)

Now, from a technological standpoint, <strong>this isn’t exactly groundbreaking anymore.</strong> On Artifacts, we’ve been talking about AI-driven search <a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/artifactstech/p/ho-parlato-con-internet?r=2d3svm&amp;utm_campaign=post&amp;utm_medium=web&amp;showWelcomeOnShare=false">since February 2024</a>. By now, <strong>many of us are already familiar with the likes of ChatGPT or Perplexity</strong> digging through the web on our behalf.

In short: <strong>we’re used to talking to the internet.</strong>

<strong>The shift already happened</strong> - from dry, scattered link lists to tight, tailored responses. But the lingering question has been: <em><strong>what is Google waiting for?</strong></em> Now we know.

And commercially? <strong>Well, this might just be the opening scene of a new era.</strong> Here’s why:

- <strong>Google</strong>, that for most of us equals the Internet, <strong>is embracing and shaping what they called <a href="https://www.theverge.com/2024/5/14/24155321/google-search-ai-results-page-gemini-overview">“a total re-imagination of search”.</a></strong> It is, in a sense, the Internet going in a whole new direction.

- This is not just a tool enabling AI search. <strong>It’s Google baking AI into everything.</strong> Search, yes, but also Gmail, Docs, Drive. The whole productivity suite is being rewired with intelligent, conversational search assistance.

And unlike Perplexity or other AI tools, <strong>Google’s shift will be impossible to ignore.</strong> It’ll be right there, front and center, for the billions who already default to it. No tutorials needed. No effort required. Just… different.

<strong>And search is just likely to be radically something else in a couple of years.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Here’s how it works, <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2025/02/26/what-is-google-gemini-ai/">according to the people building it:</a>

> <em>When you ask a complex question, Google’s AI-powered Search kicks into “advanced reasoning” mode. It uses its custom Gemini model to break your query into smaller parts and fires off multiple searches at once.</em>
>
> <em>It digs deep across the web and taps into Google’s real-time data sources like the Knowledge Graph, Shopping Graph, and even local info from Google Maps contributors.</em>
>
> <em>Then it assembles a polished answer. All of that, from just one query - and fast.</em>

As the Verge put it, it’s <strong><a href="https://www.theverge.com/google/671200/google-googling-ai-mode-project-mariner-i-o-2025">Google doing a lot of Googling.</a></strong>

But <strong>this is bigger than search.</strong>

First off, it’s what the AI folks call <strong>agentic</strong> — yes, the new favorite jargon word you’ll need to pretend to understand at conferences. But jargon aside, the idea is simple: <strong>it doesn’t just find things</strong> <em><strong>for</strong></em> <strong>you, it does the finding, the reading, the summarizing</strong> — and hands you back the insight.

Which brings us to the bigger shift: <strong>the interface itself.</strong>

<strong>Fewer clicks. More conversation.</strong> You ask, it answers, you refine, it continues. A back-and-forth, not a click-and-hope.

<strong>It’s a new User Experience</strong> — one that’s less about hunting through links and more about getting <em>usable</em> content, right away.

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HH8x!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0760492e-5168-4904-8eef-28e6296a73bf_1440x608.png" alt="">

Indeed, people are no longer <a href="https://www.bain.com/insights/goodbye-clicks-hello-ai-zero-click-search-redefines-marketing/#">clicking</a> (+ an <a href="https://chatgpt.com/share/683768fd-5bd0-800a-8bad-2e988256df2d">explanation</a> of the chart as it’s not the clearest thing lol)

As Google puts it:

> <em>The way we’ve all Googled for two decades was largely a response to the structure of the web itself: web pages in, web pages out. <strong>Good AI models are now able to get around that structure, and find and synthesize information from lots of sources</strong></em>

Put plainly: <strong>it’s just easier.</strong> And probably irreversible.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WcTd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F14ef9519-7fa7-441d-9ad1-e6125b417c9d_1024x1024.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WcTd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F14ef9519-7fa7-441d-9ad1-e6125b417c9d_1024x1024.png" alt=""></a>

if search has to be a back and forth with AI, ping pong is the best case of back and forth for sure

All of this will, of course, <strong>not come without implications.</strong>

<strong>First casualty: the humble web page.</strong> As we’ve explored before, AI search means machines read pages, rewrite the content, and feed it back to users — <strong>without users actually visiting the source.</strong> Less traffic. Less visibility. Less ad revenue.

Websites and especially media are not happy about this. They’ve called this <a href="https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/google-ai-mode-statement/">“a definition of theft”.</a> In response, Pichai (CEO at Google) said <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1IxG7ywSNXk">they expect AI to direct even more traffic to websites.</a>

<strong>Second problem: Google’s own business model.</strong> If no one’s clicking on pages, then traditional ads - <strong>the ones that made Google \$198 billion last year</strong> - lose their audience. So now Google is playing both sides: disrupting the old model while still trying to milk it.

<strong>It’s the innovator’s dilemma:</strong> evolve or protect what’s already working. In this case, Google needs web content to train and feed its AI, and publishers need Google to reach audiences. A delicate co-dependence.

<strong>Finally, the SEO apocalypse.</strong> For two decades, websites played the game of rising to the top of Google’s results. Now, the real prize is to be included in the AI-generated answer. Buried in a citation.

That’s a whole new game - <strong>not of visibility, but of</strong> <em><strong>inclusion</strong></em><strong>.</strong> Across Google, OpenAI, Perplexity, whoever ends up writing the answers the internet reads.

What does this mean for media? Business? Education? Any site that once relied on search-driven traffic?

<strong>That’s the billion-click question.</strong>

We’ve gone from a layered, intricate Internet - Google, links, websites, ads - to <strong>a flattened experience where AI intermediates it all.</strong>

<strong>The number of interfaces is shrinking.</strong> The AI now browses for us.

Sure, <strong>talking to the internet is easier than clicking through it.</strong>

But what that means for who owns attention - and who profits from it - is still very much up for grabs.

# Slicing apples
Date: 2025-05-14 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/slicing-apples
Cite as: Slicing apples by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-05-14. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/slicing-apples (CC BY 4.0)

**You’ve probably tried to buy a Spotify Premium subscription** directly from the iPhone app at least once - and **failed**. Come on, admit it.

Or maybe you were just trying to **grab that Kindle ebook from the Amazon app, but somehow… it didn’t work.** Something felt broken. Because it was.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!DQsU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0abfaabe-0462-40ac-aa47-9f3fcade75a0_1169x2086.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!DQsU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0abfaabe-0462-40ac-aa47-9f3fcade75a0_1169x2086.jpeg)

where the hell do I get my premium?!

You probably thought: *“Is my phone broken? Is my card expired? Is capitalism collapsing under its own weight?”*

Nope. **What you’re bumping into isn’t a technical glitch or a personal failure.** It’s *App Store Policy.* Or more specifically, Apple’s cut of the pie - **a 15 to 30% commission it collects on every digital transaction made through apps on iOS** to, according to Apple, guarantee the safety and privacy of payments and users.

That’s why companies like Spotify, Amazon, and many more have found creative ways to… **not sell you things in the app.** Redirecting you, vaguely and sometimes hilariously, to “go to our website” text instead (not even buttons!)

**This isn’t a bug. It’s design.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

And, well, it’s **one of the very few things the US and Europe seem to agree on these days**. (Besides the new Pope, who, btw, is [named after AI.](https://www.theverge.com/news/664719/pope-leo-xiv-artificial-intelligence-concerns) Yes, really.)

Because while the Atlantic is as wide as ever when it comes to tech policy - and just about everything else - one thing is surprisingly settled: A**pple should stop making it that hard for people to buy stuff in apps**, and for developers to keep the money they earn without giving Apple a third of it.

Let me try to make the *competition class* as short as possible.

**In the US** 🇺🇸, Epic Games, the owner of Fortnite, has been fighting Apple in court for 5 years now. Their claim? **Apple can’t take one third of any transaction made by gamers.**

They actually won a first injunction back in the day. **But Apple managed to wriggle around it by requiring developers to apply** (yes, apply!) for permission to include external links.

And even then, **Apple forced apps to display ominous pop-ups when users tried to leave for an external website** — the kind of warnings you’d expect before launching a missile, not buying a subscription.

[![Apple's outline to show text to customers indicating that they are about use an alternative payment method](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ar2l!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd9ff109d-a518-4fe5-a19b-35c558570416_314x679.png "Apple's outline to show text to customers indicating that they are about use an alternative payment method")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ar2l!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd9ff109d-a518-4fe5-a19b-35c558570416_314x679.png)

indeed, these have been called “scare screens”

**But things will now change**, for everyone and forever (maybe)!

A few weeks ago, [Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/25924283-epic-v-apple-contempt-order/) **cannot** stop developers from including external purchase links, **cannot** interfere when users choose to go to a third-party site, and **cannot** charge fees or commissions on purchases made outside the app.

So, what? App developers can now:

- **Send US users to their own checkout experience**

- **Keep 100% of the revenue**, avoiding 15-30% app store fees (minus Stripe or whoever they use)

- **Design those flows however they want** - no Apple interference.

Apple, not surprisingly, will [appeal the decision](https://www.theverge.com/news/659310/apple-confirms-it-will-appeal-the-app-store-order).

But in the meantime, they’ve started updating the [App Store guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) to reflect this new reality.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jHqb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7dabb56a-2c4c-41b8-86b4-def006f1ab77_1427x277.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Over in Europe 🇪🇺, things work a bit differently, but with the same end goal: make the digital economy more competitive for everyone. Enter the **Digital Markets Act** (DMA) - Brussels’ big new regulation aimed at taming the giants.

Specifically, **the EU Commission aims to prevent Apple from abusing of its position**, namely by allowing developers to inform users about and steer them to alternative offers and payment methods outside the App Store, and to permit alternative app stores and payment systems on iOS.

**To comply, Apple made a few changes last year:** it actually opened up to alternative app stores, enabled third-party payment systems, and even lowered its commission from 30% to (still) 17%. [We even did a whole](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/una-mela-avvelenata) *[Artifacts](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/una-mela-avvelenata)* [about it.](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/una-mela-avvelenata)

But alongside all that, Apple quietly introduced a new twist: the **Core Technology Fee** — charging developers €0.50 for every install beyond the first million each year.

**Thus, the European Commission wasn’t convinced.** In July 2024, it launched an investigation into Apple’s compliance, focusing on restrictions that hindered developers from steering users to alternative offers and payment methods.

In plain words, **it was still too complex to get your Spotify subscription.**

Then, end of April this year, **[the Commission fined Apple](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_1085) for breaching the DMA’s anti-steering provisions.** The result? A €500 million fine and a mandate to change its practices within 60 days (with Apple filing an appeal here too).

Concretely, **this means Apple will have to:**

- **allow developers to freely inform users** about alternative offers outside the App Store,

- **direct customers to those offers,** and

- **enable purchases outside the App Store without technical or commercial barriers** (and likely remove any fee on in-app payments).

So, just like in the US, the result is a much smoother experience when, say, you want to subscribe to Spotify.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We’re looking at two very different frameworks — a US court ruling here, a sweeping EU regulation there — **and yet the end goals line up almost perfectly:** break monopolistic control, give users real choice, lower prices, and let new apps and technologies actually thrive.

How and why, eventually, tech antri-trust is (just) about changing screens, what it has meant concretely and what we got out of it, is **the story of this Artifacts.**

> ### The Story

**The shift can be captured in a few screenshots.** That’s all it takes to see how big the change is:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CrJh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F74e399a2-ebf7-44bd-87a4-33d30501aba5_1920x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CrJh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F74e399a2-ebf7-44bd-87a4-33d30501aba5_1920x1080.png)

If everything plays out as planned — and yes, for once the US seems slightly ahead - **we’re moving away from closed app ecosystems towards more open ones**, where payments are smooth, not a scavenger hunt.

Why? Because developers will finally be able to:

1.  Actually **include buttons that lead out of their apps**

2.  **Avoid giving Apple a cut of every transaction**

And this isn’t theory. **It’s already happening.**

You can now buy [Kindle books](https://techcrunch.com/2025/05/06/amazon-kindles-ios-app-adds-new-get-book-button-following-apple-payments-ruling/) directly in the app again. [Fortnite](https://fortnitetracker.com/article/2364/fortnite-is-back-on-the-app-store-epic-rewards-boosted-to-20-and-more) is back on the App Store. Creators on [Patreon](https://techcrunch.com/2025/05/06/patreons-app-can-now-accept-web-payments-after-u-s-app-store-changes/) can finally get paid without jumping through flaming hoops. **And a lot more coming in these weeks.**

[![kindleios](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9s0j!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F613b81f4-0368-4e80-910a-ba64dd5564a4_1501x991.jpeg "kindleios")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9s0j!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F613b81f4-0368-4e80-910a-ba64dd5564a4_1501x991.jpeg)

What’s fascinating about all this is how **tangible** the change is. You can *feel* it. **Like when Google removed direct map links last year in the EU** - you didn’t need to read a blog post to know something had changed. **It just…wasn’t there anymore.**

The same applies here: **no need for Apple to publish a white paper on compliance.** No need to hire lawyers to explain edge-case interpretations. If the button exists, or doesn’t, everyone can see it. **Screens don’t lie.**

Despite very different regulatory tools - injunction in the US, regulation in the EU - **the outcomes are strangely aligned.**

And that matters not only to users, but **to an entire ecosystem of services.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!99DD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe249ecde-0be6-463b-a7ee-e7ea3bd87ad4_667x1108.png)](https://x.com/AzianMike/status/1917830346332332329)

**Take third-party payment providers like Stripe.** If users can finally access external pages, apps can choose which payment flow they want. **Suddenly, there’s a market.** And in that market, these players can actually compete - by building smoother, faster, cheaper options.

This opens up the arena: **user experiences can be differentiated and tailored, and platforms decide on what is better.**

Stripes and the likes of it can focus on shipping the best stuff as the market is now open for them.

In turn, prices drop. Apple’s old 15–30% cut? Optional now. Or at least newly challenged. **The playing field has shifted, and the house doesn’t automatically win.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**These are the kinds of changes good regulation makes possible.** Not just brake-pulling or compliance theatre. Not just clunky banners, mandatory pop-ups, or checkbox ethics.

**Actual, visible improvements for smoother and better user experiences.**

**It’s really about co-creating services:** suddenly, regulation isn’t a wall - it’s a seat at the product meeting. A quiet voice saying: *“Hey, what if we got rid of this pointless hurdle that no one likes anyway?”*

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-E4F!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb993144f-aaf6-4b8e-acbd-959dbf6e4326_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-E4F!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb993144f-aaf6-4b8e-acbd-959dbf6e4326_1024x1024.png)

new chair for good regulations!

**And that opens up something new.** A more competitive market. A fairer game.

**A space where getting paid is easier, user experience is better**, and — imagine this — you don’t need a customer support team just to explain that, no, you can’t buy Netflix in the app, and yes, you’ll need to go to the website [(yep, true story)](https://www.theverge.com/the-vergecast/664087/why-apple-is-trying-to-save-google)

======
# The elephant in the tube
Date: 2025-04-23 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/the-elephant-in-the-tube
Cite as: The elephant in the tube by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-04-23. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/the-elephant-in-the-tube (CC BY 4.0)

**A little more than 20 years ago**, Jawed Karim wanted to watch videos of two events that had just dominated global headlines:

- Janet Jackson’s infamous Super Bowl “wardrobe malfunction” (2004)

- The catastrophic Indian Ocean tsunami (2004)

**But he couldn’t find either online.** Nothing. No easy clips. No shareable footage. No digital archive to feed his curiosity.

A few months later (and precisely 20 years ago), **someone else posted a short video about elephants at the zoo.** He looked into the camera and said, flatly: *“The cool thing about these guys is that they have really, really, really long trunks.”*

[\[Embedded media — view original\]](https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/jNQXAC9IVRw?rel=0&autoplay=0&showinfo=0&enablejsapi=0)

That 18-second clip wasn’t just a trip to the zoo. **It was the beginning of YouTube** and a revolution of our online life, media consumption and creation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ok, this is definitely the short version. Yet, it makes the point.

Now, to be fair, **YouTube wasn’t the first online video platform.** Others like Metacafe and Vimeo were already floating around.

But in those early days, **uploading a video online was about as straightforward as launching a weather satellite.** Clunky codecs, weird download prompts, compatibility issues - **the early internet was allergic to ease.**

That’s why Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, and Jawed Karim - ex-PayPal employees - launched YouTube around a single, deceptively simple idea: **Make it dead easy to upload and share videos.**

They caught a wave of **just-in-time technical changes:**

1.  **Adobe Flash** let videos play right in the browser — no downloads, no stress, no concern about the right codec. It just worked.

2.  **Embedding** made it possible to spread videos across forums, blogs, and MySpace profiles. Every embedded clip was another stake in the ground.

3.  **Broadband** had reached about 50% of U.S. households. And digital cameras were finally decent enough to shoot not-entirely-awful footage.

So YouTube launched, burned through money, **got acquired by Google**, and then — quietly, steadily — **rewired our entire relationship with media over the past 20 years.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**And so, people - and companies, too - began familiarising with this new platform.** But YouTube wasn’t just another tool for watching media. It was something else entirely: **a gateway to new habits, a catalyst that made it easy not only to watch videos but to create them, too.**

**It kicked off a quiet revolution** - one that changed how we consume video online, and also reshaped **our entire relationship with culture, news, and content at large.**

So much so, in fact, that the slow, then sudden overtaking of television began years ago - **and by now, it’s largely complete.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fYN0!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4b22498-d455-45d9-b2a5-256424994b31_940x1268.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fYN0!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4b22498-d455-45d9-b2a5-256424994b31_940x1268.png)

What YouTube has meant (and still means), how it’s rewired our sense of time, reprogrammed our media diet, and why it remains a singular force in the online ecosystem - **all of that is what this edition of** ***Artifacts*** **is about.**

> ### The Story

The revolution YouTube triggered is **right there in the name:**

- ***“You”*** puts the viewer (or creator) at the center — a nod to agency, to personal control over media. *You* are in charge of what you watch *and* what you could create.

- ***“Tube”*** is a throwback to the cathode-ray TVs of yore, and the kind of content YouTube would gradually devour.

In other words, **your own television** or, at least, media channel.

[![the original YouTube iPhone icon : r/nostalgia](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ls4Y!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8c142104-2bed-4b61-a7c8-100dc629954f_1107x1110.jpeg "the original YouTube iPhone icon : r/nostalgia")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ls4Y!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8c142104-2bed-4b61-a7c8-100dc629954f_1107x1110.jpeg)

Apple got it right?

Besides the “Tube”, it’s the “You” that’s the real pivot of YouTube’s revolution — the part that touches at least two crucial domains: **time** and **content**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

On the ***time*** front, YouTube triggered the **shift from scheduled programming to infinite scroll.**

Before YouTube (and the broader internet-as-archive), media was **ephemeral**. TV aired and disappeared. News ran and vanished. Events were linear and irreversible. **Now, we live in an endless present.**

Put simply, **we no longer need to sync our lives to catch a particular show** — we watch at our convenience. It’s obvious now, but it was a major shift back then (we only had it with DVDs etc.)

Broadly speaking, **YouTube has, thus, reorganised our relationship to time, attention, and even memory online.**

Think of the **“Save for Later” button** - yes, the one we click before tossing content into a limbo we’ll likely never return to. Yet that button says it all: **the schedule is no longer king**, and our attention is now modular, flexible, and tailored to our whims.

Set aside the downsides for a second - this is a clear sign of what the internet at large has become: **a searchable, external, prosthetic memory** where everything is permanently accessible in hindsight.

So, yes, there’s a flood of stuff happening in real time (just scroll up and check how many hours of video are uploaded to YouTube every minute), **but we know it’ll be there later.** We’ve created a **backlog of the now.** [Present Shock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Present_Shock:_When_Everything_Happens_Now) is a great read on this.

It’s an enormous opportunity - we can consume better, deeper, smarter - but also a **breeding ground for procrastination and (digital) laziness.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inevitably, **the time element feeds into the** ***content*** **side.**

YouTube empowered a shift **from audience as passive consumer to audience as active creator.** Want to join the conversation? Fire up your camera — your content can be online in minutes.

But even if we’re not up for being creators, **we still have far more agency than we ever had with television.** We’re no longer stuck watching what the networks serve up - **we actively choose what we want to engage with**, from an endless buffet of creators.

And that’s a big deal. **It’s not just about indulging our interests; it’s about carving out niches, diving deep into weird and wonderful subcultures** - as my friend Gio aptly put it while brainstorming this Artifacts.

We all know people who learned to cook on YouTube. Or code. Or fish. Or anything else you can think of.

That said, **we should take the “actively” part with a pinch of salt.**

YouTube’s recommender algorithm plays a **huge role in shaping what we see** - and, likely, what we end up caring about. Positively framed, it helps us with curiosity; less charitably, it nudges us into filter bubbles.

So yes, **algorithmic inference drives discovery**. But it doesn’t kill agency entirely - especially because **the bond with creators tends to be stronger here than on most other platforms.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0_pX!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe299bbec-ce80-4b68-80a8-9085f63fc0be_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0_pX!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe299bbec-ce80-4b68-80a8-9085f63fc0be_1024x1024.png)

finally found out how to generate consistent pics!

And that’s precisely why, despite its TikTokification (Shorts and all), **YouTube still stands apart.**

**It’s not a social network in the traditional sense** - and probably doesn’t want to be.

For one, the ways we access it are far more diverse than with other platforms: not just smartphones, but laptops **and, increasingly, televisions.**

(According to YouTube, TV is now the primary device for watching YouTube in the United States, surpassing mobile!)

But it goes further than that. The engagement mechanics are softer. **You don’t need an account to watch videos.** And even those who *do* have accounts rarely post — instead, they use them to organise and curate their interests and favourite creators.

Not surprisingly, indeed, despite being among the most used platforms globally, **the rate of active** ***daily*** **users is much lower than the others.** We go there when we need, not to doomscrooll.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rQ6g!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F42b763f9-adfb-4ba4-bcdf-ecdc14d28c33_677x224.png)

table provided by Perplexity

In complex terms, there’s virtually no social graph. But that’s not a bug - it’s a feature. **We’re there more for the content than to socialise.** And that can raise the bar on what we watch.

Finally, and this matters: **unlike television, and unlike most social media, content on YouTube doesn’t vanish after a few hours.** It lives on for years. It keeps circulating, being discovered, and being useful.

So yes, **YouTube continues to chart its own course — not quite social media, but something well beyond television.** It profits from transcending time, while staying a platform for quality content, created by the very people who use it.

**Not too bad** for what started with someone looking for some videos online and some cool elephants.

# Services that serve?
Date: 2025-04-09 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/services-that-serve
Cite as: Services that serve? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-04-09. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/services-that-serve (CC BY 4.0)

I had the chance to talk with <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/pedrazzo/">Marco Maria Pedrazzo</a>, former Head of Design of the Italian Government and one of the minds behind <strong><a href="https://developers.italia.it/en/designers/">Design System .italia</a>,</strong> <strong>the official framework for designing digital services within the Italian Public Administration.</strong>

In plain terms? Design system italia. is the <strong>toolkit of guidelines, components, and resources aimed at creating consistent, accessible, and user-centered digital experiences</strong> across Italy's 22,000 autonomous public administrations.

In other words, <strong>if a school has to build its new website, it just takes those components without reinventing the wheel every time.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Cago!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F03bd086b-3294-4061-bc81-906878c69d2b_1920x1356.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Cago!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F03bd086b-3294-4061-bc81-906878c69d2b_1920x1356.jpeg" alt="Per designer" title="Per designer"></a>

You can find its assets on <a href="https://www.figma.com/design/wvXrFloFfHi6kd0176yqBK/prj_ITWallet---Accesso---UI-kit-baset?node-id=4705-302709&amp;p=f&amp;t=DVYtZw1V70QHClVm-0">Figma</a>, built to match national design guidelines and easy to use across platforms, or check the <a href="https://designers.italia.it/risorse-per-progettare/realizzare/sviluppo-interfaccia/">Web Development Kits</a> online (and many other resources)

But as Marco pointed out, <strong>Design System .italia was just a tool - not the end goal.</strong> The real objective of his team was far more ambitious: to <strong>build better digital services for citizens.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Our conversation was genuinely inspiring - <strong>a reminder that some of the brightest minds out there are working in the public sector.</strong>

Marco, who describes himself as a Design Manager (with a soft spot for Management Design), is an architect by training, used to work with Carlo Ratti, and is now bringing his design chops to Pininfarina.

What follows is my attempt to distill the most valuable insights from our discussion.

> ### The Interview

<em>The interview has been conducted in English. For clarity and readability, the transcript has been reviewed and lightly edited.</em>

> <strong>So, what did you do when working for the Government?</strong>

The key thing I’ve worked on is shaping and guiding the creation of Design System .italia. But let’s be clear - <strong>it didn’t start with me, and it won’t end with me</strong> - some brilliant people were there before me and others are still building great services now.

> <strong>Where did everything start?</strong>

From a simple data: the Italian public sector includes around 22,000 entities. <strong>If each designed and implemented its own digital interface from scratch, it would be incredibly costly and frustrating for citizens</strong>, who would have to figure out a new system every time they interacted with a different authority.

When the Team di Trasformazione Digitale first started working on this challenge, they had to think broadly. <strong>The first step was the creation of a design system and UI Kit, alongside <a href="https://italia.github.io/bootstrap-italia/">Bootstrap Italia</a>, which provides the code framework.</strong> Right after the time extraordinary commissioner Diego Piacentini, when I joined the team, we began assembling a larger team of designers who asked: <strong>How do we solve this in a way that scales?</strong>

That led to the first iterations of what’s now the Design System .italia, which includes <strong>extensive documentation, the contribution guidelines, and has been extensively tested in each component.</strong>

> <strong>Why is it so important that public digital services just work? How are they different from private services both in the building and delivery phases?</strong>

Public services exist for a very different reason than private ones. In the private sector, digital products are designed to create engagement, drive revenue, and foster customer loyalty. <strong>Public services, on the other hand, exist to uphold rights and fulfill obligations.</strong>

<strong>Citizens don’t “choose” to interact with public services the way they might choose between different banking apps or food delivery platforms</strong> - they have to use them.

That’s why a public digital service should be <strong>as seamless and invisible as possible</strong>. A well-designed government service shouldn’t require citizens to jump through hoops or learn a new system every time they need to interact with the State.

It should work effortlessly, without friction, because <strong>the main focus is not about delighting users — it’s about ensuring they can access what they need without unnecessary effort.</strong>

> <strong>How does this impact the way you build a digital service or product?</strong>

The key feature for public service design is <strong>openness by default</strong>. By law, any technological asset created for public administration must be open-source, for public use and scrutiny. <strong>But it’s not just about compliance</strong> — it’s about creating a genuinely open design and development process. That means having a GitHub repository, setting up clear contribution guidelines, and building a community around the project.

Then there’s <strong>privacy by default</strong>: in the public sector privacy isn’t just a feature - it’s a foundational principle.

Similarly, <strong>accessibility by default</strong> is non-negotiable. Public services exist to fulfill citizens’ rights. <strong>If they’re not accessible to everyone</strong> — including people with low digital literacy, disabilities, or other impairments — <strong>then they’re failing in their mission.</strong>

> <strong>What are the challenges of designing and building technological artifacts in such open and transparent way?</strong>

<strong>I think the first thing to ask is: What’s the alternative?</strong> If public authorities didn’t work in the open, we’d be trapped in a market of proprietary digital tools with high barriers to entry.

Becoming a supplier for the public sector isn’t like entering a commercial market - it involves navigating regulations, procurement processes, and a distinct ecosystem. <strong>If we relied on closed systems, we’d be trapped vendor lock-ins</strong>, where both institutions and citizens become dependent on a handful of companies.

What I'm trying to say is that <strong>the scenario where we don't build open and interoperable is just a non-starter for the public sector.</strong>

<strong>Take a public school website as an example:</strong> why should every school invest time and money to research, develop and test its own web page? <strong>And why should a parent learn new ways of interacting each time her kid changes school?</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sql0!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F567426a7-1cc0-4eae-9191-43c9b168f622_1024x1024.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sql0!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F567426a7-1cc0-4eae-9191-43c9b168f622_1024x1024.png" alt=""></a>

> <strong>Yet, not only the tech was open but also the process itself. How was it?</strong>

<strong>We engaged citizens including professionals and non through a multitude of channels (newsletters, LinkedIn, Instagram)</strong>, asking them for their input on services as well as for their more concrete capabilities and knowledge. And it just happened.

<strong>How many people partake? It’s hard to put an exact number on it.</strong> We’ve seen contributions from a mix of people — some from within the community who participate in public calls and workshops, and others who contribute directly via GitHub, sometimes anonymously.

<strong>The beauty of open-source is that anyone can step in and add value.</strong>

> <strong>But do people really have the time and motivation to contribute?</strong>

I think people are <strong>in desperate need of purpose</strong>. Some might contribute for altruistic reasons, others for personal or professional growth or interests in building a professional network.

<strong>But when a government, which has historically being perceived as distant, comes to your city and says, “We’re testing this, and your input could directly shape it,” people engage.</strong>

For example, when we tested new website templates for municipalities at an event at Fabbrica del Vapore in Milan, we had 20 participants, including people with disabilities, sign language interpreters, and accessibility experts. It felt great.

> <strong>Let’s move to the services you built. In “<a href="https://anatomyofpublicservices.com/">Platformland</a>”, they write that we are moving towards a future in which people’s interactions with technology tend more towards passive and real time, rather than being active and transactional. Did you see it happening?</strong>

In the private sector, digital services are designed to maximize engagement. Companies optimize for “delight” because that’s what keeps customers loyal and willing to pay. <strong>Now, take money and delight out of the equation. What’s left? A completely different set of design challenges and a higher order of priorities.</strong>

As we said, public digital services exist to enable rights and fulfill obligations, so <strong>they need to be informational and proactive so that people can be passive.</strong>

If social media wants you to spend as much time as possible online, <strong>the goal of a digital public service should be to have you there as little as possible</strong> to get what your right is.

In other words, the best public digital services are the ones that <strong>don’t require interaction at all</strong> — they just work in the background.

> <strong>For instance?</strong>

A truly proactive public administration should <strong>help people before they even ask</strong>.

If someone moves from Paris to Turin, has a child, and falls within a certain income bracket, <strong>the system should automatically suggest schools for their child and inform them of relevant tax benefits.</strong> Instead of forcing citizens to navigate bureaucratic processes, the government should anticipate their needs and provide support seamlessly.

At the end of the day, public services shouldn’t be intrusive. The government should be <strong>as invisible as possible while being as helpful as possible</strong>.

> <strong>So it’s not just about making the government more efficient - it’s about reducing the administrative burden on citizens?</strong>

Exactly. <strong>That’s the difference John Maeda draws between digitization and digitalization.</strong>

Digitization is just turning paper forms into online ones. <strong>Digitalization asks: why should a citizen keep typing in their fiscal code when their digital ID already contains all the data the government needs?</strong>

<strong>Take certificates. Nobody actually wants a certificate — they want what it gives access to.</strong> The certificate is just a bureaucratic middleman. So instead of investing in better ways to issue certificates, why not invest in getting people directly to the service?

<strong>That’s what interoperability is about: databases talking to each other, exchanging information behind the scenes.</strong> In the best-case scenario, digital services disappear entirely. All that’s left is the outcome — what the citizen came for in the first place.

> <strong>What’s the bigger picture behind all of this?</strong>

<strong>It’s about rights and duties, not purchase preferences.</strong>

Most digital products are optional — you can live with a cheap, basic phone. You might live slightly better with a smartphone. You live even better with the latest, biggest iPhone. But that’s just preference.

<strong>Public services aren’t about that. They’re not lifestyle upgrades - they’re rights and responsibilities.</strong> And that puts them in a different category altogether. We need to treat them as such when we design digital systems.

<strong>They have a higher order of priorities.</strong>

# Send good vibes
Date: 2025-03-26 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/send-good-vibes
Cite as: Send good vibes by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-03-26. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/send-good-vibes (CC BY 4.0)

Last weekend, **in just 36 minutes**, I built, developed, and deployed this [web app.](https://inthebox-newsletter.com/)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1p4f!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fadb16a82-851c-4535-9fdd-8e48e870bc65_800x493.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1p4f!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fadb16a82-851c-4535-9fdd-8e48e870bc65_800x493.gif)

*I need more newsletter recommendations!!*

It’s called **In The Box** - a repository of newsletters that I plan to expand into a full-fledged community. I’ll be focusing on it more in the coming weeks **(I’ll need to populate it - send tips if you have!)**

But what’s more striking isn’t the tool itself, which is fairly basic, it’s ***how*** **it came to exist.**

I built it entirely through **Lovable**, a sort of ChatGPT for web development, which quickly assembled the UI, set up a [GitHub repository](https://github.com/Artifacts7/in-the-box), and **handled deployment** with a custom domain.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!UxJN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F25a0be33-be7a-4393-bbbf-1bea0bc7a90c_800x435.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!UxJN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F25a0be33-be7a-4393-bbbf-1bea0bc7a90c_800x435.gif)

*feeling like Alan Turing*

**And I didn’t write a single line of code.** I just reviewed it.

Sure, I could have manually coded the database, **but not as fast as Lovable did.**

Also, **I’m not an expert in web design, but I got exactly the vintage,** Windows XP vibe I was looking for.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

What’s all this about, anyway? Andrej Karpathy, former AI guru at Tesla and X, [calls it](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383) **[“vibe coding.”](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383)** In simple terms: **you describe what you want in natural language, and AI generates the code.** No syntax struggles. No late-night Stack Overflow deep dives.

**Just vibes.**

As he put it: ***“It’s not really coding** - I just see things, say things, run things, and copy-paste things, and it mostly works.”*

**And this isn’t theoretical.** It’s happening now. **A growing wave of tools** is making software development as simple as describing a product in plain English.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-jzr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5fc3f7b-8e5a-48b7-9609-f0056c9ff97a_700x394.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-jzr!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5fc3f7b-8e5a-48b7-9609-f0056c9ff97a_700x394.png)

*and many more actually*

This goes far beyond ChatGPT writing Python snippets for your university coursework. **These tools don’t just generate code - they build and deploy infrastructure.**

You tell them what you need, and they make it happen.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ASQo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F68f1b43c-837c-4355-ae4c-2596766c577b_1200x818.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ASQo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F68f1b43c-837c-4355-ae4c-2596766c577b_1200x818.png)

The numbers say it all:

- In March 2025, **Y Combinator** reported that **25% of startups** in its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were **95% AI-generated.**

- **Bolt** scaled to a **\$20M revenue run rate**, while **Lovable** hit **\$10M** just two months after monetizing.

- And according to **Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit** (another vibe-coding tool), *“75% of Replit customers never write a single line of code.”*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Vibe-coding is part of what [Pete Sena](https://uxdesign.cc/cracking-the-code-of-vibe-coding-124b9288e551) called the ***"Great Democratization Cycle".*** We’ve seen it in photography as it evolved from darkrooms to digital cameras, which eliminated film processing, to smartphones and Instagram filters, making everyone a high-end “photographer.”

**Now, AI is lowering the barriers to coding.** If you have an idea, you’re just a few prompts away from a working product.

No, this doesn’t mean you can launch a billion-dollar startup while sipping coffee. **But you can spin up an MVP in a few hours** - something that once took weeks or months.

From a technical, economic, and product perspective, this shift is fascinating. **And worth digging into.**

In this edition of **Artifacts**, we’ll break down: the tech that makes vibe coding possible, the ripple effects across the software development chain, what this (may) mean for the future of product - and who gets to build it.

> ### **The Story**

Before moving any forward, **good to understand a bit of how these systems work.**

**Imagine you have an idea for an app - a simple task manager with login functionality.** Instead of coding it yourself, you describe what you want in plain language. That’s where the system takes over, breaking your request down into components and assembling them into a working application.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_Vqe!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39146d4a-51a5-4b69-b532-ec21e8bf5c61_1536x779.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_Vqe!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39146d4a-51a5-4b69-b532-ec21e8bf5c61_1536x779.png)

*pls nerds don’t kill me*

**1. Understanding Your Request: The Role of the LLM**

The Large Language Model (LLM) is the brain of the operation. It takes your prompt - *“Build a task manager with login support”* - and translates it into structured code. **It understands that you’ll need a front-end UI, a backend to handle tasks, and user authentication.** More than just generating code, the LLM anticipates what’s needed, ensuring that each piece fits together logically. If you later say, *“Add dark mode”* or *“Make it mobile-friendly”*, the LLM adjusts accordingly, refining the app iteratively.

**2. Bringing It to Life: The Agent Runtime**

The LLM doesn’t work alone. The Agent Runtime acts as an orchestrator, making sure everything generated by the LLM is functional, cohesive, and follows best practices. **It’s like a project manager, coordinating tasks, managing dependencies, and integrating external tools when necessary.** If your app needs a workflow to send reminder emails, the Agent Runtime ensures the right services are wired in properly.

**3. Your Control Panel: The UI**

You interact with this whole process through a user-friendly interface. Instead of writing complex commands, you type in your idea, and the UI streams responses in real time. **As the LLM generates code, the UI displays it dynamically, showing a preview of your app as it takes shape.** Want to make changes? Just describe them, and the system updates the app accordingly.

**4. Expanding Capabilities: Third-Party Integrations**

Some app features require specialized services. **Rather than reinventing the wheel, the system pulls in third-party components based on what your app needs:** *Resend* handles email notifications, *Supabase* provides a backend database and authentication, *Clerk* manages user identity.

**5. Testing on the Fly: Execution Environments**

Before you deploy your app, you’ll want to see it in action. This is where execution environments come in. With **WebContainers**, your Node.js app runs directly in the browser - no local setup needed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**All of this comes with a set of potential implications** I’ve been parsing, gathering, and brainstorming.

Vibe coding could split ***developers*** into two camps:

- Those who **understand the foundations** and can wield AI effectively.

- Those who **rely entirely on AI**, oblivious to what’s happening under the hood.

**Less coding, more reviewing.** Instead of writing code, engineers will vet, optimize, and integrate AI-generated solutions. (especially as code generated by these tools seems to be a bit dirty as of yet)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bTHS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F533e4d58-4157-4be7-8ada-3ea6eea71df8_720x666.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bTHS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F533e4d58-4157-4be7-8ada-3ea6eea71df8_720x666.png)

*a lot of memes today*

***For product managers***, it’s an opportunity - and a reckoning. Non-technical folks would get a seat at the table, but they couldn’t hide behind wireframes and docs. Prototypes are just clicks away. No excuses.

***As for products?*** Interfaces could be [churned out by LLMs](https://medium.com/paychex-ux/interfaces-are-disappearing-are-you-ready-fffc298595b7), built on existing templates and past designs. Good for efficiency. Bad for originality. We may expect sameness.

***And coding itself?*** More disposable, less reusable. Open-source libraries and Stack Overflow might fade as AI generates fresh code on demand. Already, starting a new project is easier than editing an old one - because context is hard. If this trend holds, things could get weird.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This raises big questions. Pete Sena put it well: ***What happens when makers are separated from their materials?***

Would we celebrate a world where painters never touch paint? Where sculptors never feel clay? Where chefs never taste their ingredients?

**It’s not just about shipping software.** It’s about understanding systems deeply - so when things break (and they will), you can actually fix them.

One CTO warned that AI reliance leads to “hidden complexities” - quick fixes that spiral into chaos at scale. It’s also about creating elegant, maintainable solutions that last. **Good software isn’t just functional; it endures.**

**The job market could also shift.**

**AI will take over repetitive coding** - web development, scripting, testing, deployment - shrinking the need for junior developers who typically start with those tasks. At the same time, companies will prioritize mid-to-senior engineers who understand AI-assisted workflows and system architecture.

Entry-level jobs won’t disappear, **but they’ll get harder to land.**

Instead of cutting their teeth on grunt work, **newcomers will be expected to think strategically from day one.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lj1E!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F407ea2b5-4a83-41a9-a9ac-bdde83297181_1536x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lj1E!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F407ea2b5-4a83-41a9-a9ac-bdde83297181_1536x1024.png)

One thing, however, will stay the same - maybe even grow in importance: **what drives new products and the ideas behind them.**

More than ever, **the real skill will be identifying concrete problems and crafting solid solutions (and ideas of products) to tackle them.**

If vibe coding takes off, the technical barriers between idea and execution will shrink. Moving from concept to a working product will be faster, but **the hardest part - figuring out what’s worth building - will still be the priority.**

# Shedding a light
Date: 2025-03-05 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/shedding-a-light
Cite as: Shedding a light by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-03-05. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/shedding-a-light (CC BY 4.0)

This is how turning off data collection in ChatGPT <strong>does (not) work.</strong>

<em>(Yes what you should do if you've ChatGPT writing confidential emails)</em>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZDlW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4309fe54-76f5-494d-b284-9354f49cbac0_800x493.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZDlW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4309fe54-76f5-494d-b284-9354f49cbac0_800x493.gif" alt=""></a>

Or rather, you can pull it off - eventually. But <strong>it’s not exactly intuitive</strong>, nor is it easy. And that’s for a few reasons:

- first of all, it takes <strong>4 (!) clicks</strong> to get there;

- the language is - to say the least - convoluted: <em>"improve the model for everyone"</em> sounds almost noble, like some crowdsourced act of AI altruism. <strong>It subtly frames opting out as selfish</strong>, as if withholding your data means stalling progress, depriving the world of some grand technological enlightenment;

- This setting is <strong>ON by default</strong>;

- If you want out, there’s no simple “Off” button. Instead, <strong>you get a chevron ( \> ) - a tiny, easily missed nudge toward another screen.</strong> More friction, more effort, more chances to give up and leave the setting as it is.

To be clear, <strong>I’m not picking on OpenAI specifically.</strong> They do get some things right - like warning users that AI-generated answers can be wrong. A reminder that, despite its confidence, <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2023/04/03/the-great-pretender/">ChatGPT is the Great Pretender.</a>

<strong>And they’re not alone.</strong> Take Perplexity. It doesn’t exactly set a gold standard for transparency either.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!eTLB!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F612a696d-78cb-4805-8dbf-2a555d8a0628_1276x724.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!eTLB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F612a696d-78cb-4805-8dbf-2a555d8a0628_1276x724.png" alt=""></a>

But I’m not here to talk about AI or data collection. <strong>This is just the hook</strong>, the spark that led to this edition of Artifacts.

Because what really matters is what all these frustrating UX journeys have in common: a specific, insidious concept - <strong>dark patterns.</strong>

Back in 2010, UX designer <strong>Harry Brignull</strong> gave this name to something we’ve all experienced: <strong>deceptive design choices that subtly push users toward actions they might not otherwise take.</strong>

He even cataloged them, putting together a <a href="https://www.deceptive.design/hall-of-shame">hall of shame</a> full of the most <strong>shameless examples.</strong>

And he was onto something. Fast-forward to today, and <strong>“dark patterns” are recognized in tech regulation</strong>, from the EU’s Digital Services Act to California’s CCPA

------------------------------------------------------------------------

What he got right is that design matters and, importantly, shapes users’ behaviour.

<strong>Because design isn’t just about aesthetics.</strong> It’s a language - one that dictates what we notice, how we navigate, and what choices feel possible and, eventually, our agency over the (digital) world

Like words in a sentence, <strong>design structures our experience.</strong> It can clarify or obscure, guide or mislead. <strong>It can empower users</strong> - or trap them in a maze of friction, confusion, and manipulation, as dark patterns do.

In this edition of Artifacts, <strong>we’re shining a light into that darkness.</strong> And tracing it back to some core principles of design—not just digital UX, but the very fundamentals of how we interact with everyday things.

> ### The Story

At its core, <strong>design is a system of control.</strong> The real question isn’t <em>how</em> something is designed, but for <em>whom</em> —\> <em>Whose interests are being served?</em>

This isn’t just a theoretical musing - it’s baked into the very nature of how we interact with the world, both physical and digital. A door handle, a software setting, a checkout button - <strong>each one is designed to nudge us toward an intended action.</strong>

<strong>Don Norman</strong>, in <em>“The Design of Everyday Things”</em>, breaks this down into a <strong>set of principles & criteria</strong> that make objects easy to use. They’re just as relevant to websites and apps as they are to coffee makers and light switches:

- <em><strong>Affordances</strong></em> <strong>tell us what something can do.</strong> A handle invites pulling, a button suggests clicking. When design is done well, this feels obvious. When it’s not, you push when you should pull - or worse, click when you shouldn’t.

- <em><strong>Signifiers</strong></em> <strong>guide where to act.</strong> A blue underlined link looks clickable. A toggle switch with unclear states? That’s bad signification - you’re left wondering if it’s on or off.

- <em><strong>Mapping</strong></em> <strong>is how controls relate to their effects.</strong> A volume knob turns right to increase sound. But in a digital setting, mapping can be twisted: a privacy setting buried deep inside a “General” menu is mapped to be hard to find on purpose.

- <em><strong>Feedback</strong></em> <strong>lets you know something happened.</strong> Click “Delete Account,” and you should get a confirmation. If you don’t? You’re left in limbo, unsure if your action even worked.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0BML!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe02de39b-d52d-41fc-bad7-c6cd45ca4663_3431x3431.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0BML!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe02de39b-d52d-41fc-bad7-c6cd45ca4663_3431x3431.jpeg" alt="Affordance - Sketchplanations" title="Affordance - Sketchplanations"></a>

For instance

These lead to two broader design principles:

- <em><strong>Discoverability</strong></em><strong>,</strong> whether we can figure out what actions are possible and <em>where</em> and <em>how</em> to perform them;

- <em><strong>Understanding</strong></em>: How a product is supposed to be used and what do all the different controls and settings mean.

These are the criteria we can use to evaluate the design of anything - <strong>the worse it performs, the closer we get to a dark pattern</strong> or, more simply, to a design that harms users.

Now, here’s where things get interesting. If an interface lacks these qualities by accident, <strong>it’s just bad design.</strong> <em>Annoying</em>, but not sinister.

<em>But when these principles are deliberately weakened?</em> <strong>That’s when we enter the realm of dark patterns.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uUni!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F559cb115-8725-4a41-99c6-0707f226e09f_1024x1024.webp"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uUni!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F559cb115-8725-4a41-99c6-0707f226e09f_1024x1024.webp" alt=""></a>

Which is, actually, well different from a <em>bad</em> design.

Dark patterns don’t make a product <em>unusable</em> - <strong>they make it work against you.</strong> They constrain options, push defaults, and make it harder to act in your own interest. <strong>They turn users into passengers rather than drivers of their own experience.</strong>

And where does that lead? <strong>To a world where control shifts from the user to the designer</strong> - not in service of usability, but of someone else’s bottom line.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

So, what? Playing around with Don Norman’s toolkit—more understanding, more discoverability—<strong>we can rethink how OpenAI’s opt-outs work.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JYAq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F52f3ee43-d179-48c6-8e6e-404d5d60185d_2158x1358.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JYAq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F52f3ee43-d179-48c6-8e6e-404d5d60185d_2158x1358.png" alt=""></a>

as a reminder

Which, again, doesn’t just mean <em>fixing</em> what’s broken. <strong>It means making the system explain itself so users don’t have to reverse-engineer it.</strong>

Right now, the setting has a vague phrase paired with an <strong>On</strong> toggle. What does “improve” mean? What data is being collected? Can I see what’s shared? These are <strong>black boxes where transparency should be</strong>.

And then there’s the toggle itself - <strong>a tiny, unclear switch with no real signifier of its state.</strong> Does “On” mean I’m sharing data? Does “Off” mean I’m private? A simple binary like:

✅ <strong>“Allow my chats to be used for AI training”</strong>

🚫 <strong>“Do not use my chats for AI training”</strong>

…would be far clearer. Even better? <strong>A proper switch component</strong> - one that explicitly changes state instead of a vague, text-based indicator.

And that’s it for <em>signifiers</em> and <em>affordances:</em> <strong>we know better what to do and are better guided.</strong>

On top of this, <strong>we can reimagine the</strong> <em><strong>mapping.</strong></em>

Currently, this option sits under <strong>“Data Controls,”</strong> which sounds neutral, almost administrative. But <strong>data-sharing is a privacy decision, not just a settings toggle.</strong> It belongs under <strong>Security</strong> - or at least should be cross-referenced there. If a user has to hunt for it, they’re already at a disadvantage.

Needless to say, <strong>making it less than 4 clicks away</strong>, possibly in the home page, <strong>would make things even more understandable and usable.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

These aren’t sweeping changes or demands for a full system overhaul. They’re small but meaningful adjustments—simple ways to make the system clearer, giving users more control and, ultimately, more power over their own data.

<strong>So they’re not left in the dark.</strong>

> ### Nerding
