# Breaking the chains
Date: 2025-02-11 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/breaking-the-chains
Cite as: Breaking the chains by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-02-11. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/breaking-the-chains (CC BY 4.0)

Back in November 2022 - feels like ages ago, doesn’t it? - ChatGPT took off because it was… <em>a chat</em>.

Sure, OpenAI had a powerful model, but that wasn’t new. The real breakthrough? <strong>They made AI</strong> <em><strong>simple</strong></em><strong>.</strong> No coding, no weird interfaces - just a basic, familiar format: dialogue. <strong>One of the oldest interfaces of (online) life.</strong>

<strong>Just type, hit enter, and get a response.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rPcB!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F408942e2-6bce-47c7-a392-fa4efbdb81d7_1080x924.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rPcB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F408942e2-6bce-47c7-a392-fa4efbdb81d7_1080x924.jpeg" alt=""></a>

Isn’t it like that?

A lot has happened since. But one thing remains clear: <strong>the more</strong> <em><strong>natural</strong></em> <strong>(I’m not using “human” on purpose) the interaction, the more engaging AI becomes.</strong>

That’s why voice was the next big leap - why OpenAI’s advanced voice mode and NotebookLM felt so uncanny. AI now writes, speaks, listens, and draws, <strong>mimicking what we instinctively recognise as intelligence.</strong>

The missing piece? <em><strong>Thinking</strong>.</em>

Or at least, something that <em>resembles</em> it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<strong>And that’s where DeepSeek comes in.</strong>

The latest big name in AI didn’t just ride the wave of better models, more GPUs, and geopolitics. It introduced something else: <strong>an AI that appears to</strong> <em><strong>think</strong></em><strong>.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lA6l!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F005b5f77-f2d7-465e-84ed-075856c6112f_1198x1304.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lA6l!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F005b5f77-f2d7-465e-84ed-075856c6112f_1198x1304.png" alt=""></a>

Using it through Perplexity as I tend to care about my personal data

<strong>Yet, this “thinking” is more a design choice</strong>. A nice one, but a design one, as claimed by <a href="https://www.platformer.news/deepseek-design-user-interface-chain-of-thought-ai/">Casey</a> and <a href="https://darioamodei.com/on-deepseek-and-export-controls">Amodei</a>. It has relatively little to do with the actual inner functioning but it reveals a lot about the training of Deepseek’s models.

For the IT guys reading Artifacts, this DeepSeek’s “thinking” is, rather, <strong>exposing its chain of thought</strong> - <em>what you see above.</em>

Which is not, actually, a brand new thing as OpenAI released it before, but DeepSeek made it popular, widespread.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vQPj!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F59f2adf4-dc3f-4df6-9ead-544b9cf170ad_1280x827.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vQPj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F59f2adf4-dc3f-4df6-9ead-544b9cf170ad_1280x827.jpeg" alt="zdnet.com" title="zdnet.com"></a>

Is AI really thinking? What does this reveal about DeepSeek’s inner workings? <strong>And why does it matter?</strong> This <em>Artifacts</em> is here to unpack it all.

> ### The History

To fully grasp what is going on, it’s good to understand what a <strong>chain of thought</strong> even is.

Chain-of-thought in DeepSeek is a reasoning technique that enables the AI models to <strong>break down complex problems into logical,</strong> sequential steps before providing a final answer. It:

1.  articulates its thought process step by step.

2.  reflects on its own reasoning.

3.  even double-checks itself along the way.

Remember when AI experts told you to prompt models step by step to improve responses? <strong>Now, AI does it on its own.</strong> The gurus can rest.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<strong>What’s different about DeepSeek is</strong> <em><strong>how</strong></em> <strong>it learned this.</strong> Instead of traditional supervised learning (where models are fed labeled examples) or unsupervised learning (where they find patterns in data), DeepSeek’s training relies on <em><strong>reinforcement learning</strong></em><strong>.</strong>

This reinforcement learning of DeepSeek is something worth scrutinising. With <strong>an example</strong>, of course, trying to unraveling <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948">their complex paper.</a>

<strong>Imagine solving a math problem by writing down each step in a notebook.</strong> DeepSeek's AI does something similar internally, <strong>breaking complex questions into smaller steps.</strong> What's unique is how it <em>learned</em> this skill:

1.  <strong>Self-Teaching Brain</strong>: Instead of being shown examples of step-by-step solutions first, t<strong>he AI figured out how to break down problems on its own through trial and error</strong>.

2.  <strong>Built-In Fact Checker</strong>: As it works through problems, the AI automatically double-checks its steps (like re-doing calculations) before finalizing answers. This wasn't programmed - <strong>the AI developed this error-checking ability naturally.</strong>

Importantly, along this process, these models earn rewards for <strong>good thinking steps</strong>, not just correct answers.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Even more importantly, DeepSeek does not rely on trial and error one step at a time but on <strong>multiple solutions simultaneously.</strong>

<strong>For each problem, it generates several potential answers, evaluates them collectively, and ranks them.</strong> By comparing different approaches, it learns to prioritize the most effective strategies over weaker ones..

In jargon, this is called <strong>Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO),</strong> namely like teaching a group of students who can share what they learn with each other instead of single students studying in isolation.

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2gdz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F688fed65-e0e7-49d1-8ffe-a0c57f8adc45_710x335.png" alt="">

This process is what enables DeepSeek to display its <em>chain of thought</em> so clearly. It even has <em><strong>aha</strong></em> <strong>moments</strong> - instances where it retraces its steps and realizes it made a mistake.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EhQ4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7e3467b7-5c6e-46a5-b37e-ef14e6543cbb_1600x1008.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EhQ4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7e3467b7-5c6e-46a5-b37e-ef14e6543cbb_1600x1008.jpeg" alt="DeepSeek R1 exhibits an &#x27;aha moment&#x27; during training" title="DeepSeek R1 exhibits an &#x27;aha moment&#x27; during training"></a>

read the red!

DeepSeek has undeniably pushed AI training forward, making models appear more cautious and deliberate.

But let’s be clear: <strong>AI is</strong> <em><strong>not</strong></em> <strong>thinking.</strong> Not even close.

The chain of thought is the reflection of a real training technique, j<strong>ust made it digestible to human beings.</strong>

Internally, <strong>AI models do not "think" in words or sentences as we do.</strong> Instead, they process input data through layers of mathematical computations, resulting in output that can be interpreted as text.

The CoT approach is a way to structure these computations to <em><strong>mimic</strong></em> <strong>a step-by-step reasoning process</strong>, making the model's operations more interpretable to users.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tsdM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7211e686-5f64-4f1d-89d5-c1d8ce71c1e2_1024x1058.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tsdM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7211e686-5f64-4f1d-89d5-c1d8ce71c1e2_1024x1058.png" alt=""></a>

So what does this mean? The exposure of a chain of thought isn’t a window into the model’s actual inner workings - <strong>it’s a design choice, a tool for making AI seem more understandable.</strong>

This may seem obvious (is it?), but it’s worth repeating. Human minds <em>think</em>. <strong>Statistical models don’t.</strong> Words aren’t even a concept to them—they’re just patterns.

None of this is meant to diminish DeepSeek’s achievements. In fact, making AI reasoning more transparent is a win for AI safety and usability. But we should recognize it for what it is: <strong>an interpretative layer, not a fundamental shift in machine intelligence.</strong>

# Not every fish is worth it
Date: 2025-01-28 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/not-every-fish-is-worth-it
Cite as: Not every fish is worth it by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2025-01-28. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/not-every-fish-is-worth-it (CC BY 4.0)

You’ve probably heard the buzz: **Meta’s doing a big shake-up.**

**What’s allowed (and not allowed) to be said** on its platforms is about to look a whole lot different. **And how they’ll check and control what you say?** That’s shifting too.

In complex terms, Meta is overhauling its **content moderation policies** (only in the US, for now).

Mark Zuckerberg kept it brief - **5 minutes**, to be exact:

[![Meta official blasts CEO Mark Zuckerberg for 'buckling to political pressure'](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3BOp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F44d7192c-cd24-4a8b-bdb5-05b93445c49d_700x1024.jpeg "Meta official blasts CEO Mark Zuckerberg for 'buckling to political  pressure'")](https://about.fb.com/news/2025/01/meta-more-speech-fewer-mistakes/)

Zuck in his new style!

Here’s the breakdown:

- **Fact-checking? Out.** They’re replacing it with something called Community Notes, which sounds a lot like X’s approach. Instead of expert fact-checkers tagging content, they’re putting the responsibility in the hands of the users - free of charge, of course.

- **Restrictions on harmful speech? Relaxed.** Now, you can say that, for instance, a gay person is mentally ill. Call it “freedom of expression,” if you wish.

- **Moderation overhaul.** Meta’s recalibrating its automated systems to focus only on the big, truly harmful violations—like drugs or child exploitation. The rest? They’ll scrutinise less.

- **Politics are back in play.** Meta’s resurrecting political content, which they were trying to bury just a couple of years ago, as we saw [here](https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/la-piazza-al-centro-del-villaggio) on Artifacts.

- **Moderators are moving.** Goodbye, California. Hello, Texas. Because, well, Texas has different ideas.

In a [tagline](https://about.fb.com/news/2025/01/meta-more-speech-fewer-mistakes/) (provided by Meta), they want ‘**More Speech and Fewer Mistakes’**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The comms strategy around this announcement has been pretty straightforward. In Zuck’s words, Meta wants to **“get back to our roots”**, which happens to coincide with (at least) **2019**, when he delivered [this speech,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nYMX-ArjYz8) he referenced to.

**Not a random year.** That was before the Biden administration took the reins, when Trump was president, and when platform accountability laws—like the DSA in the EU—were still in the making. **A pivotal time, indeed.**

**This is 100% an about-face for Meta.** Remember, the fact-checking program kicked off in 2016 amidst accusations of misinformation flooding its platforms. **By 2021, Meta was actively reducing political content**, and Zuck wasn’t exactly holding back his disdain for Trump:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!28yX!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3932bda7-7c7c-4173-9b6e-58c100d7d1fc_762x619.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!28yX!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3932bda7-7c7c-4173-9b6e-58c100d7d1fc_762x619.png)

**But political tides shift, and so do corporate strategies.** What we’re seeing is a repositioning—Meta tracing back its steps to protect its interests and its business. Predictable? Sure. Surprising? Not so much.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Let’s leave the politics aside, though.** I don’t have all the pieces to comment on that, and much has already been said.

What’s more fascinating is what lies beyond politics. Behind the mantra of “more speech and fewer mistakes” are **calculations, statistical trade-offs, and artifacts—the tools and decisions shaping it all.**

> ### The Story

First, Meta isn’t changing how it handles **illegal content**. The definition of what’s illegal might be fuzzy and context-dependent, but it’s ultimately grounded in the law. That stays.

Yet, **illegal content are just a** ***limited*** **part of the issues of speech online.**

What Zuck seems to be changing his mind about is ***harmful content,*** which is inherently a slippery middle ground between legality and illegality.

Harmful content encompasses speech or media that isn’t outright illegal **but may have negative consequences.** Think of cyberbullying, disinformation, or glorification of eating disorders. These are - bear with me - **also** forms of freedom of expression. **Which can be harmful, but still not illegal.**

**This is where platforms exercise discretion.** They decide how safe—or how harmful—they want their spaces to be. By making these choices, they define the boundaries of their communities.

Yet, [as Florent Joly brilliantly puts it](https://www.threads.net/@florent.joly/post/DEiVXuJpIV2), **framing this as a battle between “censorship” and “free speech” is oversimplifying things.** Relaxing harmful content policies isn’t just about “freedom”—it’s about the real-world consequences that come with that freedom. **There’s more at stake than just free speech.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Zuck, for his part, seems to **care deeply about ensuring no one gets censored.** The cost of this? As Zuck puts it, they’re *“gonna catch less bad stuff but also reduce the number of innocent people whose content is taken down”.*

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bp5O!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F57e1af79-5096-43d3-aab5-d4f0ddfe2cad_210x362.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bp5O!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F57e1af79-5096-43d3-aab5-d4f0ddfe2cad_210x362.gif)

Please appreciate the gif replacing the video

You see: **fewer mistakes, more speech.**

Which brings us to the concept of **precision vs. recall**—yes, the dreaded terms that sound more like a math exam than content moderation. But stick with me.

Now, before moving forward, it’s worth **defining** these two seemingly complex terms. Borrowing from [Simon Cross](https://www.simoncross.com/p/precision-and-recall):

- *“Precision”* is a measure of the **accuracy** of a detection system.

- *“Recall”* is a measure of the **coverage** of a detection system.

  [![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!defk!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb47b86d0-eac6-467c-931d-c763be5e2661_350x637.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!defk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb47b86d0-eac6-467c-931d-c763be5e2661_350x637.png)

To make things simpler, **picture a fisherman looking for fish with golden scales.**

A **precision fisherman** casts their line carefully, catching only 20 golden fish without wasting time. They might miss a few, but every catch is golden. A **recall fisherman** throws a wide net, catching 100 fish to ensure no golden ones escape—but they have to sort through a lot of plain fish too.

**Meta wants to be the precision fisherman.** They’d rather remove 20 harmful pieces of content with near certainty than remove 100 less harmful pieces and risk taking down some innocent posts by mistake.

**Content moderation is always a trade-off between precision and recall.** A (new) decision has been taken at Meta. Only some very harmful fishes are worth it.

*(Ok, I may be spending too much time in markets when in Paris)*

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nTOG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F95ee8b4d-b419-46af-9d6f-75ef19ff9adc_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nTOG!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F95ee8b4d-b419-46af-9d6f-75ef19ff9adc_1024x1024.png)

A basic fish, *created with DALL-E*

This is where we are: **Meta**, a private company, **deciding how to handle harmful content based on its own priorities.**

What does this mean for us? Simply put, **social media is a business.** The people in charge will adjust their policies to serve their interests, **even if that means relaxing standards for harmful content to maximize engagement.**

As frustrating as this might be, we have to accept these decisions for what they are. While we often view online platforms as public spaces, **they’re ultimately private, managed by entities whose goals don’t necessarily align with ours.**

Despite years of effort to create healthier online spaces—driven by companies and, to some extent, nudged by regulators—**social media platforms prioritize engagement and the time we spend there.** This often comes at the expense of some harmful discourse slipping through.

This isn’t about excusing or condemning these platforms.

It’s about recognizing the realities of how they operate and the **shifting incentives** behind them. Expecting the same level of safety and moderation as we might in public spaces? **That’s wishful thinking.**

> ### Save for Later

All the AI models rolled out in the past 12 months, [here](https://huggingface.co/spaces/reach-vb/2024-ai-timeline) + a new [AI tool](https://storm.genie.stanford.edu/) to generate Wikipedia-like pages.

[What’s a fact](https://www.newyorker.com/news/the-weekend-essay/whats-a-fact-anyway), nowadays? And why we’re not [distracted](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2025/01/27/the-sirens-call-chris-hayes-book-review) but just focused on something else.

TikTok was dead, [then no longer](https://www.platformer.news/tiktok-restored-immortal-app/). And why it has won a [different battle.](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2025/01/tiktok-already-won/681343/)

# A gift from builders and makers
Date: 2024-12-27 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/a-gift-from-builders-and-makers
Cite as: A gift from builders and makers by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2024-12-27. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/a-gift-from-builders-and-makers (CC BY 4.0)

**Every day this year, I set out to read something interesting**—or at least remarkable—in pursuit of a simple goal: to stay curious and, hopefully, interesting.

Most of what I read had to do with technology, **but not always.**

**The common thread, I’d say, was people who built something.** An artifact, a process, a company, a government—you name it.

And every day, **I jotted down a sentence that resonated with me.**

I kept them all in a small Moleskine notebook I carried everywhere.

By now, that’s about 366 quotes.

I went back through them, picked a handful of favorites, **and turned them into a short digital book for all the subscribers of Artifacts.**

# Pulling linchpins
Date: 2024-12-03 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/pulling-linchpins
Cite as: Pulling linchpins by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2024-12-03. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/pulling-linchpins (CC BY 4.0)

<em><strong>“Google is a monopolist,</strong> and it has acted as one to maintain its monopoly\[…\]in general search services and search text advertising <strong>through a web of anticompetitive practices</strong>”</em> declared Judge Mehta last August.

Some stats for perspective:

- <strong>9 out of 10</strong> online searches are conducted via Google.

- Nearly <strong>2 out of 3</strong> internet users browse with Google Chrome.

It’s no wonder that <em>“Googling”</em> has become shorthand for browsing the web.

But the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) seems ready to rewrite the thesaurus. <strong>They’ve proposed a series of remedies aimed at dismantling what they describe as Google’s monopoly on digital search and advertising.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The DOJ’s wishlist of reforms is as ambitious as it is disruptive.

At the top of the docket is a headline-grabber: <strong>Google should sell Chrome,</strong> its flagship browser. The idea is simple<strong>—stop letting Google use its interconnected web of services to steer users deeper into its ecosystem</strong>.

But that’s not all. Google <em>may</em> also be expected to:

- <strong>Share its treasure trove of user data</strong> with competitors, giving other search engines a shot at closing the quality gap.

- <strong>Cease exclusive deals</strong> that keep Google Search preloaded on Apple devices and others.

- <strong>Halt its acquisitions spree,</strong> which has often swallowed up competition before it can bloom.

- <strong>Give advertisers more transparency</strong> and control over their campaigns.

- And, in a nuclear scenario, <strong>sell Android</strong> if the softer measures don’t stick.

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Pb2t!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F95f97109-8aea-4695-a120-f108ed9d8bb1_1106x434.png" alt="">

If you wish to read the summary, <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1UNLi2woayYhsQzF-wPPsDmTm7Zm58eKb/view?usp=sharing">here</a> the version highlighted by Artifacts

Once again (thinking of Microsoft in the 90s), competition policy is stepping in to fix (and try to break) entrenched structures. The aim? <strong>Forcing users and companies to imagine an Internet that is just different from the one we’re accustomed to.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now, a looooot has been written and said on these solutions in the past weeks, especially on selling Chrome.

<strong>And many are the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/26/opinion/google-chrome-antitrust.html">skepticals</a>, pointing to several reasons:</strong> users would still gravitate back to Google even if it weren’t the default, that selling Chrome might just transfer monopoly power to its new owner, and that banning exclusive deals could <a href="https://fortune.com/2024/08/05/mozilla-firefox-biggest-potential-loser-google-antitrust-search-ruling/">threaten the survival of smaller browsers like Mozilla.</a> <strong>The list goes on.</strong>

Yet, this Artifacts isn’t the space to weigh the pros and cons of those solutions.

Instead, we take a step back to ask bigger questions. <strong>Where are these ideas coming from?</strong> What do they reveal about the juggernaut Google has built? And most importantly, <strong>what do they hint at for the future of search and the internet at large?</strong>

> ### The Story

<em>Why Chrome?</em> <strong>Because it’s more than a browser.</strong> It’s the linchpin, the gateway, the cornerstone, and the top of the funnel of the Google universe.

<strong>Open Chrome, and the gravitational pull begins.</strong> It nudges you to log in to your Google account (you don’t <em>have</em> to, but come on, you will), funnels you to Google Search, and then whisks you into Gmail, Docs, Maps, and beyond.

<strong>Chrome isn’t just software; it’s the</strong> <em><strong>operating system</strong></em> <strong>of your Google account.</strong> <em>Sorry product managers :)</em>

And, therefore, <strong>the problem is not Google Chrome itself</strong>, but <em>what it represents and enables.</em>

And that’s precisely why <strong>breaking up Chrome from Google, the DOJ argues, would shatter this synergy.</strong> A Chrome under new ownership wouldn’t have the same incentives to tie itself to Google’s broader services.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dAro!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd142b1c8-a889-4548-8fb3-b0094cc5d07f_1024x1024.webp"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dAro!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd142b1c8-a889-4548-8fb3-b0094cc5d07f_1024x1024.webp" alt=""></a>

A linchpin, <em>meticulously crafted by DALL-E</em>

But <strong>Chrome is not the only linchpin of this alleged monopoly.</strong> There is something more, maybe less tangible and identifiable, that has been fuelling this monopoly: <strong>data</strong>

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MJ0P!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe67c4d19-170c-4f6c-972d-489b3ea4fe63_1424x346.png" alt="">

<strong>Google’s dominance is powered by two self-reinforcing feedback loops,</strong> straight out of Shoshana Zuboff’s <em><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2019/oct/04/shoshana-zuboff-surveillance-capitalism-assault-human-automomy-digital-privacy">Surveillance Capitalism</a></em><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2019/oct/04/shoshana-zuboff-surveillance-capitalism-assault-human-automomy-digital-privacy">:</a>

1.  <strong>User cycle (bottom):</strong> Google collects data to improve Search. Better Search attracts more users, who generate even more data, which further improves Search. Rinse, repeat.

2.  <strong>Advertiser cycle (up):</strong> More users generate better targeting data, making Google the holy grail for advertisers. More ad dollars mean more resources for better services, which draw in yet more users.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!11bR!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fabe0594d-da60-4c9d-9bb2-e314516bd270_560x565.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!11bR!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fabe0594d-da60-4c9d-9bb2-e314516bd270_560x565.png" alt="Diagram of behavioral surplus and prediction products in surveillance capitalism" title="Diagram of behavioral surplus and prediction products in surveillance capitalism"></a>

The DOJ’s remedies aim squarely at the <strong>first cycle,</strong> the one below.

By forcing Google to share its data hoard with rivals, <strong>the hope is that alternative engines</strong>—think Bing or DuckDuckGo—<strong>won’t lag behind due to Google’s outsized head start.</strong>

Instead of playing catch-up on raw search quality, <strong>they could focus on differentiators like privacy or user experience.</strong> Concretely, they could focus on building features of a search engine instead of a search engine from scratch.

In theory, <strong>it’s a chance for competitors to finally get a foot in the door.</strong>

Since data at scale is the essential raw material for “building, improving and sustaining” a competitive general search engine, <strong>the DOJ now aims to force Google to make this data available and at disposal of other engines.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ultimately, the DOJ’s goal is plain: <strong>crack open the search market</strong>—or, if you’re feeling cynical, break up Google and cross your fingers that a fairer ecosystem emerges from the rubble.

<strong>But fairer</strong> <em><strong>for whom</strong></em><strong>?</strong> At first glance, the answer seems obvious: competitors like Bing, DuckDuckGo, and other underdog search engines. <strong>Yet, as is often the case, the reality is more nuanced.</strong>

<img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hz0f!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2712bb0b-883b-458e-8157-5f1350791198_1786x904.png" alt="">

Nice read, btw!

Interestingly, <strong>the DOJ’s proposals look beyond traditional search engines.</strong> The plaintiffs have pointed to <strong>“query-based AI solutions”</strong> as the next big thing.

As seen earlier, ChatGPT with a Search plugin, Perplexity, Arc—these conversational, AI-powered tools <strong>could represent the future of how we search online.</strong>

If search is shifting from ten blue links to AI-driven dialogues, then the <strong>remedies need to make room for that transformation</strong>.

The goal is not just to dethrone Google, but to <strong>foster innovation and ensure the search landscape evolves.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<strong>Of course, this is all a big “if.”</strong> The DOJ’s proposals are just that—proposals. The final ruling isn’t expected until next summer, and <strong>Google will appeal any decision it doesn’t like.</strong>

Regardless of the outcome, the DOJ’s case is <strong>a rare glimpse into the mechanics of Google’s dominance</strong> and, indirectly, how it managed to get that big.

For now, one thing is certain: “Googling” isn’t fading away anytime soon. But its grip on the internet? <strong>That’s about to face its toughest test yet.</strong>

# Talking to the Internet
Date: 2024-11-03 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/talking-to-the-internet
Cite as: Talking to the Internet by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2024-11-03. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/talking-to-the-internet (CC BY 4.0)

Halloween this year, **OpenAI played a trick.**

No flashy new model, no major tools or apps. Instead, they slipped in a small but seismic shift: ***SearchGPT***, [an internet browsing feature in ChatGPT.](https://openai.com/index/searchgpt-prototype/)

Sure, they had something similar before, but let’s face it—**it was clunky, often unreliable, and sources were murky at best.**

Now? It's something else. Smooth and seamless, like this:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fYN7!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F50821141-e7ec-40de-b5f4-d05c2b247f29_600x338.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fYN7!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F50821141-e7ec-40de-b5f4-d05c2b247f29_600x338.gif)

It’s easy to dismiss as OpenAI just catching up to Google’s Gemini or Perplexity. **But there’s something deeper here.**

This isn’t just an upgrade; **it’s a marker of where AI and search are heading.**

AI-driven search isn’t a *nice-to-have* feature.

**It's an epistemological change.**

And it's not a stretch. Just take a look down here:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!n5G5!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F486bb2ff-8965-4e94-b395-1a7df5b34fbe_1808x1002.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!n5G5!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F486bb2ff-8965-4e94-b395-1a7df5b34fbe_1808x1002.png)

Searching the Internet like this is just **easier, smoother, and quicker.**

The old dance was simple: search, click, read, repeat. **Now we cut right to the answer.** No more scanning lists of links or opening a dozen tabs.

**Now, we ask; it answers.**

But there's more to it. **Instead of hyperlinks, we’re served sentences.** Instead of fragmented pages, we get a full conversation.

And instead of keywords, we use questions, **as if we’re** ***talking*** **to the web.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Everything is getting more and more conversational.**

Until now, we stretched our language to adapt to machines—those stripped-down, choppy search terms we fed Google. But now, **the flow is reversed.**

**The language of AI search is becoming our natural language.** We’re seeing the first glimmers of a future we’ve only dreamed about: ***talking*** **to the Internet, like we might talk to a friend.**

It’s a leap toward something that could be **AI’s killer feature**, something actually *useful*—not just another machine churning out empty paragraphs for LinkedIn posts.

*But here’s the thing:* even if the pieces are falling into place, **we’re still a long way from the future of search we imagine.** The potential is huge, but there’s work to be done to make it a reality.

Why that is—and what might be required to steer the future of search—are the questions this edition of *Artifacts* aims to answer.

> ### The Story

**People are not using AI for Search.** Data are clear:

[![Immagine](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!329f!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F28543eef-de45-45dd-9b25-872bc9a04cac_2012x1414.jpeg "Immagine")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!329f!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F28543eef-de45-45dd-9b25-872bc9a04cac_2012x1414.jpeg)

**Critical masses are still anchored to Google**, and unseating a habit that ingrained won’t happen overnight.

This is why it matters when big players like ChatGPT enter the scene, bolstering the ranks of AI search challengers.

Even so, **it’s just a drop in the ocean**.

**As with any technology, adoption is key.** But widespread adoption is a steep hill to climb.

[![https://x.com/joshm/status/1852064574607880253](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!udWf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6e1517b-a3e8-4eb3-a2d1-97eb71fc2de9_1191x933.png "https://x.com/joshm/status/1852064574607880253")](https://x.com/joshm/status/1852064574607880253)

Arc and Perplexity’s CEOs know this story of adoption well

*Bottom line?* **As long as Google remains the default on most browsers, it will continue to wall off the search market from outside innovation.**

Or, at least, this would be the case as long as they don’t decide to go full steam on AI Search (as they're trying to do with AI Overviews) and being those ushering in the revolution.

But here’s the kicker: **for the time being, other contenders—OpenAI, Perplexity, and the like—aren’t making it to users’ devices**, and the reasons aren’t exactly fair.

(And that's why they are pushing own plug-ins and calling for for a new era.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The reality is, piecemeal solutions won’t be enough. **Structural remedies are needed to give AI search a real shot.**

Enter competition policy—the **Digital Markets Act in the EU**, for instance, aims to make search engine choice more transparent to citizens, though writing the rule is far easier than enforcing it.

Or consider the **Google antitrust case in the U.S.**, where the potential breakup of services could crack open the walls around search.

These structural moves, intended to curb Google’s dominance, might, ironically and unexpectedly, **create room for AI search to gain traction with the general public.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

But here’s a caution: **adoption is only part of the puzzle.**

Underlying this shift are **economic incentives and dynamics** that are causing headaches for everyone involved.

In a snippet: **AI Search could upend the economic model of online search.**

If AI tools like Perplexity and ChatGPT answer questions directly, users won’t visit websites as they used to, **disrupting the entire advertising-based ecosystem that search engines and content creators rely on.**

The equation is simple: **if users stop visiting websites, ad revenues plummet.** Google and other ad players lose a primary revenue stream, and media outlets—already under pressure—face further erosion of their advertising income.

So, what? **The advertising model may soon be outdated and a new one is yet to come.**

**The tension is especially fraught for media.** Many are wary of having their content scraped and repurposed without compensation, especially as AI models depend heavily on existing online material.

Some publishers are striking deals with AI providers, agreeing to license their content in exchange for a cut of the benefits. Others, like the *New York Times*, are taking a harder line, suing providers for “stealing” content.

But here’s the irony: media do not just need to defend from a "steal" but **they may hold the stronger hand.**

AI providers depend on high-quality content to generate useful responses. Without access to reputable sources, AI search tools are just glorified aggregators.

**That’s why media outlets have leverage to negotiate—AI providers desperately** ***need*** **their content.**

Yet, what these agreements may entail and the shape they'll take is still unclear.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NVae!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4f44359c-35ea-4960-98f7-fb6191cda01a_1024x1024.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NVae!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4f44359c-35ea-4960-98f7-fb6191cda01a_1024x1024.webp)

Finally, the rise of AI search **is a foundational change in both knowledge and business.**

There are still many moving parts, **and it will take time for them to settle.**

But as the landscape of search, knowledge, and business continues to shift, **it’s a puzzle worth watching**—and worth searching for solutions to solve.

# As we speak
Date: 2024-10-08 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/as-we-speak
Cite as: As we speak by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2024-10-08. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/as-we-speak (CC BY 4.0)

<strong><a href="https://artifactstech-substack-com.translate.goog/p/as-we-speak?_x_tr_sl=auto&amp;_x_tr_tl=it&amp;_x_tr_hl=en-US&amp;_x_tr_pto=wapp&amp;_x_tr_hist=true">\[To read this in 🇮🇹\]</a></strong>

Take a minute (or two, or however long you want) to listen in—<strong>just click below</strong> or <strong><a href="https://notebooklm.google.com/notebook/c8b3bda2-b156-4405-8fc4-4ee28d551ae8/audio">here</a></strong>. (I swear the newsletter will be shorter)

0:00-12:54

<a href="https://artifactstech.substack.com/api/v1/audio/upload/91a9f5d2-cb84-4284-afc3-aabed39981c9/src">\[Embedded media — view original\]</a>

It’s just a lady and a gentleman chatting about EU politics and party manifestos. <strong>They’re also big fan of Artifacts - lovely!</strong>

Except, here’s the kicker: <strong>these two don’t exist.</strong> The entire podcast? Completely AI-generated. <strong>And it took me less than three minutes to make it, for free.</strong>

All I did was drag and drop a <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/posts/lorenzo-ancona-1b02b31a7_not-the-platforms-you-were-thinking-about-activity-7203289310840655872-_2kQ?utm_source=share&amp;utm_medium=member_desktop">guide I wrote about the upcoming EU elections</a>, and <strong>voilà—the AI did the rest.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oUBu!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F284926f6-5bf3-4643-934b-77ade2e2881e_600x361.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oUBu!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F284926f6-5bf3-4643-934b-77ade2e2881e_600x361.gif" alt=""></a>

As simple as that

Now, what you hear are <strong>two eerily smooth voices having a conversation.</strong> They <em>sound</em> human, even throwing in a few attitude shifts depending on the topic.

As someone who actually <em>wrote</em> the guide, I can confirm they’re hitting all the right points. Sure, <strong>they get a bit superficial at times and lean a little too heavily on certain sections</strong>, but still—it’s shockingly accurate.

Yet, what strikes me is that this AI made my dry-as-dust EU election guide sound almost… <strong>fun.</strong>

And it didn’t require a single line of code, no complicated instructions, no need for tech or AI expertise. <strong>Just drop your content in, and</strong> <em><strong>bam</strong></em><strong>, you’ve got a podcast.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is <strong>Google’s NotebookLM</strong>, the latest shiny AI toy from Big G to engage with any type of content and, as they claim, <em><strong>“go from information to insights”.</strong></em>

You upload your material, and it’ll spit out summaries, key points, outlines—<strong>basically anything that would’ve taken a student or intern hours.</strong>

<a href="https://notebooklm.google.com/">Give it a whirl.</a>

I remember the first time I used ChatGPT—that “wow” moment when I realized, okay, this is something. I’ve had similar moments with other AI tools over the years, and <strong>NotebookLM gave me that same feeling.</strong>

But here’s the thing: this isn’t just a “wow” moment. <strong>It’s a chance to take a step back</strong> and think about Gen AI and the hype, AI-generated content, and what it means for the future of information. And who (or what) is actually intelligent in all this?

That’s Artifacts for today—just a bit more aware that my future competition might be synthetic :)

> ### The Story

<strong>To make matters more ironic</strong>, the elections guide I uploaded was also partially AI-generated (or at least co-created) with Claude, <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/posts/lorenzo-ancona-1b02b31a7_not-the-platforms-you-were-thinking-about-activity-7203289310840655872-_2kQ?utm_source=share&amp;utm_medium=member_desktop">as I mentioned back in June.</a>

So, one AI helped draft the report, and another turned it into a podcast.

<strong>Does this mean machines are getting smarter?</strong> Well, not exactly.

One key takeaway here is that <strong>there’s no real intelligence at play.</strong> Rather, intelligence is in what we perceive and in our understanding, but not in the machines.

<strong>Let me break it down.</strong> Tools like ChatGPT, NotebookLM, and others don’t possess intelligence in the traditional sense. They rely on statistics and computation to process input and produce output.

<strong>But they don’t</strong> <em><strong>understand</strong></em> <strong>the content and what they’re processing, nor do they attach any meaning or emotion to it.</strong>

<a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4358789">As Floridi brilliantly puts it</a>, <strong>AI is “</strong><em><strong>agency without intelligence”.</strong></em> In other terms, it’s something performing actions that would require intelligence (doing a podcast) without any actual intelligence to do so.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<em>So, where is the intelligence?</em> <strong>It’s in our perception of the text, audio, or images produced as the final output.</strong> We associate intelligence with this because, traditionally, these kinds of outcomes have required human intellect. <strong>But that’s not what’s happening in the process itself.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WxjL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F96142294-9bd1-46b1-a706-953006151e07_360x360.gif"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WxjL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F96142294-9bd1-46b1-a706-953006151e07_360x360.gif" alt=""></a>

Now, someone might ask, <em><strong>“So what? Isn’t the output what really matters?”</strong></em> Well, that’s debatable. Think of any work of art or human creation—<strong>we value not just the finished piece</strong>, but also the process, the intention, the creativity behind it.

<strong>The painter at work is just as important as the final painting.</strong>

This isn’t to dismiss AI, which clearly generates impressive outputs. But it’s key to remember that <em><strong><a href="https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/5338/Artificial-CommunicationHow-Algorithms-Produce">“What algorithms \[and AI\] are reproducing is not the intelligence of people but the informativity of communication.”</a></strong></em>

Again, AI excels at creating content bearing information value, like the podcast you heard. <strong>But it’s an artificial form of</strong> <em><strong>communication</strong></em> <strong>rather than</strong> <em><strong>intelligence.</strong></em>

We need to be mindful of this distinction so we don’t overstate what these tools are really doing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Still, even though the processes lack intelligence, the results are increasingly indistinguishable from what humans can produce. <strong>And that’s something we have to sit with.</strong>

This shift, in my view, has two major implications:

1.  <strong>Mediocrity is at stake.</strong> AI-generated content can match the quality of low to mid-tier content, and it’s faster and cheaper to produce. But if mediocrity becomes unacceptable, how will one push the boundaries to grow toward excellence? It’s an open question.

2.  <strong>We’re facing a flood of content.</strong> Social media already boosted content creation and sharing. GenAI is about to supercharge that—making it easier, quicker, and more accessible for anyone to generate and share on-demand content.

This will create a <strong>synthetic internet</strong>, where more and more content is machine-generated, <strong>yet strikingly similar to what humans used to make.</strong>

As discouraging or even threatening as this might seem to those passionate about content creation, <strong>I still believe that human processes—intelligence, passion, and creativity—will remain valuable.</strong>

Even if, at first glance, mediocre content from a human and a machine will look almost indistinguishable. <strong>And this is already playing out, as we speak.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fARI!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b3a429d-8797-4586-b4c6-aeaea6a2c7b2_2160x2160.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fARI!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b3a429d-8797-4586-b4c6-aeaea6a2c7b2_2160x2160.png" alt=""></a>

# Who made the iPhone boring ?
Date: 2024-09-24 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/who-made-the-iphone-boring
Cite as: Who made the iPhone boring ? by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2024-09-24. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/who-made-the-iphone-boring (CC BY 4.0)

Last Friday, as I’ve done for years now, I found myself in the ritual of standing in line (not more than 10 mins) to see <strong>the new iPhone.</strong>

We’ve all heard the familiar refrain: <strong>Apple’s just recycling the same old stuff.</strong> And sure, there’s some truth to that. <a href="https://disconnect.blog/smartphone-innovation-is-dead-and-thats-fine/">Innovation in phones has hit a plateau,</a> which makes sense—<strong>it can’t always be fireworks.</strong>

Yet, when I finally got my hands on the new iPhone, <strong>I couldn’t shake the feeling that this one took an even smaller leap than usual.</strong> More like a skip, really.

<em>Why?</em> There’s a meme floating around online that cuts to the heart of it:

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c3_r!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb1c4e731-3650-4103-9166-823e0f3719b6_800x673.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c3_r!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb1c4e731-3650-4103-9166-823e0f3719b6_800x673.jpeg" alt="Image preview" title="Image preview"></a>

<strong>Apple’s will not roll out its AI</strong>—its so-called “Apple Intelligence” and not “Artificial”(!)—<strong>in the EU.</strong> The same AI supposed to be the big thing this year, <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PugKQZHPut8">with some nice features</a> soon to be released worldwide.

It won’t be in the EU not because Brussels banned it someway, but <strong>due to Apple’s “regulatory concerns” tied to the Digital Markets Act (DMA)</strong>, the EU’s grand effort to make digital markets more open and competitive.

<em>In plainer terms?</em> <strong>Apple’s being vague, to say the least</strong>. They’ve said that the <em>“the interoperability requirements of the DMA could force us to compromise the integrity of our products in ways that <strong>risk user privacy and data security.”</strong></em> But they haven’t offered any concrete examples to back that up.

Artifacts managed to talk to a senior Apple employee, though the details were thin. The hint? <strong>The company might run into trouble because, right now, the list of external AI providers is short (basically just OpenAI), and it’s unclear if that will change anytime soon.</strong>

Therefore, as iPhone users won’t have much control over what AI providers to use, <strong>Apple would be stifling competition and users’ choice.</strong>

<strong>More precisely, there would be a problem also for interoperability</strong>—one of the DMA’s key goals aimed at breaking down the walls between online services.

Think of being able to message from WhatsApp to Telegram, for example. That’s the DMA in action.

<strong>So yes, the iPhone feels like more of the same.</strong> But the real story is bigger than just Apple.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6Ssd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe2094bee-310a-49ee-b41d-d4e7975da75f_1024x1024.webp"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6Ssd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe2094bee-310a-49ee-b41d-d4e7975da75f_1024x1024.webp" alt=""></a>

It is said that the DMA wants to break open gatekeepers.

For once, we can confidently say, <em><strong>“The EU lacks innovation because of regulation”</strong></em>—<em>but not in the usual sense</em>. It’s not that we’re failing to create or develop technology; <strong>it’s that we’re simply not</strong> <em><strong>receiving</strong></em> <strong>it.</strong>

One may even question <strong>whether we actually</strong> <em><strong>want</strong></em> <strong>this kind of innovation.</strong> It’s fair to assume regulations exist to protect us from things we don’t want. And that, therefore, maybe we’re fine without it.

<strong>Still, this is part of a larger trend:</strong> tech companies are starting to withhold features or services from Europe. This also raises eyebrows about consumer protection as well as questions the strength of the so-called “Brussels Effect”, the EU’s ability to set global standards.

Fewer answers, more thoughts, and plenty to chew on in today’s Artifacts.

> ### The Story

<strong>The clash over Apple’s closed systems has been a recurring theme in its history.</strong> Even the two co-founders & Steves—Jobs and Wozniak—argued about it, with Jobs ultimately winning out.

Steve Jobs made it clear he preferred closed systems, not to chase profit, but because <em><strong>“we want to make great products, not crap like Android.”</strong></em> He believed in tightly controlling hardware and software to <em>“create a seamless and unique user experience”</em>

<strong>If you’ve ever tried using AirDrop, you’ve likely noticed this</strong>—especially when your Android-using friend gets left out.

Yet, if you use AirDrop, you can see that <strong>there’s an economic upside too.</strong>  Apple’s closed ecosystem encourages users to stay locked in, buying more and only Apple devices.

<strong>And that’s exactly what the EU’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) aims to challenge</strong>—making sure Android and Apple users aren’t cut off from each other’s ecosystems.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We saw this play out last year <strong>when Apple switched to a USB-C charger from lightning worldwide</strong>, thanks to an EU directive.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jQrv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe73d4ca8-e533-4730-98c4-e2c838dcd05a_800x800.jpeg"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jQrv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe73d4ca8-e533-4730-98c4-e2c838dcd05a_800x800.jpeg" alt=""></a>

One of the few times the EU got right the comms :)

<strong>The tech world hailed it as a win for the “Brussels Effect”</strong>—an EU rule causing global change, with Apple quietly adapting across the board.

The assumption (never confirmed, tough) was that <strong>Apple found it easier and cheaper to make one version of the iPhone for everyone.</strong>

<strong>Yet, the Brussels Effect seems not to hold here with AI.</strong> While hardware is hard to customise regionally, software - and therefore AI - is flexible.

This is a new, interesting, turn: this time, Apple is rolling out two different versions of its operating system. <strong>The same iPhone will have different features depending on where it’s sold and used.</strong>

<strong>This shift suggests not only that the Brussels Effect has less sway over software but also that Apple isn’t backing down.</strong> We saw something similar with Meta, which chose <a href="https://www.theverge.com/2024/7/18/24201041/meta-multimodal-llama-ai-model-launch-eu-regulations">not to release its latest AI model and features in Europe</a>, citing regulatory concerns.

The walls are still up—<strong>for now.</strong>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<strong>The DMA is proving to be a tough challenge for Apple, which is <a href="https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_24_4761">now under scrutiny</a></strong> for blocking developers from informing users about cheaper options outside the App Store, making it difficult to install alternative app stores, and limiting integration with non-Apple devices.

This is, in many ways, <strong>the natural consequence of a regulation like the DMA.</strong> It’s trying to reshape how tech companies operate, pushing them to rethink their systems and make substantial changes.

As expected, <strong>this has led to friction,</strong> with Apple either finding clever (sometimes sneaky) ways to comply or holding back features—like its AI—altogether to avoid scrutiny.

<strong>In the end, it’s the users who feel the impact</strong>. We could either enjoy a more flexible and funnier iPhone <a href="https://www.theverge.com/2024/8/24/24226946/iphone-eu-regulation-app-stores-fortnite">(as The Verge claimed)</a> with greater choice, thanks to the DMA, or end up with a less exciting device because of the very same regulation.

For now, this is where things stand. Apple says it’s working on bringing its latest innovations to Europe, <strong>so we’ll see if the European iPhone actually gets better.</strong>

# Artifacts, once again
Date: 2024-09-10 | Language: en
Canonical: https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/artifacts-once-again
Cite as: Artifacts, once again by Lorenzo Ancona, Artifacts, 2024-09-10. https://artifactstech.substack.com/p/artifacts-once-again (CC BY 4.0)

<a href="https://artifactstech-substack-com.translate.goog/p/artifacts-once-again?_x_tr_sl=en&amp;_x_tr_tl=it&amp;_x_tr_hl=it&amp;_x_tr_pto=wapp&amp;_x_tr_hist=true">\[For my Italian friends\]</a>

I have to admit, <strong>this might be one of the toughest Artifacts I’ve ever written.</strong>

Not because we’re making a leap from Dante’s language to Shakespeare’s.

It’s more about the challenge of speaking to both longtime subscribers, who know Artifacts inside out, and those of you who are just stepping aboard <em><strong>(welcome, by the way).</strong></em>

Now, <strong>I don’t want to rehash what this newsletter is about</strong>—that would be mind-numbing. But at the same time, I can’t skip over the basics of what I’m doing here, why it matters, and who it’s for.

After mulling this over for hours, <strong>I came to a question</strong> I first needed to answer for myself:

<em><strong>Why is reflecting, writing, and discussing technological artifacts not just idle speculation, but something urgent today?</strong></em>

In other words, <em><strong>why should anyone subscribe to and read this newsletter?</strong></em>

<strong>The answer are two simple lines,</strong> that I try to unfold below.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hbDF!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa6c1e654-a91d-4147-b45b-ceea038b103a_3200x2160.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hbDF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa6c1e654-a91d-4147-b45b-ceea038b103a_3200x2160.png" alt=""></a>

Keep reading to fill this in

<em>Your <strong>comments, thoughts, and critiques</strong> aren’t just appreciated—they’re what will make this newsletter even more valuable.</em>

<em>And if you’re ready to trust Artifacts, <strong>just hit the button below :)</strong></em>

> ### The Answer

<strong>With the term “artifacts”,</strong> I’m casting a wide net: it covers everything from physical devices (like the latest iPhone) to AI tools, online platforms, websites, digital services, self-driving cars—you name it.

In short, <strong>anything born of technical expertise</strong>, often connected to the internet, and helping define <strong>what we now think of as our digital society and life.</strong>

But more importantly, <strong>these artifacts are the tools that—whether we realise it or not—shape our daily existence.</strong> They mediate our interactions and have woven themselves so deeply into our lives that they’re almost invisible or granted (think of your phone).

As straightforward as it may seem, <strong>we can’t afford to be passive about these artifacts or assume they just</strong> <em><strong>happen</strong></em> <strong>to us by chance.</strong>

If a technology produces a certain effect, <strong>it’s because someone designed (or misdesigned) it to do just that.</strong> Again, we can’t ignore that.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Since the days when Homo habilis crafted the first tools—probably weapons for hunting—<strong>artifacts have embodied specific beliefs, intentions, and a clear view of the world.</strong>

Creating technology isn’t just some side note in human history—<strong>it’s what has, in many ways, made us more human.</strong> <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2023/01/chatgpt-ai-technology-techo-humanism-reid-hoffman/672872/">Reid Hoffman would likely back me up on that.</a>

<strong>But with that power comes responsibility.</strong> As Winston Churchill sharply put it, <em><strong>“We shape our buildings, and thereafter they shape us.”</strong></em> He was talking about palaces, but those are just another form of technology—another artifact.

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7U9u!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F12029695-5e5c-49d8-a44e-17d50d9b7675_629x620.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7U9u!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F12029695-5e5c-49d8-a44e-17d50d9b7675_629x620.png" alt=""></a>

A building, drawn by <a href="https://huggingface.co/spaces/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-schnell">Flux</a>

The bottom line to this? <strong>We ought to think through how technologies are built to understand why and how they mediate and shape our lives in a certain direction.</strong> But also to react and give technologies the shape we aim for.

That’s why it’s crucial to push back on the tired claim that <em>“technology is neutral—it’s all about how you use it.”</em>

<strong>No, that’s completely misguided!</strong> And our two lines unfold right from here.

> #### Two lines

<strong>The design of any technological artifact is infused with values and political structures long before it even reaches the user.</strong> This is what <a href="https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf">Langdon</a> <strong><a href="https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf">Winner</a></strong>, the godfather of this newsletter, argued when he examined the low-hanging bridges in Long Island <strong>designed to keep Black people from reaching the beach.</strong>

Luciano <strong>Floridi</strong> echoes this, claiming <strong><a href="https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13347-023-00661-4">there’s no such thing as neutral technology.</a></strong> The construction phase—the very <em>design</em> of any artifact—is shaped by various forces, <strong>and it’s on those designing to ensure the right values win out.</strong>

In that sense, <strong>design is a moral act</strong>, placing significant responsibility on us when we build and deliver something new.

<strong>Safety, ethics, and considerations like these can’t be an afterthought.</strong> They need to be woven into the design process from the beginning. In other words, <strong>they must be considered</strong> <em><strong>by design</strong></em> <strong>throughout the design phase.</strong>

<strong>And that’s the first line Artifacts walks —</strong> moving from technology to us, politics, and society.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

But, of course, this isn’t always possible. Some technologies are already out in the world, and we can’t just send them back to the factory or rebuild them from scratch. <strong>This is exactly where politics, policies, and regulations come into play.</strong>

Not as roadblocks to innovation, as many claim. Rather, <strong>they serve to guide technology toward what we collectively define as good.</strong>

A prime example of this is the <strong>European Union’s Digital Markets Ac</strong>t, which compels online services to revisit their interfaces—essentially requiring a redesign to address what went wrong the first time.

Now, let’s be clear: <strong>I’m not suggesting tech policies and regulations are just second-chance efforts.</strong> While they may have functioned that way in the past, well-crafted rules can do more than clean up the mess—<strong>they can shape how future technologies are built from the outset.</strong> The AI Act might be a proving ground for this, but we’ll have to wait and see.

<strong>And that’s the second, other line of Artifacts</strong>—this time, moving from politics to technology<strong>.</strong>

<a href="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!r98B!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a389166-4312-4a81-b74d-0b5cc9f39459_3200x2160.png"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!r98B!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a389166-4312-4a81-b74d-0b5cc9f39459_3200x2160.png" alt=""></a>

Promise kept

In the end, <strong>it often comes down to design, whether we’re talking about the artifacts themselves or the regulations governing them.</strong> And I find it fascinating that the same word—<em>design</em>—can stretch to cover both.

> #### So, what?

I’ve probably said enough by now. <strong>Hopefully, it’s clear why talking about artifacts isn’t just some niche obsession for tech nerds</strong>—it’s an urgent priority for us all.

We’ll be diving deep into artifacts here in <em>Artifacts</em>. <strong>This will be a space, a playground, to bring together facts, ideas, and reflections on how these technologies have been, and continue to be, shaping us.</strong>

And just as importantly, <strong>we’ll explore how politics and institutions are grappling with the meaning of technology.</strong>

We’ll do this <strong>every other Tuesday.</strong> Most of the time, I’ll be sharing my thoughts, <strong>but we’ll also bring in technologists, policy experts, and other curious minds to join the conversation.</strong>

<strong>Each edition of</strong> <em><strong>Artifacts</strong></em> <strong>will follow the format you see here:</strong> a deep dive into a key topic, food for thought from different sources, a book recommendation, a quote from someone sharper than me, and a tool I’d suggest you try.

It’ll be a journey we take together, and <strong>I’m excited to kick it off, once again.</strong>

<em>Thank you to everyone who’s joining us for the first time today, and to those who’ve been here from the beginning for your continued support.</em>

> ### Someone said this before

> ### Nerding
